issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Extend the DRA plugin (and other in-tree plugins) to have a notion of in-memory resource reservations, so that the kube-scheduler could perform quick in-memory rescheduling without causing any physical allocation. In turn, the scheduler should be able to requesting resource allocation in the binding phase.

### Why is this needed?

A recent DRA enhancement proposals introduces intra-node dependencies (see [KEP-4815 DRA Partitionable devices support for multi-host](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5069)), which in fact introduce an implicit topology that scheduler needs to be aware of while taking scheduling decisions.

It's unfortunately not possible to do it right without a notion of group scheduling, so that scheduler could quickly reconsider initial pods placements to either avoid running into dead-end paths ([scheduling on one node, restricts possible placements for other pods](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-scheduling/4815-dra-partitionable-devices#multi-host-scheduling-limitations)) or to try a better placement before taking the binding decision.

Currently DRA plugin does not have a notion of in-memory reservations (like assumed pods) without triggering resource allocation. Currently dynamic allocation is triggered at the Reserve extension point, but gang-scheduling gate that is later at the Permit extension point. In case a subset or the whole group of pods is rejected at Permit, resources may be already in the process of their allocation (binding).

Recent enhancements makes things even worse as they leaves a possibility of resource allocation to a secondary scheduling cycle after the binding decision was taken (see a discussion in [KEP-5007: DRA Device Binding Conditions](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5012#discussion_r1951772957)). Scheduler should enforce in-tree plugins to adhere to the scheduling principles.
issues.title: Extend the DRA plugin with ability to reserve resources (without their allocation) before the binding phase

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

In #119987 and #121954, the scheduling framework introduced `NodeInfo` as a parameter in the `RunPreScorePlugins` and `RunScorePlugins` functions of the `PluginsRunner` interface. Thank @Huang-Wei and @AxeZhan for these improvements that have made the framework easier to use. However, `NodeInfo` is still not exposed to the functions of the `ScorePlugin` and `PreFilterPlugin` interfaces (see [relevant code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.32/pkg/scheduler/framework/interface.go#L929)), which remains inconvenient for plugin users like [Koordinator](https://github.com/koordinator-sh/koordinator).

For instance, Koordinator aims to support [directive preemption](https://github.com/koordinator-sh/koordinator/blob/main/docs/proposals/scheduling/20220609-resource-reservation.md). To achieve this, it has had to propose [specific extensions](https://github.com/koordinator-sh/koordinator/blob/main/docs/proposals/scheduling/20220513-enhanced-scheduler-extension.md) to construct `NodeInfo` with reserved resources during the scheduling cycle.

Currently, while the `RunScorePlugins` function of the `PluginsRunner` interface accepts `NodeInfo` as a parameter, it does not pass it directly to the individual `Score` plugins. The relevant interface definitions are as follows:

```golang
type ScorePlugin interface {
	Plugin
	Score(ctx context.Context, state *CycleState, p *v1.Pod, nodeName string) (int64, *Status)
	ScoreExtensions() ScoreExtensions
}

type PreFilterPlugin interface {
	Plugin
	PreFilter(ctx context.Context, state *CycleState, p *v1.Pod) (*PreFilterResult, *Status)
	PreFilterExtensions() PreFilterExtensions
}

type PluginsRunner interface {
	RunPreScorePlugins(context.Context, *CycleState, *v1.Pod, []*NodeInfo) *Status
	RunScorePlugins(context.Context, *CycleState, *v1.Pod, []*NodeInfo) ([]NodePluginScores, *Status)
	RunFilterPlugins(context.Context, *CycleState, *v1.Pod, *NodeInfo) *Status
	RunPreFilterExtensionAddPod(ctx context.Context, state *CycleState, podToSchedule *v1.Pod, podInfoToAdd *PodInfo, nodeInfo *NodeInfo) *Status
	RunPreFilterExtensionRemovePod(ctx context.Context, state *CycleState, podToSchedule *v1.Pod, podInfoToRemove *PodInfo, nodeInfo *NodeInfo) *Status
}
```

We propose exposing `NodeInfo` in the `ScorePlugin` and `PreFilterPlugin` interfaces to allow plugin developers to access and utilize node information more conveniently. This would greatly enhance the flexibility and functionality of plugin development.

The interface can be updated as follows:

```golang
type ScorePlugin interface {
	Plugin
	Score(ctx context.Context, state *CycleState, p *v1.Pod, node *NodeInfo) (int64, *Status)
	ScoreExtensions() ScoreExtensions
}

type PreFilterPlugin interface {
	Plugin
	PreFilter(ctx context.Context, state *CycleState, p *v1.Pod, nodes []*NodeInfo) (*PreFilterResult, *Status)
	PreFilterExtensions() PreFilterExtensions
}
```

### Why is this needed?

Just like PR #119987 mentioned:

> - consistent function signature - all use NodeInfo
> - unleash more potential to use scheduler framework natively w/o hacks

We aim to align with and enhance the upstream framework for the following reasons, and we believe this change will benefit both the Kubernetes community and third-party plugin developers:

1. **Consistency**: Ensure that all plugins, including `ScorePlugin` and `PreFilterPlugin`, use a consistent `NodeInfo` parameter to simplify plugin development and reduce errors from mismatched data structures.

2. **Enhanced Flexibility**: Exposing `NodeInfo` directly allows plugin developers to implement advanced scheduling logic without workarounds, promoting cleaner and more maintainable code.

3. **Eliminate Workarounds**: Projects like [Koordinator](https://github.com/koordinator-sh/koordinator) currently need custom extensions to construct `NodeInfo` with reserved resources. Direct exposure of the `NodeInfo` would eliminate these workarounds.

4. **Future-Proofing**: Aligning with the upstream framework ensures easier adoption of future Kubernetes scheduler enhancements.

Looking forward to your feedback and support!
issues.title: Sched Framework: Request to expose NodeInfo to PreFilter plugins and Score plugins

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Improve the error reporting for Declarative Validation when validating lists that use listType=map semantics. Currently, validation errors when using listType=map (see: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130349) report the list index of the problematic element when it could instead show the key for the field.

### Why is this needed?

Declarative Validation uses list indices in its error messages (e.g., spec.conditions[2]: Invalid value). For cases such as listType=map this can make it difficult for users to correlate errors with their configuration, as mapping the index to field might be difficult for a user to derive.

A potentially more user-friendly error message would be to reference the key of the list item, rather than its index. For example, instead of:
```
spec.conditions[2].status: Invalid value: "Foo": must be "Bar"
```

the error message might look like:
```
spec.conditions[name=Ready].status: Invalid value: "Foo": must be "Bar"
```

This would allow a user to more directly locate the problematic item in their configuration. 

This issue originated from a discussion in PR #130349, which introduces the Declarative Validation feature:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130349#discussion_r1968068374
issues.title: [Declarative Validation] Improve Error Reporting for listType=map

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

We need to decide on a consistent policy for how code generators in `kubernetes/kubernetes` (specifically `validation-gen`, but this likely applies more broadly) handle unrecognized `+k8s:` prefixed tags in comments.  Currently, `validation-gen` silently ignores unknown tags.  We need to decide whether to:

1.  **Ignore unknown `+k8s:` tags:**  (Current behavior) This allows older generators to process code that includes newer tags they don't understand, maintaining backwards compatibility.  The downside is that typos in tag names will go undetected.

2.  **Warn on unknown `+k8s:` tags:** This would provide a middle ground, alerting users to potential typos or misconfigurations without breaking existing workflows.  The downside is that users might ignore warnings.

3.  **Fail (error) on unknown `+k8s:` tags:** This would prevent typos and ensure that all tags are explicitly understood by the generator. The downside is that it breaks backwards compatibility: older generators would fail when processing newer code, even if the newer tags are irrelevant to that generator.

This decision impacts `validation-gen` directly but probably should be a consistent policy across all code generators.


### Why is this needed?



This issue was raised during review of PR #130349, which introduces the `validation-gen` code generator. See this comment thread:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130349#discussion_r1970588825 

The main trade-off is between:

*   **Strictness/Correctness:**  Failing on unknown tags prevents typos and ensures that all declared behavior is understood.
*   **Backwards Compatibility/Flexibility:**  Ignoring unknown tags allows older generators to process newer code without modification.

Without a consistent policy, we risk introducing subtle bugs or unexpected behavior due to misspelled or misunderstood tags.  A decision will inform how we handle tags going forward, and whether existing generators need to be updated. Also, the answer to this question will determine if a linter rule should be created to enforce this behaviour.

/sig api-machinery
issues.title: [Declarative Validation] Decide Policy on Unknown +k8s: Tags in Code Generators

### What would you like to be added?

We encountered an issue where one or two pods in our application lost network connectivity. While the exact root cause is unclear, we suspect it may be related to iptables. As a result, application requests intermittently fail whenever traffic is directed to the affected pod. The liveness and readiness probes do not fail because the kubelet can still reach the pod. This impacts all users relying on the application. Looking for a feature in Kubernetes to handle this failure mode.

To replicate this issue, I used a network policy that mimics the behavior. Apply a network policy to deny both ingress and egress traffic to one application pod using a label selector. Then, perform requests to the application service; you'll notice intermittent failures. The liveness and readiness probes will not fail because the network policy does not apply to the node or kubelet. How can we configure the application to be robust enough to handle this failure mode?

Feature to detect network failures that only impact pod-to-pod network failures that can detect above failure mode.
May be the ability for the service to do necessary health checks on the pods.

Throughout the code base, instead of just using the feature gates to check if a feature is enabled or not, there are several unconventional use of feature gates:

- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/df030f3851ac8c125fa50642b967a8399b935c2c/staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/logs/api/v1/kube_features.go#L64-L65 are used to promote new format options configurable. 
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/df030f3851ac8c125fa50642b967a8399b935c2c/pkg/features/kube_features.go#L98-L116 are used to allow for new options to fine-tune the cpumanager policies
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/df030f3851ac8c125fa50642b967a8399b935c2c/pkg/features/kube_features.go#L684-L700 are used to allow for new options to fine-tune the topology manager policies.

These feature gate do not progress in lifecycle, while the underlying available options progress over the stages. 
As it is right now, we would not be able to emulate these options in compatibility mode. For example, if a new option is moved from Beta to GA feature from 1.32 to 1.33, this option would be available as a GA option when we are emulating 1.32. 

Ideally, we would want these new options to be tracked by a dedicated feature gate for each option. 
If that's not feasible, we would need a mechanism to track when these options are moved from one stage to another. 
Otherwise, these options are not emulatible, and we will always have the options at the binary version, even when the emulation version is different.
issues.title: [CompatibilityVersion] Unconventional use of feature gates

#### Summary
If `MatchLabelKeys` of `PodSpec` contains duplicate keys, the validation should fail with an explicit error.

#### Details
If `MatchLabelKeys` of `PodSpec` contains duplicate keys, validation will fail as follows.

`sample-affinity.yaml`
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: sample-affinity
  labels:
    app: sample-affinity
spec:
  containers:
  - image: nginx
    name: nginx
  affinity:
    podAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
      - labelSelector: {}
        topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
        matchLabelKeys:
        - app
        - app
```
 
```console
$ kubectl apply -f sample-affinity.yaml
The Pod "sample-affinity" is invalid: spec.affinity.podAffinity.requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution[0].matchLabelKeys[1]: Invalid value: "app": exists in both matchLabelKeys and labelSelector
```

It is caused by duplication between `matchLabelKeys[1]` and the key added to the `labelSelector` corresponding to `matchLabelKeys[0]`, so strictly speaking, key duplication in `matchLabelKeys` is not validated.
I think it should be explicitly validated.

#### Special notes:
#130534, which adds `matchLabelKeys` validation for `PodTemplateSpec`, is in progress.
In the case of `PodTemplateSpec`, the duplication of keys in `matchLabelKeys` is explicitly validated because the key-values corresponding to `matchLabelKeys` will not be added to the `labelSelector`.
If #130534 is merged and this issue is not addressed, the error message will differ between `PodTemplateSpec` and `PodSpec`.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0ab306a08655c72fe26c01090a154264648fd2ba/pkg/apis/core/validation/validation.go#L8032-L8040


/kind feature 
/sig scheduling
issues.title: Duplicate keys in MatchLabelKeys of PodSpec should be explicitly validated

This is a feature suggestion for ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (VAP).  It may depend on other enhancements to workload types before it becomes tractable.

Writing a VAP that verifies all PodSpecs is difficult/impossible.  PodSpecs are embedded in multiple built-in types (Deployments, Jobs...) as well as CRDs.

Even writing a VAP to validate the containers in Pod requires writing validation code in triplicate to handle `containers`, `initContainers` and `ephemeralContainers`.

Writing a VAP against Pod and all the other built-in types that embed PodSpec is even more difficult and is at risk of not validating types that are introduced AFTER the VAP is authored.

If CRDs were to clearly identify where PodSpecs were embedded, and VAP had a way to match "all resources that embed PodSpec", this could become feasible.

This idea has come up multiple times and relates to topics such as CRX and "workload type embedding", so I'd like to open this tracker to allow for discussion.

/sig api-machinery

cc @cici37 @cheftako @thockin
issues.title: Validating Admission Policy: Uniform workload type policy enforcement

### What would you like to be added?

Currently, CEL expressions are validated only at runtime when a resource is submitted to the cluster. To address this, we propose expanding the existing[ kubectl-validate](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kubectl-validate) repository to provide a shift-left validation tool that allows users to test CEL expressions against incoming object files locally before deploying them.

https://docs.google.com/document/d/1QzEXIEdAjbPtaFnAtuHzot16Lp2X4vTpQ1AokfPFv1w/edit?tab=t.0

Kubernetes has increasingly leveraged Common Expression Language (CEL) to enhance policy enforcement and resource allocation. Features such as ValidatingAdmissionPolicy and Dynamic Resource Allocation rely on CEL to define the matching resources and how resources should be validated. However, one major challenge is the lack of a shift-left validation tool that enables developers and operators to test CEL expressions against real objects before deploying them to a cluster.

### What would you like to be added?

Raised at https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/129698#issuecomment-2614641760.

We should somehow tell end-users (i.e., not the cluster admin who has access to the scheduler logs) why pods are pending if `PreEnqueue` has been rejecting those pods.
That being said, we cannot simply make API calls for kube-apiserver within the scheduling queue because the queue is very performance sensitive.

### Why is this needed?

Currently, when PreEnqueue rejects pods, pods are just kept in the scheduling queue without any visible changes to pod objects. i.e., users cannot see why pods are pending at pod condition, status, events etc. The only way to figure out is to look at the scheduler's logs.

The scheduling gate feature is avoiding this problem at kube-apiserver; add a condition to pods if the scheduling gate is specified.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3f26d005571dc5903e7cebae33ada67986bc40f3/pkg/registry/core/pod/strategy.go#L821
We cannot do the same for any PreEnqueue plugins in general because kube-apiserver doesn't know which pods will be rejected by the scheduler's PreEnqueue plugins.

issues.body:
### What happened? ### Summary: The Kubernetes Controller Manager (KCM) Informer caches experiences read/write mutex contention at scale. KCM controllers frequently acquire a read lock on the Informer cache to list objects from the store, which can starve the CacheController's DeltaFIFO processing from acquiring a write lock to update the Store/Cache during high throughput. This contention can lead to a backlog in DeltaFIFO, delaying delta event processing and stale cache. ### Impact A high backlog in DeltaFIFO results in stale Informer cache data, affecting KCM controllers that rely on it for resource reconciliation. This can lead to incorrect decisions, such as unnecessary resource creation or unnecessary load to APIServer and etcd from KCM Controllers. More details of impact/analysis on Statefulset controller, DaemonSet Controller is provided later in the example section. ### Code Flow : 1. Cache controller [processLoop](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/controller.go#L205-L216) pops from DeltaFIFO queue to [processDeltas](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/controller.go#L552-L584). 2. As cache controller processes deltas, it [adds](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/controller.go#L571) or [updates](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/controller.go#L566) the store based on[ ADD/UPDATE etc events ](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/controller.go#L564) from DeltFIFO queue. 3. For Add/Update operations to store, it acquires lock [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/thread_safe_store.go#L236-L242) to update the store. 4. Meanwhile controller, in the process of [listing pods](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d386d6880e57556f7fe19e65e89f60501aa0aa25/pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set.go#L314) , it acquires read lock on store [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6549f52b97d4d0837d9d0c2c1758320b19b38472/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/thread_safe_store.go#L296-L310) while DeltaFIFO in the above is trying to update the store at the same time. I believe [Delete in Store](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6549f52b97d4d0837d9d0c2c1758320b19b38472/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/thread_safe_store.go#L244-L251) is also prone to this, this code path was not exercised in the test. ### Mutex pprof for KCM showing RW and Rlock on Cache/Store from CacheController Loop and StatetfulSet controller getPodsFromList ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d3dff4d4-0e1f-41bd-8c24-bd852c565917) #### Impact/Analysis examples : ##### 1. Statefulset Controller In statefulset controller case, if/when cache is stale and Pod phase status reflects[ nil](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set_utils.go#L470) in cache, even though kubelet has patched the pod to `Running` phase, Statefulset controller will keep trying to [create pods and get 409's - conflict as it exists in etcd ](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7b6c56e5fb530c80e3510977a752be5ce6e23a27/pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set_control.go#L397) as this [condition](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set_control.go#L388) will evaluate to true When I patched the KCM Statefulset controller, I can see that just `LISTING` pods from informer cache in statefulset controller when there are lots of pods in single namespace can take upto at peak `~980 ms `, which creates a huge backlog in DeltaFIFO during this time. In Statefulset controller, in the process of [listing pods](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d386d6880e57556f7fe19e65e89f60501aa0aa25/pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set.go#L314) , it acquires read lock on Store [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6549f52b97d4d0837d9d0c2c1758320b19b38472/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/thread_safe_store.go#L296-L310) while DeltaFIFO in the above is trying to update the Store at the same time ( will cover on this more below) ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8904f4cf-140b-4b17-b750-b8c04ea7d8f1) **Example of DeltaFIFO backlog** ``` 12 trace.go:236] Trace[410148869]: "DeltaFIFO Pop Process" ID:kube-system/kube-proxy-fv428,Depth:229809,Reason:slow event handlers blocking the queue ... (total time: 321ms): ``` ##### 2. DeamonSet Controller : In DS conttoller it does similar thing , [listing all pods from cache](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6d0ac8c561a7ac66c21e4ee7bd1976c2ecedbf32/pkg/controller/daemon/daemon_controller.go#L702) holding a read lock, which blocks all that time from updating the store in Process Deltas. Consequence of stale cache can make DS controller to create more DS pods for same node. ### What did you expect to happen? Ideally Controllers should be isolated from each other to avoid noisy neighbor problem, which isn't possible due to Controllers sharing Shared InformerCache. **Long Term**: Food for thought: - Introduce a dedicated Indexer/Cache solely for DeltaFIFO writes and syncing it in a separate routine to a separate Indexer/Store for controllers to read from can reduce lock contention from list from downstream controllers. - However, this means controllers will operate on slightly delayed data, which is much better than super stale data at scale, we need to ensure this copy is light weight unlike Huge lists that controllers do today which worsens the contention. This will help APIMachinery code has more control on these components performance instead of depending on implementations of downstream controllers. - Main thing about this theory is that - we need to ensure we are not shifting the problem to second cache to reduce overhead in first cache :) , we can something similar to what etcd does today, if difference between applies and commits b/w first cache and second cache is like say `X` , we will stop read lock to second cache from controller, to ensure second cache (i.e controller relies on) catches up to first cache, to guarantee controllers are not reading stale data - This comes with a con of increasing the memory overhead because its essentially storing a separate cache copy. This requires changing pieces of API Machinery architecture as it stands now. This approach might not only help KCM controllers but any controllers relying on caches built out of API Machinery code that runs on Dataplane Nodes. **At the minimum in short term**: - we should ensure all Controllers under KCM avoid heavy list operations on the Informer Cache/Store to reduce lock contention. - Build and utilize Indexers where applicable to minimize the number of items fetched, reducing read lock duration and improving cache update efficiency. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? - Create 200 Statefulsets of 1000 pods each at once. - Ensure all those pods are Schedulable to the nodes. ### Anything else we need to know? _No response_ ### Kubernetes version
```console $ kubectl version dev-dsk-hakuna-2c-2122d141 % kubectl version Client Version: v1.32.1 Kustomize Version: v5.5.0 Server Version: v1.32.2 ```
### Cloud provider
AWS
### OS version
```console # On Linux: $ cat /etc/os-release # paste output here $ uname -a # paste output here # On Windows: C:\> wmic os get Caption, Version, BuildNumber, OSArchitecture # paste output here ```
### Install tools
### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)
### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)

### What would you like to be added?

We have a `Service` resource using type `LoadBalancer` and `externalTrafficPolicy: Local`. We have set `allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false` because we do not rely upon node ports in our setup. However, there does not seem to be a way to disable the health check node port.

### Why is this needed?

Without the ability to disable the health check node port, we have to add network policy so that this port will not be exposed to the public internet. Since this port is not required in our setup at all, it would be great if we could just disable it instead of having closing the port with a network policy. We can close this port since we are using Calico's GlobalNetworkPolicies which we can apply to entire nodes. AFAIK the `networking.k8s.io/v1` NetworkPolicies offer no such feature and thus there is no built-in feature to disable/close the health check node port.

From @johnbelamaric https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130764/#discussion_r1993803425
```
For 1.34+: Theoretically, ResourceSlices are just, well, slices of a larger resource pool. Thus, the CapacityPools (and later the Mixins), could be considered unique across the resource pool rather than within the resource slice. If that's true, we could move to a place where we define capacitypools and mixins in one slice, and the devices in different slices. This would allow very large devices partitionable devices that share capacity pools and mixins (think: very large multi-host partitionable devices). Now, we don't do that today because this makes validation hard (impossible?) at admission time. But I want to at least introduce the idea that we might want to do it at some point. Further validate the incoming resources.
```

### What would you like to be added?

propagated from https://github.com/containerd/containerd/issues/10692

@ningmingxiao mentioned that containerd creates the logs but doesn't handle deleting them, that's done by kubelet if using K8s

-----------------

**What is the problem you're trying to solve**

We use daemons (fluent-bit, vector, etc) to suck up all of the logs for all pods that run on K8S nodes and send them to an aggregator (cloudwatch).

For short-lived pods that start and exit very quickly it turns out that the log files are deleted from disk before the daemon has a chance to read the log file.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

A configuration parameter in containerd to keep the log files around for an amount of time like 60s before they are deleted. This would allow me to configure the daemon to ensure it can find the files and read them before they are deleted.

**Additional context**

I'm generally running on AWS EKS, so I'd be looking at configuring containerd via cloud-init but that is already supported.

https://github.com/vectordotdev/vector/issues/20541

Is there a better way to do this than what I'm proposing? I believe containerd is managing the lifecycle of those logfiles, but maybe that isn't correct? If not, I'd appreciate being pointed in the right direction!

-------------------

if I'm correct, this would be done in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/logs/container_log_manager.go potentially...? 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/logs/container_log_manager.go#L202-L226 looks to handle cleaning up logs today, we'd just need a configurable delay mechanism in there?

_Note: ideally we wouldn't set this to a high value, to avoid consuming disk space for unnecessary amounts of time. if a hardcoded maximum value was to be configured for node resiliency reasons, that would be wise. maybe 90 seconds?_

### Why is this needed?

to avoid logs from short lived containers not being shipped off to centralised logging systems, due to the file being deleted before it can be read by the log shipping daemon

issues.body:
I propose introducing `topology.kubernetes.io/rack` as a standardized label key in Kubernetes. This label would complement the existing well-known topology labels (`topology.kubernetes.io/region`, `topology.kubernetes.io/zone`) by enabling rack-level topology awareness.

**Why is this needed:**

**1. Rack-Level Collocation**
Some workloads—such as those with low-latency or high-throughput requirements—benefit from being placed on the same or nearby racks. Currently, there is no established “rack” key in the well-known topology labels, making it difficult to consistently label and schedule workloads by rack boundaries.

**2. Granularity Between Zone and Node**
While `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` offers a broader grouping of resources and `kubernetes.io/hostname` identifies individual nodes, there is a gap in the middle. Many data centers manage hardware and networking at the rack level; a standard label would help reflect that common topology layer.

**3. Consistency with Existing Label Patterns**
Kubernetes already uses the `topology.kubernetes.io/*` pattern for recognized topology labels (region, zone). Following the same pattern for rack labeling would align with best practices and reduce confusion.

**4. Enhanced Scheduling Strategies**
With a well-known rack label, advanced scheduling plugins or custom schedulers can use rack information for optimized workload distribution, fault tolerance, or data locality in distributed applications (e.g., databases, analytics, or HPC workloads).
issues.title: introduce topology.kubernetes.io/rack label

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

#### Problem Statement
Currently, when a node fails, Kubernetes reschedules pods onto other nodes even if another healthy replica exists on a different node. This behavior can lead to unnecessary resource usage, overloading of remaining nodes, and increased costs in environments where resource optimization is critical.

#### Proposed Solution
Introduce a new field in the Deployment or Pod spec, such as `preventRescheduleIfHealthy: true` or `maxUnavailable: 1`. When this field is set, the Kubernetes scheduler would check if another healthy replica of the same application is running on a different node. If a healthy replica exists, the scheduler would skip rescheduling the failed pod until the healthy replica becomes unhealthy or the node is restored.

#### Alternatives Considered
I explored using Pod Anti-Affinity to ensure replicas are not co-located on the same node, but this does not prevent rescheduling when a node fails. I also considered writing a custom controller to enforce this behavior, but this approach is complex, error-prone, and not scalable. A native Kubernetes feature would provide a more robust and maintainable solution.

#### Example Implementation 1
Here’s an example of how the new field could be added to a Deployment spec: The `preventRescheduleIfHealthy`  specifies to prevent reschedule if any other pod is already healthy.
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: my-app
    spec:
      preventRescheduleIfHealthy: true
      containers:
      - name: my-container
        image: my-image
```

#### Example Implementation 2
Here’s an example of how the new field could be added to a Deployment spec: The `maxUnavailable` specifies that at most one replica can be unavailable at any time.
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: my-app
    spec:
      disruptionBudget:
        maxUnavailable: 1
      containers:
      - name: my-container
        image: my-image
```

### Why is this needed?

#### Use Case
In my deployment, I have a stateful application that runs two replicas for high availability. When a node fails, Kubernetes reschedules the failed pod onto another node, even though the second replica is already healthy and running on a different node. This results in unnecessary resource consumption and potential performance degradation. I want to ensure that the second replica is not rescheduled unless the first replica is unhealthy, to optimize resource usage and reduce costs.

#### Impact
This feature would help users optimize resource usage, reduce unnecessary pod rescheduling, and lower costs in environments where resource efficiency is critical. It would also simplify the management of stateful applications and improve the overall stability of deployments.

#### References
- [Pod Topology Spread Constraints Documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/topology-spread-constraints/)

### What would you like to be added?

When watching from etcd, apiserver sets `WithPrevKV` flag so the  returned watch events include information about previous version. This is used by apiserver to handle watch with selector, where it needs to be aware of  what were fields/labels of previous object to notice changes. This is always done on etcd3 layer.

When watch cache is enabled, the watches to etcd3 never include those selectors as they are handled by cache and prevKV is replaced with value from cache. This allows us to deallocate the object, but only after it was decoded on etcd3 layer.

I would propose to stop setting PrevKV when watch cache is enabled.

Pros:
* Reduces lock contention in etcd MVCC by reducing number of reads by 50% and increases write throughput by 20% (from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/131862)
* Watch no longer will break when there is a missing PrevKV field. Etcd doesn't guarantee PrevKV as the field is filled just before sending event and can race with compaction.
* Doubles capacity of watch stream, which was proved that can be overloaded with bad consequences. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/123448
* Halfs allocations needed to handle watch events.

Cons:
* Complicates watch code as it creates special cache for watch cache

/cc @wojtek-t @deads2k


### Why is this needed?

Presented benefits are nice, so I think we might want to consider it, however I don't think there is a strong "need". Would need to measure the direct impact of reducing watch reintializations due to PrevKV, reducing allocations and watch capacity problem.
issues.title: Removing dependence on PrevKV when watch cache is enabled

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

I would like to be able be able to specify unix domain socket paths in my kubeconfig, e.g.:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
clusters:
- cluster:
    server: unix:/run/user/1000/ops-staging.sock
  name: proxy-ops-staging
```

(bonus points if it's possible to use something like `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` or the systemd `%t` placeholder for `/run/user/1000`, but that would introduce templating into the kubeconfig and is *far* out of scope for this request)

### Why is this needed?

#64783 was closed with the [justification](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/1749#issuecomment-755738311) that users who require alternative authentication mechanisms should use a proxy server. The comment even touched upon maybe enhancing kubectl with unix domain socket support.  
Right now [my proxy](https://github.com/orbit-online/step-plugin-kmsproxy) binds to a port on `127.0.0.1`. This works, but is not ideal from a security standpoint: Any user with network access on the current machine is able to authenticate towards the cluster.  
Unix domain sockets reduce the attack surface by allowing users to restrict read/write access to a socket through filesystem permissions.
issues.title: Support unix domain sockets for `cluster.server` in kubeconfig

We（AlibabaCloud）has recently introduced [Regional EBS](https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/ecs/user-guide/regional-essd-disks?spm=a2c63.p38356.0.i1). a new type of EBS that enables pod(app) to utilize it across all zones within a specific region, thereby achieving higher availablity.

Meanwhile, users can modify their existing EBS to a regional EBS by openapi to use the EBS in the other zone. However, after changing the EBS type, we cannot modify the current PV's nodeAffinity to enable the new feature, as it remains limited to its original zone.

current state
```
  nodeAffinity:
    required:
      nodeSelectorTerms:
      - matchExpressions:
        - key: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          operator: In
          values:
          - cn-hangzhou-i
```

desired state
```
  nodeAffinity:
    required:
      nodeSelectorTerms:
      - matchExpressions:
        - key: "topology.kubernetes.io/region"
          operator: In
          values:
          - cn-hangzhou
```

therefore, we want to make nodeAffinity editable to transition PVs from their current state to the desired state. 

We also note that [Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/disks/hyperdisks) in GCP has a similar definition, may suggesting similar requirements. 

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0e5a1c4f-b573-4195-9b12-988256fc4b12)

issues.body:
The current evented PLEG implementation in CRI generates container events (create/start/stop/delete) to trigger `syncPod`, but it fails to accommodate the in-place pod resizing feature. During in-place pod resizing, after completing container resource updates via `UpdateContainerResources/UpdatePodSandboxResources`, we need to re-trigger `syncPod` to update the container status.

In the generic PLEG implementation, this is achieved by forcing a synthetic container event during the next PLEG relist after doPodResizeAction, which triggers `syncPod`. However, for evented PLEG (where events originate directly from the container runtime via CRI), there is no native event generated when resource updates occur. Currently, In PR #131024, I implemented a temporary workaround by simulating container runtime-generated events to achieve this behavior. While this approach unblocks testing, it remains a short-term fix.

To fully align with evented PLEG's design, we need container runtimes to emit a dedicated "Update" event when their `UpdateContainerResources` or `UpdatePodSandboxResources` CRI interfaces are invoked. This event should notify the Kubelet to trigger syncPod, ensuring consistent behavior between generic and evented PLEG implementations.

/sig node
/kind feature
issues.title: Add Container Event Notification for CRI's Update*Resources Interface to Support In-Place Pod Resizing

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

I didn't find any open or closed issue regarding this topic, so I thought to ask here for feedback.

Today, TopologySpreadConstraints allow us to express distribution conditions focused on how many domains or topologies are created when scheduling a particular workload.

We're managing large multi-tenant clusters and often feel the need to express a "limit" in the topology, such as "I want this workload to be distributed as per maxSkew, but not more than X replicas per node or no more than 10% of the replicas per node."

I'm not an expert in scheduling terminology, but I think adding something like "maxReplicas" (which could be an integer or a percentage) would help with this scenario, expressing the additional conditions mentioned above.

### Why is this needed?

In large multi-tenant clusters, where different applications are expected to run on shared nodes, it's useful to specify a further degree of distribution (not more than X replicas per node or not more than Y% per node). This ensures that, in case of node loss, we can control how many replicas per application we can afford to lose. This is particularly important with spot offerings (nodes that can be reclaimed at short notice by the cloud provider).
issues.title: TopologySpreadConstraints to specify "max number or % of replicas"

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Our users rely heavily on eviction and pod disruption budgets for stability and for fleet management, see [this previous talk on rotating nodes](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KQ1obaC-ht0) for more context.

An issue our users often run into is that temporarily they do not want their pod to be evicted. The readiness probe is not an option because the pods critically do still need to serve traffic.

## Proposal

The proposal is to add an additional probe the kubelet would perform, similar to [liveness and readiness](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes/). See [probe definition](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/api/core/v1#Probe), an example portion of the pod spec:

```
"readinessProbe": { # existing
    ...
},
"disruptionProbe": { # new
    "failureThreshold": 3,
    "httpGet": {
        "path": "/disruptable",
        "port": 8484,
        "scheme": "HTTP"
    },
    "initialDelaySeconds": 60,
    "periodSeconds": 30,
    "successThreshold": 1,
    "timeoutSeconds": 1
},

```

Similarly there will be a corresponding status on the pod, an example portion of the pod status:

```
"status": {
"conditions": [
...
    { # existing
        ...
        "status": "True",
        "type": "Ready"
    },
    { # new
        "lastTransitionTime": "2025-02-05T20:26:15Z",
        "status": "True",
        "type": "Disruptable"
    },
    ...
  ]
```

### Behavior, Implementation, and Details

If the disruption probe is defined, only pods with a `True` `Disruptable` condition status (see above status) will count towards the quota for disruption. The disruption controller will need to take this into account _instead_ of the `Ready` condition of pods it looks at today. To maintain current behaviour, if no disruption probe is defined, the kubelet will sync the `Ready` status to the `Disruptable` condition.

It's important that the system we build to support this use case fails closed. Meaning that if it doesn't work correctly we don't accidentally allow evictions that should not be allowed. Probes give this, because having a disruption probe initiated by the kubelet keeps the failure domain consistent with the kubelet, meaning that the eviction won't happen unless the kubelet is a healthy member of the cluster _and_ the kubelet gets an OK response from the relevant pods. An alternate solution could be to have a centralized gate controller effectively manage the `Disruptable` condition. This alternative disruption gates solution is not selected here since among other problems it would be difficult to make its behaviour fail closed.

### Why is this needed?

There are several examples where application owners had to build workarounds for the current behavior to distinguish between these two states:

### Example 1)

We are running a custom-built distributed database. On pod startup, it is assigned a shard and synchronizes data with its siblings in the background. It can be configured to serve traffic once it has replicated enough data while continuing to sync in the background.
This means that the cluster is in a state where we need to serve traffic for stability reasons, but can't afford to lose another pod of the same shard during that time.

Readiness probes could be used by increasing the shard replica count, but it's tightly connected to the total cost of the application, which will increase significantly when running many small clusters.

### Example 2)

The Elasticsearch operator has a similar problem. Elasticsearch clusters can be in different [health states (green / yellow / red)](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/cluster-health.html). If the cluster health is not green, it means that it could still be ready, but the system shouldn't disrupt any of the pods.

Unfortunately, they can't rely on readiness probes only. If a [cluster is in a yellow state](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/red-yellow-cluster-status.html), it means, for example, that one of the shards is missing replicas. So there should not be any disruption to prevent cluster stability issues, but the cluster nodes should still be ready to be able to serve traffic.

To mitigate the problem, the operator maintains logic to [update the cluster's PDB](https://github.com/elastic/cloud-on-k8s/blob/v2.16.1/pkg/controller/elasticsearch/pdb/reconcile.go#L193-L197) and change the `minAvailable` count depending on the health.

### Impact

There are more cases like this, especially for stateful workloads. We have built multiple workarounds, such as implementing custom eviction API endpoints that behave similarly to the Kubernetes API but give more control to our users.

In all these cases, the failure domain is moved from pod level to an external controller. Ensuring application cluster stability is therefore coupled with the health of this controller, which is often less maintained and monitored. Furthermore, users have to actively work against Kubernetes primitives to reflect business needs.

The request is to have a mechanism provided by Kubernetes that can distinguish between whether a pod should be routable (readiness) and whether a pod should be disruptable. If not provided, the behavior will be as is today with readiness controlling disruptability. The solution outlined here is to have a disruption probe and pod status, similar to readiness.

## Next steps

We are hoping to gauge interest with a lighter weight issue, if there is interest we will convert to a KEP.

Besides that, the issue might be related to the newly created [node-lifecycle WG](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/pull/8396). We would be happy to present the topic in that context too.

cc: @K8Y @ryanmcnamara
issues.title: Enhancement: Add a new probe to distinguish between application is ready to serve traffic and when it is safe to disrupt.

issues.body:
**Labels:**
/sig node

**Problem Description:**

Under node memory pressure scenarios where the kernel OOM killer acts before kubelet eviction, critical system pods running with 'Burstable' QoS can be OOM-killed before lower-priority pods that are consuming significantly more memory. This happens because the current `oom_score_adj` calculation for Burstable pods does not take `PriorityClass` into account.

**Observed Scenario:**

* **Node:** 4Gi Total Memory
* **Critical Pod:** konnectivity-agent
  * **QoS:** Burstable
  * **Request:** 30Mi
  * **PriorityClass:** system-cluster-critical
* **Memory Hog Pod:** Application Pod
  * **QoS:** Burstable
  * **Request:** 1Gi
  * (Observed high memory usage: ~1Gi + swap)
  * **PriorityClass:** Lower than system-cluster-critical (default)

During rapid memory pressure, the kernel OOM killer terminated the 'konnectivity-agent' before the memory hogging pod. Kubelet eviction, which *does* respect priority, did not have a chance to act.

**Current Behavior:**

Kubelet sets `oom_score_adj` to influence the kernel OOM killer.

* For `Guaranteed` pods & `system-node-critical` pods: `oom_score_adj = -997` (highly protected)
* For `BestEffort` pods: `oom_score_adj = 1000` (most likely to be killed)
* For `Burstable` pods: `oom_score_adj = min(max(2, 1000 - (1000 * memoryRequestBytes) / machineMemoryCapacityBytes), 999)`

This formula for Burstable pods means:

* **Priority is not considered**: `system-cluster-critical` is treated the same as any other priority within the Burstable class regarding OOM score.
* **Lower requests get higher scores**: Pods with smaller memory requests (like many system agents) receive a higher `oom_score_adj`, making them more likely to be OOM-killed compared to other Burstable pods with larger requests.

This contradicts the intent of `PriorityClass`, where `system-cluster-critical` pods should be protected over lower-priority application pods.

**Expected Behavior:**

The `oom_score_adj` calculation for pods with `Burstable` QoS should incorporate the pod's `PriorityClass`. A `Burstable` pod with a higher priority (e.g., `system-cluster-critical`) should receive a lower (more protected) `oom_score_adj` compared to a `Burstable` pod with a lower priority on the same node, aligning the OOM killer's preference more closely with kubelet eviction logic and the user's intent.

**Why this Matters:**

Premature termination of `system-cluster-critical` pods (like `konnectivity-agent`, `coredns`, CNI components) can lead to node isolation, loss of cluster functionality, cascading failures, and overall cluster instability, especially during high load or resource contention events.

**Suggestion:**

We propose investigating a modification to the `oom_score_adj` calculation logic within kubelet specifically for `Burstable` pods to factor in `PriorityClass`. This could involve adjusting the score based on the priority value, ensuring higher priority leads to a lower score.

*(Context: This issue was discussed briefly in a SIG-Node meeting where it was suggested to file an issue/enhancement request to explore this potential improvement).*
issues.title: kubelet: oom_score_adj for Burstable pods ignores PriorityClass, causing premature kill of high-priority pods

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

We want to add flag zone-full-disruption-eviction-rate. This is used to limit number of nodes per second on which pods are deleted in case of node failure when some zone is disruption.



### Why is this needed?

Currently the node-lifecycle-controller has three types of state categories corresponding to different eviction QPS.


| state| condition| QPS|
|  ----  | ----  | ---- |
|Normal| NotReady nodes accounts for less than 55%| depends on node-eviction-rate, Default: 0.1|
|PartialDisruption|NotReady nodes accounts for large than 55% |depends on secondary-node-eviction-rate,  Default: 0.01|
|FullDisruption|All nodes are not ready|depends on node-eviction-rate, Default: 0.1|
|AllZoneFullDisruption|All zones are `FullDisruption`| The eviction QPS is 0|




With the flag zone-full-disruption-eviction-rate, we can control `FullDisruption` states：

| state| condition| QPS|
|  ----  | ----  | ---- |
|Normal| NotReady nodes accounts for less than 55%| depends on node-eviction-rate, Default: 0.1|
|PartialDisruption|NotReady nodes accounts for large than 55% |depends on secondary-node-eviction-rate,  Default: 0.01|
|FullDisruption|All nodes are not ready|depends on zone-full-disruption-eviction-rate, Default: 0.1|
|AllZoneFullDisruption|All zones are `FullDisruption`|0|


Some systems already have similar capabilities:
1. The control plane does not apply the node.kubernetes.io/unreachable=NoExecute taint to the nodes if the zone is fully disrupted.  https://www.redhat.com/en/blog/openshift-edge-disruption-mitigation
2. If all nodes in a zone are unreachable, Kubernetes cancels pod evictions for the nodes in that zone. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/hybrid-nodes-network-disconnection-best-practices.html

Preview disscussion: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/110114

Please take a look. Will this be accepted?
issues.title: Kube-Controller-Manager add flag zone-full-disruption-eviction-rate

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

As part of the implementation of Dual Stack and also the new nftables backend, kube-proxy now does a validation if IPv4 and IPv6 can be used, for instance https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/88dfcb225d41326113990e87b11137641c121a32/cmd/kube-proxy/app/server_linux.go#L112

The improvement here is that while kube-proxy does check if IPTables support IPv6 (and nftables is right now hardcoded, but with a pending action), it doesn't really check if IPv4 and IPv6 kernel subsystem are enabled on the operational system.

So before taking the action of checking the filter service support, I would like to propose that we do a check, on Linux, if "/proc/sys/net/ipv4" exists and if "/proc/sys/net/ipv6" exists before moving on to the specific IPtables and nftables checks

One example of the implementation can be found at https://github.com/rikatz/kubernetes/commit/6c72306bf29b30378412fbf90dcc13cc6f3a23c6, tho this implementation doesn't use the filesystem list, but instead the utilsysctl, which may not be ideal in this case

### Why is this needed?

Some very specific Linux distributions don't load all the iptables or nftables modules by default, and also don't have auto load (x_tables) working properly due to restrictions and modifications made to work. 

Some other distributions disable IPv6 during boot time with ipv6.disable=true. Generally disabling IPv6 doesn't mean the IPv6 rules cannot be added, but on some very specific cases that I could't define why, not all IPv6 filter modules are compiled to the kernel and will partially fail during IPv6 apply, blocking kube-proxy to work.

This is more a proposal to be early defensive on these cases
issues.title: Improve IP protocol detection on kube-proxy

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Kubernetes clusters on top of GCE should use community maintained binaries, the CSI Proxy binary used in kubernetes/kubernetes comes from a release pipeline owned by the GKE team.

### Why is this needed?

The current process to use a new CSI Proxy binary is as follows:

- A CSI Proxy owner makes a release cut e.g. https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/csi-proxy/releases/tag/v1.2.1
- In GKE, an automated pipeline detects a new tag and builds the binary and makes it available in a staging bucket.
- In GKE, a GKE dev promotes the binary to the prod bucket `gke-release`
- In upstream kubernetes/kubernetes, we use the binary promoted to the `gke-release` bucket e.g. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/131146

Ideally, upstream kubernetes should rely on binaries created in upstream build pipelines. The process could look like the following:

- A CSI Proxy owner makes a release cut e.g. https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/csi-proxy/releases/tag/v1.2.1.
- A post tag Github Action runs automatically and builds the binary and attaches the artifacts to the release.
- In upstream kubernetes/kubernetes, we use the binary available as attached resources in the new tag.

Mirror bug in CSI Proxy: https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/csi-proxy/issues/83

/cc @sunnylovestiramisu @tonyzhc
issues.title: Refactor GCE Windows bootstrap to use a community maintained release of CSI Proxy

Now, if we want to try a preemption of a pod and no candidates are found, `nominatedNodeName` is cleared for a pod in the preemption code:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/88dfcb225d41326113990e87b11137641c121a32/pkg/scheduler/framework/preemption/preemption.go#L316-L324

But, because we return `framework.NewPostFilterResultWithNominatedNode("")` anyway when there are no candidates:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/88dfcb225d41326113990e87b11137641c121a32/pkg/scheduler/framework/preemption/preemption.go#L263-L276

The nominatedNodeName will be cleared in the `handleSchedulingFailure` in the scheduling cycle:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/88dfcb225d41326113990e87b11137641c121a32/pkg/scheduler/schedule_one.go#L1088-L1096

So, we can remove the `ClearNominatedNodeName` in `findCandidates`, because it's a duplicated effort.

Reducing number of API calls could improve performance.

/kind feature
/sig scheduling
issues.title: Don't clear nominatedNodeName in preemption if no candidates are found, because it is cleared later anyway

### What would you like to be added?

Add some kind of mechanism to "shutdown event monitor" in `managerImpl.start()` waits before terminating Pods with `m.processShutdownEvent()`.

### Why is this needed?

The main reason for this mechanism is to make Pods termination action be dependant on some external condition.

In my case this condition is controlled by a separate systemd unit that installs systemd inhibitors. This component delays Node shutdown to give an administrator some time to take care of specially labeled Pods (think of critical virtual machines, or atomic CronJobs, or ...).

### PoC

I've patched `managerImpl.start()` to sleep until a well-known-file disappears. It works fine for my case.

What would you suggest as a more universal way for this scenario? Some kind of rpc server like device plugin API, or another mechanism? A list of inhibitors names in the kubelet configuration?

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Currently, it always returns `Unschedulable`. But, if node's `.status.Capacity` (not `.Allocatable`) is smaller than the pod (= even if the node is empty, the pod wouldn't be able to go there), we can return UnschedulableAndUnresolvable for the node because the preemption wouldn't help for sure.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/30469e180361d7da07b0fee6d47c776fa2cf3e86/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/noderesources/fit.go#L469

### Why is this needed?

In large clusters, there could be various sizes of pods and nodes. It's fairly possible that a small node's capacity is smaller than a large pod's resource request. 
Given the preemption is a heavy calculation vs checking the capacity at the resource fit plugin shouldn't be a heavy calculation, we should do it so that we can reduce the number of candidate nodes that we have to calculate in the preemption process.

That being said, we should make sure this change wouldn't impact the normal scenarios where the preemption doesn't get involved. (via scheduler_perf)
issues.title: scheduler: return UnschedulableAndUnresolvable when a node's capacity is smaller than the pod size

### What would you like to be added?

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Current default eviction threshold is hardcoded as 100MiB, this works for default linux default (66MiB). But this can be adjusted, and with swap use-cases, kubernetes environments will likely see this sysctl parameter adjusted to a higher value than default.

This proposal suggests to set the sysctl parameter based on the observed value instead:

`max( DefaultHardEvictionThresholdValue , NodeMinFreeKbytes + SafetyMargin )`

Where:
- `DefaultHardEvictionThresholdValue` is the current default (100MiB).
- `NodeMinFreeKbytes` is the value read from /proc/sys/vm/min_free_kbytes, converted to MiB.
- `SafetyMargin` is a buffer (e.g., 50MiB or a percentage of min_free_kbytes) to ensure eviction triggers comfortably before the kernel's absolute minimum is reached. 

Proposal discussed at SIG-Node: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1qBkCuB7hPbCfCkTc7ilYwwDzyG_ykpP7losidyuOiTU/edit?usp=sharing
 

### Why is this needed?

This is required to ensure Kubernetes handles eviction before the OOM killer starts handling for memory pressure. This is particularly important for swap use-cases as the swap watermarks are directly influenced by this sysctl parameter.
issues.title: Default memory eviction-hard threshold in kubernetes should be set more than `vm.min_free_kbytes`

issues.body:
### What happened?

Let's say I have a containerized app which take about 75 seconds to start.
When a startupProbe is configured for its pod as below:
```
    startupProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /actuator/health/livenessState
        port: 9080
        scheme: HTTP
      failureThreshold: 30
      periodSeconds: 10
      successThreshold: 1
      timeoutSeconds: 3
```
it reports in Kubelet events Warning 7 times:
```
Events:
  Type     Reason     Age                From               Message
  ----     ------     ----               ----               -------
  Normal   Scheduled  38s                default-scheduler  Successfully assigned my-pod-86f77646d5-vd8ks
  Normal   Pulling    38s                kubelet            Pulling image "artifactory...."
  Normal   Pulled     32s                kubelet            Successfully pulled image "artifactory...." in 5.709s (5.709s including waiting). Image size: 232274542 bytes.
  Normal   Created    32s                kubelet            Created container my-pod
  Normal   Started    32s                kubelet            Started container my-pod
  Warning  Unhealthy  18s (x7 over 90s)  kubelet            Startup probe failed: Get "http://100.65.0.75:9080/actuator/health/livenessState": dial tcp 100.65.0.75:9080: connect: connection refused
```

That is logical, but **not practical nor semantic**.

The startupProbe's sole reason of existence **is to get** the initial **failures**. So it should not report them as `Warning`, because it's not wrong. If the app really did not start at the end, the probe which should report the problem should be the livenessProbe after the startupProbe reached its maximum (failureThreshold * periodSeconds), not the startupProbe. So the only `Warning` or `Error` situation the startupProbe should report, is if it exceeded its maximum livespan without any successful attempt.

### What did you expect to happen?

The startupProbe should not report failures, except at the end, if it exceeded its maximum livespan without any successful attempt.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Declare a `startupProbe`, use `kubectl describe pod` and see the `Warning` in the `Events` section.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### What would you like to be added?

It is currently a requirement for all custom scheduler plugin developers to have a dependency on the entire k8s mono repository even though this has been explicitly discouraged (See https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/79384#issuecomment-505627280)

To implement different plugins (e.g. `framework.PermitPlugin` or `framework.ReservePlugin` etc.) there is no choice today but to include the dependency of the entire k8s github as framework interfaces have not been exposed separately. This not only violates your own `strong-recommendation` but it also bloats the custom scheduler plugin development go.mod.

Would you consider moving the framework interfaces and expose it via the existing [kube-scheduler](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/kube-scheduler/) go module?

### Why is this needed?

To not have dependency on k8s github mono repository which requires a lot of unnecessary replace directives to be added to dependencies that are not even used by the custom scheduler plugins. It also results in lean scheduler plugin go modules.

Of course one needs to have a dependency on k8s mono repository when using `app.NewSchedulerCommand` but this could be a completely different go module. This enables custom plugin go modules to be lean and only the custom-scheduler-builder go module to have k8s mono repo dependency.
issues.title: Expose all scheduler framework interfaces via existing staging/src/k8s.io/kube-scheduler

### What would you like to be added?

I am asking for a new feature request where the 'kubectl drain' command would be only the initiator of a job inside the Kubernetes control plabe.

Problem statement:
- there is a lot of interaction between the kubectl and the actual low level drain sub-operations
- user should really just trigger a drain and leave the client and monitor a K8s control plane job instead

### Why is this needed?

reduce non-productive time
move away from client environment executing an administrative task into more controlling task
reduce network latency between the client and control plane
if client terminates, operation of draining terminates immediately - client becomes a single point of failure and we could lose insight where it left, where a control plane job could be still there and provide insights into the status, including issues
issues.title: Worker node draining should be fully managed by the control plane as a job

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

With the continued advancement of image volumes https://kubernetes.io/blog/2025/04/29/kubernetes-v1-33-image-volume-beta/ I would like to see an ability to mount the volume as rw.

I do *NOT* want the actual changes to be written to the registry (local or remote) but rather simply want the mount point to be ephemeral in much the same way a rootfs is of a running container.

### Why is this needed?

My specific use-case it to use the volume essentially as a rw cache. For example let's say I have a large git repository I wish to share across CI builds running in a cluster. I would like each build to use the image as a 'starting place' and each build will then simply (ephemerally) do a `git pull` and `git checkout` etc on the mount point and be able to generally function as a rw volume. Once the build is done the modified data is simply discarded and the source image is left untouched.

A side-benefit is that each relevant node will only store the data of the repo once (ie: copy-on-write-like semantics) reducing storage requirements. The source image can periodically be updated to the latest upstream content and inherit the goodness of image deltas for that process as well.

Thanks for the consideration!
issues.title: support ephemeral rw image volume mounts

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

The updated [KEP-5073](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-api-machinery/5073-declarative-validation-with-validation-gen/README.md) proposes a user-experience-focused approach for ratcheting `structType=atomic` and `mapType=atomic` collections in built-in types. Specifically, it suggests that re-validation during an update should only occur for the sub-fields or key-value pairs that have actually changed, rather than re-validating the entire atomic collection if any part is modified.

This behavior differs from the current, stricter interpretation for atomic collections in CRDs under [KEP-4008](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-api-machinery/4008-crd-ratcheting/README.md#atomic-lists-and-maps).

#### Proposal

* **Built-in Types**: Solidify the decision for this granular ratcheting behavior (only revalidating changed parts) for structType=atomic and mapType=atomic in built-in types as per KEP-5073.

* **CRD**: Align the ratcheting behavior for `structType=atomic` and `mapType=atomic` in CRDs (KEP-4008) so that CRDs also adopt this more granular, user-experience-focused approach of only revalidating the changed sub-fields or key-value pairs within atomic collections, ensuring consistency across built-in types and CRDs. 

### Why is this needed?

Aligning the ratcheting behavior for atomic structs and maps across built-in types and CRDs is needed to:
* Provide a uniform and predictable validation ratcheting experience for users.
* Uphold the core principle of minimizing update rejections due to validation failures on fields or map entries that were not modified by the user, even as "atomic".
* Clearly distinguish the "atomic" nature for ownership purposes from the granularity of re-validation during ratcheting.
issues.title: Align Ratcheting behavior for "atomic" data type between Built-ins and CRDs

issues.body:
Add Fallback to Static Version File in Shallow Clones.

**Background:**
In environments where the Kubernetes source repository is cloned with the `--depth=1` option 
(e.g., in CI/CD pipelines or containerized builds), the full Git history and tags are not available. 
As a result, the git describe command used in `kube::version::get_version_vars()` fails to produce a valid semantic version. 
This leads to the version being set to a default like `Kubernetes v0.0.0-master+$Format:%H$`, which is not informative or consistent with release expectations.

**Problem Statement:**
When git describe cannot determine the version due to a shallow clone or lack of tags, the current versioning logic does not provide a meaningful fallback. This can cause downstream tooling and image tagging logic to behave incorrectly or inconsistently.

**Proposed Enhancement:**
Introduce support for a static version fallback file [build/build-image/cross/VERSION](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/build/build-image/cross/VERSION) within the kube::version::get_version_vars() function. 
If git describe fails to determine the version, and if [build/build-image/cross/VERSION](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/build/build-image/cross/VERSION) exists, the script will read and use its contents as the 
KUBE_GIT_VERSION and we get version like `Kubernetes v1.33.0+5596991555fa21 `

**Benefits**
	•	Ensures consistent and predictable versioning in restricted Git environments.
	•	Supports reproducible builds by decoupling versioning from Git state when needed.
	•	Minimal impact on existing logic; activated only when git describe fails.
issues.title: Add Fallback to Static Version File in Shallow Clones.

t1: pre-stop done, kubelet starts to stop container
between t0 and t1, readiness probe didn't failed,  pod is still ready, traffic is forwarded to  the abnormal container.

# Suggestion

Set container ready condition to false once liveness probe failed.

### What would you like to be added?

In package [`k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/errors`](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/errors):
1. implement the `func Unwrap() []error` method on the `aggregate` type (the concrete type behind the [`Aggregate`](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/errors#Aggregate) interface). Implementation already exists under the `func Errors() []error` name.
2. handle the `func Unwrap() []error` and `func Unwrap() error` interfaces in the implementation of `aggregate.visit()`
3. switch the implementation of all function of the package to use the `func Unwrap() []error` method instead of the `func Errors() []error` method of the [`Aggregate`](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/errors#Aggregate) interface
4. deprecate the `func Errors() []error` method of `Aggregate` and point

Note: At this point I think that to preserve forward compatibility it is not possible to extend [`Aggregate`](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/errors#Aggregate) interface to the `Unwrap() []error`. However we could add an `AggregateUnwrap` interface that would have that method (and not the `Errors()` method) and could serve as documentation point for the new behavior. 

### Why is this needed?

Go 1.20 introduced [`errors.Join`] and the `func Unwrap() []error` method that may be implemented by errors. They fit most needs for the [`Aggregate`](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/errors#Aggregate) interface and the [`NewAggregate`](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/errors#NewAggregate) func.

Any new use of `NewAggregate` should be discouraged (Deprecated?). Any inspection of an `Aggregate` should be done using the standard `func Unwrap() []error` interface and stdlib [errors](https://pkg.go.dev/errors) utilities. However **this is not yet possible** because the `aggregate` type doesn't yet implement the `func Unwrap() []error` method.
issues.title: apimachinery/pkg/util/errors: retrofit integration with std errors.Join

issues.body:
### What happened?

When we create a 1-GPU pod on a machine with 8 NUMA nodes (AMD CPU + NVIDIA 4090D), the hint providers for CPU, memory, hugepages, and GPU each generate approximately 255 hints. During the hint merging phase, the topology manager needs to evaluate 255^4 (over 4.2 billion) possible hint combinations. In our testing, this process took nearly 21 minutes.
- _The time mentioned here refers to the duration from when the CPU, memory, and device managers each generate their hints, to when the topology manager computes the best hint._

### What did you expect to happen?

Optimizing the computation efficiency of a pod’s best hint down to the second level.

Here are some simple yet high-impact optimization ideas I’ve identified:
- When the restricted topology manager policy is selected, hints with preferred=false returned by hint providers can be filtered out early, and excluded from the subsequent hint merge logic. This would significantly reduce the computational overhead and improve the efficiency of best hint calculation.
- The number of NUMA nodes involved in the hints returned by the device manager should match the number of requested devices.
For example, when creating a pod requesting 1 GPU, the GPU device manager currently returns 255 hints, but in reality, only 8 of them are valid (e.g., 01, 10, 100, 1000, 10000, 100000, 1000000, 10000000).
The rest are redundant and cause a more than 30-fold decrease in the efficiency of computing the best hint.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0525accb-ede1-449b-b096-bf8271272c8d)

These optimizations could greatly improve pod admission performance, especially on systems with many NUMA nodes.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- Kubelet with topology manager configurations. The main configurations:

```yaml
cpuManagerPolicy: static
memoryManagerPolicy: Static
topologyManagerPolicy: best-effort
topologyManagerScope: pod
featureGates:
  CPUManagerPolicyAlphaOptions: true
cpuManagerPolicyOptions:
  distribute-cpus-across-numa: "true"
```

- Create a 1-GPU pod on a node with 8 NUMA nodes and no GPUs currently allocated

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### What would you like to be added?

Kubernetes components are careful to write all log records with a single write call, which then hopefully translates into a single system call. When passing that output through kube-log-runner with [-log-file-size non-zero](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/094466539e0781bfc3d6184983edeaa90a04245d/staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/logs/kube-log-runner/README.md?plain=1#L34-L41) (added in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/127667), kube-log-runner will split the stream of bytes without considering log record boundaries.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/compare/master...pohly:kubernetes:log-runner-torn-writes?expand=1 demonstrates the problem.

If kube-log-runner were to use Unix Domain [sequential packet sockets](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/22955226/unix-domain-socket-name-in-go-language) for redirecting the command's output, each write syscall of the command turns into a datagram which can be received completely by kube-log-runner.

/sig instrumentation

cc @zylxjtu 

### Why is this needed?

Ensure that each log file contains complete log records.
issues.title: kube-log-runner: avoid torn log records when using log rotation

### What would you like to be added?

Add a way for kube-apiserver to present client certificate while requesting to a ConversionWebhook. Maybe we add a new entry for ConversionWebhook as well like:

```
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: AdmissionConfiguration
plugins:
- name: ValidatingAdmissionWebhook
  configuration:
    apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
    kind: WebhookAdmissionConfiguration
    kubeConfigFile: "<path-to-kubeconfig-file>"
- name: MutatingAdmissionWebhook
  configuration:
    apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
    kind: WebhookAdmissionConfiguration
    kubeConfigFile: "<path-to-kubeconfig-file>"
- name: ConversionWebhook
  configuration:
    apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
    kind: ConversionWebhookConfiguration
    kubeConfigFile: "<path-to-kubeconfig-file>"
```
And use it while creating a client for ConversionWebhooks.
As the client for all the ConversionWebhooks will be same i.e. kube-apiserver, so it makes sense to keep it in kube-apiserver configuration.

### Why is this needed?

After we implement mTLS between the kube-apiserver and webhooks using the steps mentioned in: https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/extensible-admission-controllers/#authenticate-apiservers 

When ConversionWebhook is added to the same server manager as AdmissionWebhooks using `AddToManager`, then conversion webhooks keeps failing for error
```
2025/05/15 18:33:43 http: TLS handshake error from 192.168.128.0:42658: tls: client didn't provide a certificate

```
Suppose we have `conversionReviewVersions: ["v1", "v1beta1"]`. Here the requests for v1 CRDs goes through without any errors as the conversion is not triggered. But when the v1beta1 CRD is applied the ConversionWebhook returns tls errors.

Also going through the code we can confirm that this discrepancy is the cause of errors here:
For AdmissionWebhooks: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/webhook/generic/webhook.go#L74 , here the client is created with kubeconfig for client auth.

For ConversionWebhooks: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apiserver/conversion/webhook_converter.go#L77 , here the client is created without any client auth.

kube-apiserver as a client should behave in similar way when connecting to the webhook server hosting all 3 enpoints.

Workarounds that were thought of:
1. Use `tls.RequestClientCert` but it defeats the security purpose of introducing authentication in the first place.
2. Run conversion webhooks in a separate server inside the controller instead of re-using the admission webhooks server. This should work in theory but it would be good to consolidate all webhooks in a single server.
issues.title: Add option for mTLS for conversion webhook
