issues.body:
### Context

"[KEP-3521](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-scheduling/3521-pod-scheduling-readiness): Pod Scheduling Readiness" had graduated to GA in 1.30. It allows gating the scheduling of a pod, hence delaying it until the gate is removed.

This feature is useful for multiple use-cases, one of them being to allow out-of-tree quota management solutions to integrate well with Kubernetes. In fact, in a [post](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2022/12/26/pod-scheduling-readiness-alpha/#use-cases) in the Kubernetes blog the outlined use-case is the following:
> An important use case this feature enables is dynamic quota management. Kubernetes supports [ResourceQuota](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/resource-quotas/), however the API Server enforces quota at the time you attempt Pod creation.
> ...
> Scheduling gates allows an external quota manager to address the above limitation of ResourceQuota.

In addition, in the "[What problem does it solve?](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2022/12/26/pod-scheduling-readiness-alpha/#what-problem-does-it-solve)" section, it writes:
> Clearing the gates is the responsibility of external controllers with knowledge of when the Pod should be considered for scheduling (e.g., a quota manager).

As can be seen from the above, the Pod Scheduling Readiness feature was specifically designed to allow out-of-tree quota management solutions to integrate well with Kubernetes.

### The problem

The [In-place Update of Pod Resources](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/1287-in-place-update-pod-resources) KEP allows to modify pod's resources without re-scheduling them. While this feature is absolutely useful, it removes the assumption in which every pod that uses new resources would be scheduled.

The current behavior contradicts one of the main goals of Pod Scheduling Readiness, which is a GAed feature, and is effectively breaking existing out-of-tree quota solutions.

### Possible solutions

**Idea 1**: Introduce a resize gate, which operates similarly to a scheduling gate, meaning it will gate resizes until removed. This will allow external quota managements to become aware of the resize request, being able to perform custom logic.

**Idea 2**: Re-use the current scheduling gates as resize gates. In other words, delay resize requests until the scheduling gate is removed. (As far as I remember, scheduling gates are immutable, which could challenge this approach).

**Idea 3**:  ??

### Effected projects

I'm aware of two projects that are effected by this, being
* Kueue: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue.
* AAQ (Application Aware Quota): https://github.com/kubevirt/application-aware-quota. 

### Related discussions

Issue opened to Kueue: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/issues/5257.
Old issue about the same subject: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/4304.
issues.title: [KEP-3521]: Integrate well with out-of-tree resource quota solutions

**What would you like to be added**:

I would like to be able to see resource consumption for all pods running on the specific node only.
```
kubectl top pods --field-selector spec.nodeName=<name>
```

Currently this command is failing with:
```
➜  ~ kubectl top pods --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node> -A
Error from server (BadRequest): "spec.nodeName" is not a known field selector: only "metadata.name", "metadata.namespace"
```

**Why is this needed**:

This is useful when investigating node resource pressure. Let's say that I run `kubectl top nodes --sort-by='memory'` and see that one of my nodes is on 95% memory usage. The next logical thing to do is to find what are the most memory intensive pods.

I can run `kubectl describe node <name>`, this will give me list of pods and their memory requests and limits but not the usage.

Currently this can be fetched by the following overly-complicated command:

```bash
kubectl get pods --field-selector spec.nodeName='<name>' -A -o custom-columns=NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name --no-headers | \ 
   xargs -I {} sh -c "kubectl top pod --no-headers -n {}" | \
   column -t
```

### What would you like to be added?

Currently, Apiserver disable event watchcache by default. We did this to make test faster. See https://github.com/kubernetes/perf-tests/issues/561. We could disable it in tests, but keep it enabled in the default settings.

### Why is this needed?

Watchcache is critical in reducing etcd pressure. We have ran into some serious issue due to lack of event watchcache. 

We used to have a failure rate over 80% in a proction cluster with 14k nodes and 560k pods. With watchcahe enabled, the failure rate droped to near zero.

The etcd is really not good at handling large range requests. Without watchcache, the list/watch goes directly to etcd, which cause a serious lock contension. We saw some large range requests took over 1m and kept hodling the lock, while others starved.

issues.body:
### What happened
When using GPU resources in Kubernetes pods, I found that GPU resource definitions don't allow limits to be greater than requests. In fact, they must be equal. This limitation prevents using GPU virtualization capabilities in modern device plugins like [hami](https://github.com/Project-HAMi/HAMi), where multiple pods can share a single physical GPU.

### Current implementation
The current code in `helpers.go` defines what resources can be overcommitted:

```go
func IsOvercommitAllowed(name core.ResourceName) bool {
    return IsNativeResource(name) &&
        !IsHugePageResourceName(name)
}
```

This function only allows native Kubernetes resources (except HugePages) to be overcommitted. Extended resources like GPUs must have equal requests and limits. The validation logic in `validation.go` enforces this:

```go
if quantity.Cmp(limitQuantity) != 0 && !helper.IsOvercommitAllowed(resourceName) {
    allErrs = append(allErrs, field.Invalid(reqPath, quantity.String(),
        fmt.Sprintf("must be equal to %s limit of %s", resourceName, limitQuantity.String())))
}
```

### What you expected to happen
With modern GPU virtualization technologies like NVIDIA MPS, vGPU, MIG, and various device plugins (e.g., hami), it's now common to share a single physical GPU among multiple containers, especially for inference workloads. In these scenarios, it should be possible to overcommit GPU resources similar to CPU and memory.

### Feature request
I propose to modify the `IsOvercommitAllowed` function to allow specific GPU resource types to be overcommitted, especially `nvidia.com/gpu`:

```go
func IsOvercommitAllowed(name core.ResourceName) bool {
    // Original logic (native resources except hugepages)
    if IsNativeResource(name) && !IsHugePageResourceName(name) {
        return true
    }

    // New: Support overcommit for nvidia.com/gpu
    if strings.HasPrefix(string(name), "nvidia.com/gpu") {
        return true
    }

    return false
}
```


### Related issues
- Issue #52757 (Is sharing GPU to multiple containers feasible?)

/kind feature
/sig node
/area gpu
/area hw-accelerators

### Why is this needed?

This change would enable running multiple inference workloads on a shared GPU, making better use of GPU resources in clusters and supporting common patterns in AI/ML deployments.
issues.title: Support resource overcommit for virtualized GPUs

### What would you like to be added?

Implement `HealthCheckable` interface for controllers to include the informer cache readiness. So that each controller has real health check on whether it is running and ready to process requests.

### Why is this needed?

Currently we use default ping health checker for controllers without custom health check functions defined (all controllers don't have it implemented now). As a result, it always returns healthy regardless of its running state. 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d96cfeb7de7742733c1c83a5cf0f3675b2910d6e/cmd/kube-controller-manager/app/controllermanager.go#L762-L778

Although controllers will wait for informer cache to be synced before starting processing any requests, we are lacking visibility into whether the controller is actually healthy/ready for processing requests in the work queue.

For example for job-controller it waits cache to be synced in `jm.Run` function
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bbb42911531af4cd9206e7646c0af3ace157404e/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L248-L258

If the cache fails to be synced the job-controller routine would exit here
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bbb42911531af4cd9206e7646c0af3ace157404e/cmd/kube-controller-manager/app/batch.go#L50

But the registered ping check will still return healthy. 

The registered health checks are also exposed as `kubernetes_healthcheck` metrics emitted by KCM through `/metrics/slis`. Having custom health check for controllers will increase the user visibility into controller's runtime healthiness.

There was a similar issue created before but didn't get attention https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/128233, reopening new one with focus on improving the health check functions for each controller. The informer cache sync can be the first one (and generic one) included in all custom health check functions

### What would you like to be added?

Kubernetes currently supports raw block device volumes via volumeMode: Block (see [raw block volume support](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2019/03/07/raw-block-volume-support-to-beta/)). However, there is no support for raw character devices.

I would like Kubernetes to support a new `volumeMode: CharDevice` option for local volumes, allowing pods to consume character device files directly from the host (e.g., `/dev/stX` for tape drives).

### Why is this needed?

Some specialised workloads rely on hardware accessible via character devices. Without native support, these workloads cannot be containerised using standard Kubernetes volume mechanisms.

Adding support for `volumeMode: CharDevice` would enable static provisioning of local PersistentVolumes backed by character devices. This would make Kubernetes a more viable platform for tape-based systems or other software relying on character devices.

issues.body:
## What would you like to be added?

The API Priority and Fairness (APF) mechanism effectively protects the Kubernetes API server from CPU-bound overloads. However, it currently falls short in preventing memory exhaustion, particularly from large LIST responses. The size of LIST responses can vary drastically, ranging from a few kilobytes to hundreds of megabytes. APF's current cost estimation for requests does not adequately account for the memory footprint of these responses. This oversight can lead to API server memory exhaustion (OOMs), reduced stability, and inefficient resource utilization.

Goals
* Reduce the maximum memory usage of API server without impact on throughput.

Non-Goals
* Model non linear relations in memory usage, this should be reserved for future where we might use a proper model.
* Load shedding that happens when cost of upcoming request eshauses CPU causing GC to starve and leak memory.

## Proposal

To mitigate memory overloads and prevent OOMs, I propose to incorporate the object size as a primary signal into the APF LIST work estimator. This will allow APF to better reflect the memory cost of these requests and allocate "seats" proportionally, as based on experiments in most cases it is a linear relation.

Specifically, I propose the following changes to the LIST work estimator:
* Replace the existing object count estimator with a size-based model:
  * Requests served from etcd: Assign 1 seat per 100 KB of objects response size. 
  * Requests served from cache: Assign 1 seat per 100 KB of objects response size, however limit it to 1MB. Over that value the cost becomes non-linear which we not model for now.
* Increase the global maximum seats from the current 10 to 100. We need bigger range of request cost to properly weight bigger requests.

EDIT: Removed idea to account borrowing into maxSeats estimate based on results in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/132233#issuecomment-3084310266

Above changes could be done one by one, to verify impact of the change on the project.

### Why 100KB?
The choice of 100KB per seat is an arbitrary tuning parameter, similar to the current guess of 1 seat per 100 objects. The proposed 100KB value is based on the following observations:

* Granularity and Object Size: The maximum object size is 1MB, so a value larger than that would not be effective. A smaller value like 100KB allows the system to better distinguish the cost of single object operations, such as a 100KB put versus a 1MB put.
* Memory Variance: We observe a large variance in memory usage for responses of 100KB and 1MB. For 100KB requests, the memory variance is about 2x (between 0.5GB and 1GB), which is within acceptable user expectations. For 1MB requests, memory usage can grow by almost 7x (to 3.2GB), which is not a safety buffer we can reasonably ask users to accommodate.

## Experiments

The aforementioned proposal is informed by experiments in which the following behavioral observations were made regarding memory usage when serving LIST requests:
* APF nicely scales max QPS to type of request as in most cases thanks to feedback loop that happens during overload. When API server becomes overloaded, the request duration increases reducing number of requests allowed through APF. This works a certain point where cost of accepting requests starts starving GC, however this is realm of load shedding that is outside the scope of this proposal.
* There is no linear relation between memory cost of request and number of objects. Rather it increases the CPU cost of allocations and garbage collection, which can indirectly influence memory used. In most cases this is compensated by APF ability to scale to CPU. 
* In most cases Memory consumption is directly proportional to the object size:
   * For etcd this relation holds on hide range due to memory mostly coming from needing to load etcd response into memory. 
   * For serving from cache it holds if streaming is disabled. When we enable streaming it this holds well up to 1MB responses, after which it becomes non-linear. This comes from fact that memory comes from encoding and compressing response. 

### Setup

Experiments were conducted on a Kind cluster with an API server configured with 16 cores and a maximum of 800 concurrent requests. This value was selected because at 800 concurrent requests, the global-default priority level reaches its maxSeats limit of 10. At that value global-default requests are able to borrow up to 500 seats. The cluster utilized the latest Kubernetes build from the master branch, incorporating a patch that allowed the explicit setting of request seats to values of 1, 10, or 100 (bypassing the maxSeats configuration for experimental control).

### Metod

For each combination of input parameters (response size, object count, and etcd/cache serving), the following procedure was executed:

1. Initialize the number of allocated seats to 1.
2. Determine the maximum Queries Per Second (QPS) that the API server could sustainably serve without hitting any "Too many requests" responses. Run for at 80 seconds to ensure that it's longer than request timeout (default 60s)
3. At the determined maximum QPS, measure the API server's peak memory usage for different enforced seat values: 1, 10, and 100.

### Results

#### etcd

Observations
* Number of objects causes increased CPU usage, however doesn't necessarily higher memory usage for objects number below 10`000.
* Assigning seats proportionally to Response size results reduces the memory with minimal impact to error rate. For 10MB+ 100 seats might be too much, so will consider lower value but for simplicity we avoided using non linear estimator.

issues.body:
## What type of Issue is this?

/kind feature
/sig scheduling

## What this Issue does / why we need it:

This issue proposes adding memory tracking capabilities to `scheduler_perf` to detect memory leaks and regressions before they reach production.

### Background

The Kubernetes scheduler has experienced critical memory leaks in production:

- **#120622**: QHint inFlightPods memory leak
- **#111773**: Preemption strategy memory leak
- **#83895**: Work queue timer memory leak
- And your custom scheduler plugins?

These issues were discovered only after deployment to production, causing a significant operational impact. The variety of root causes (watch operations, preemption logic, queue timers, map cleanup) demonstrates the need for systematic memory tracking.

### Proposed Solution

Add memory tracking to `scheduler_perf` that monitors:

- **HeapMemoryInUse**: Current heap memory usage (MB)
- **GoroutineCount**: Number of active goroutines
- **MemoryGrowthRate**: Rate of memory increase (MB/min)

Frankly, what to monitor is debatable. I welcome your opinion.

PoC is https://github.com/utam0k/kubernetes/tree/scheduler-perf-memory/test/integration/scheduler_perf/memory/demo, and confirm PoC can detect #120622 case.

Here is the summary by PoC:

- **Workload**: 150,000 pods
- **Duration**: ~1.5 minutes

| Metric                     | Baseline    | Memory Leak | Difference         |
| -------------------------- | ----------- | ----------- | ------------------ |
| HeapMemoryInUse (Average)  | 4418 MB     | 4941 MB     | +523 MB (+11.8%)   |
| HeapMemoryInUse (Max)      | 6626 MB     | 7770 MB     | +1144 MB (+17.3%)  |
| MemoryGrowthRate           | 1946 MB/min | 2801 MB/min | +855 MB/min (+44%) |
| GoroutineCount (Average)   | 2,475       | 2,483       | +8 (+0.3%)         |
| GoroutineCount (Max)       | 3,015       | 3,221       | +206 (+6.8%)       |
issues.title: scheduler_perf: Add Memory Tracking to Detect Memory Leaks

issues.body:
A little background just in case: `ImageMinimumGCAge` options controls after how much time **after the image was first seen** it can be deleted by GC in case of disk pressure:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8f1f17a04f62ab64ebe4f0b9d7f5f799bf56a0d9/pkg/kubelet/images/image_gc_manager.go#L486

`ImageMaximumGCAge` in turn controls how much time **image was unused** before it can be removed: 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8f1f17a04f62ab64ebe4f0b9d7f5f799bf56a0d9/pkg/kubelet/images/image_gc_manager.go#L430

There's currently a requirement for `ImageMaximumGCAge` to be less than `ImageMinimumGCAge`:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8f1f17a04f62ab64ebe4f0b9d7f5f799bf56a0d9/pkg/kubelet/apis/config/validation/validation.go#L93

I believe this requirement is incorrect, as these two min/max parameters are not closely related as they're counted from different moments. The more specific example when one would want to set max < min is the following situation happening in our production workloads.

We have a multi-container pod with multiple large images. Our hosts are experiencing disk pressure often, so GC tries to clean up the images every time. If the deployment strategy is `RECREATE`, the old pod is removed first when deploying a new version. The individual container's images between sequential deployments usually intersect a lot, so there's no reason to remove and pull these images again until the new pod is created. However, if GC is run between the old pod is removed and the new one is created, it collects the images based on `MinAge` (because it's counted since the first time image appeared, i.e. a week ago and the start of the previous deployment). It makes sense to set a high `MinAge` (more than our usual deployment interval) and a small `MaxAge` (a bit higher than we expect for all images to be pulled). Small `MaxAge` would lead to the leftover images to be removed after the new pod is created, and large `MinAge` (or even to disable this option altogether, which is currently impossible as well) would ensure the GC is not removing images before the new pod is created.
issues.title: ImageMaximumGCAge's requirement to be less than ImageMinimumGCAge is incorrect

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Feature Request: Observability-Based Runtime Overcommit for Burstable Workloads
Kubernetes currently enforces static ResourceQuota at the namespace level, which becomes counterproductive in clusters where workloads are predominantly burstable (i.e., requests < limits). The quota model effectively flattens all container limits into a hard ceiling, preventing efficient shared resource utilization—even if most workloads are well below their limits.

This rigid enforcement eliminates the benefits of burstable QoS and contradicts the shared-resource philosophy of Kubernetes.

Proposed Solution:
Introduce a runtime-level overcommit model with observability, inspired by financial risk management practices. In banking, individual and corporate customers are assigned credit limits that often exceed the institution’s total liquidity—assuming not all customers will utilize their full limit simultaneously. Real-time monitoring and risk engines ensure the system stays within safe operating bounds.

Kubernetes could adopt a similar model:

Replace (or complement) static quota enforcement with runtime metrics-aware policies.

Allow overcommit beyond namespace quotas as long as the cluster has available headroom.

Introduce observability hooks or admission plugins that warn, throttle, or deny burst if global limits are at risk.

Benefits:
More efficient resource utilization in shared environments.

Preserves burstable QoS semantics.

Closer alignment with real-world elastic demand patterns.

This model could optionally be opt-in via a new feature gate, scheduler policy, or dynamic admission controller.

Happy to collaborate for a draft KEP if there's interest from the community.

### Why is this needed?

For more efficient resource utilization in shared environments within namespase/project/cluster level budgets/quotas.
issues.title: Proposal: Runtime-Level Overcommit Model for Burstable Workloads Inspired by Financial Systems

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

As In Place Pod Vertical scaling is maturing, there is interest in using this feature for apps or batch workloads.

I can imagine a world where someone wants to change an existing job to lower the cgroups of a workload or scale up. One interest is to rebalance workloads to match their actual utilization. As stated in the in place pod vertical scaling, some apps have high startup resources and then they are able to have their resources scaled down. Most of these workloads do not use pods but higher level objects so it is important to consider how this feature will eventually work with higher level controllers like Jobs, Deployments and StatefulSets. 

Another use case I have heard is the ability to patch/update workloads before they are scheduled. Some use cases I've heard are using an external service to select requests/limits for workloads based on model size or historical data. One implementation idea is to submit a Job in a suspended state and allow the service to patch the Job to reflect the intended state of the resource request and unsuspend with the updated request. This is forbidden today in validation logic so it would be worth considering how to relax this.

For Job, Deployment, and StatefulSet we assume PodTemplates are immutable. In some cases, for Job, we did relax the immutability for scheduling directives but we did not change resource/requests. I was curious how we can start the discussion on how to relax this to further enable In Place Pod Vertical scaling and other use cases where the workloads have not yet been scheduled.

I am opening this up to see how we could tackle this overall.

One possibility is to take this in smaller KEPS:

- [KEP - 1]: Relax immutability of container requests/limits when suspended for Jobs
- [KEP - 2]: In Place Pod Resizing of Job while running.
- [KEP - 3]: In Place Pod Resizing of Deployments
- [KEP - 4]: In Place Pod Resizing of StatefulSets


### Why is this needed?

See above.

issues.body:
Add 'optionalSelf: true' config for consistency with 'optionalOldSelf: true'

Labels:

/kind feature
/sig api-machinery



### why we need it?

This is a feature request to add a new optionalSelf boolean field to the x-kubernetes-validations rule definition.

When set to true, this configuration would change the type of the self variable within the Common Expression Language (CEL) expression to be an "optional". This would mirror the existing optionalOldSelf: true configuration, which does the same for the oldSelf variable.

This addition would provide a consistent and more readable syntax for writing rules that need to check for the presence of fields, especially for rules that must work across both CREATE and UPDATE operations.

### Motivation:

A common validation use case is to prevent a field, once set, from being unset. For example, a user may set an optional field like spec.replicas. Future updates should not be allowed to remove this field from the object.

With the current tooling, this rule is written using the 

```
// Prevent spec.replicas from being unset
'!has(oldSelf.replicas) || has(self.replicas)'

```
This rule correctly implements the logic: "either the old object did not have the field, or the new object must have the field".

This rule needs to define on the parent object, far from the field is defined. 

### Proposal:

Introduce a new boolean configuration field, optionalSelf, to the validation rule definition. When optionalSelf is set to true, the self variable in the CEL expression will be treated as an optional, gaining the same hasValue() and value() helper methods that oldSelf gets via optionalOldSelf: true.

With this change, the rule above could be present on the field itself.
// The proposed, more readable syntax.
// This would require both `optionalOldSelf: true` and the new `optionalSelf: true`.
oldSelf.hasValue()  == self.hasValue()

**Advantages:**

- Improved Readability and Symmetry: The proposed syntax is cleaner and more self-documenting. The parallel structure of oldSelf.hasValue() and self.hasValue() makes the rule's intent immediately obvious.
- Consistency: It provides a single, consistent mechanism for checking field presence on both object states (oldSelf and self), removing the need to mix methods and global functions.



**Example Use Case**
Consider a CRD where the replicas field is optional but should be immutable in its presence after being set.

Current Implementation:

```yaml
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: mycrds.example.com
spec:
  # ...
  versions:
  - name: v1
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          spec:
            type: object
            x-kubernetes-validations:
            - rule: "!has(oldSelf.replicas) || has(self.replicas)"
               message: "replicas can't be unset"
            properties:
              replicas:
                type: integer
                format: int32

```

Proposed Implementation with optionalSelf:

```yaml
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: mycrds.example.com
spec:
  # ...
  versions:
  - name: v1
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          spec:
            type: object
            properties:
              replicas:
                type: integer
                format: int32
                 x-kubernetes-validations:
                 - rule: "!oldSelf.hasValue()  || oldSelf.hasValue()  == self.hasValue()"
                   message: ".spec.replicas cannot be unset once it has been set."
                  optionalOldSelf: true
                  optionalSelf: true
```
issues.title: CEL Validation: Add 'optionalSelf: true' config for consistency with 'optionalOldSelf: true'

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Enable support for the `objectSelector` field in `ValidatingWebhookConfiguration` for webhooks that handle `CONNECT` operations, such as `pods/exec`. This would allow webhook invocations to be filtered based on pod labels, similar to how `objectSelector` works for `CREATE` and other operations.

### Why is this needed?

We are currently using a `ValidatingAdmissionWebhook` to intercept `CONNECT` operations (e.g., `pods/exec`) across the entire cluster. However, this broad scope is inefficient and introduces unnecessary overhead. We want to scope the webhook to only target specific pods based on labels, reducing impact and avoiding unintended side effects in case the webhook pods are down. 

**For example, if the webhook pods are unavailable, all `pods/exec` operations throughout the cluster are blocked; effectively making the entire cluster inaccessible for interactive debugging or remote command execution.**

While the `objectSelector` field works as expected for `CREATE` operations, it appears to be unsupported or non-functional for `CONNECT` operations. For example, using the following configuration causes the webhook not to trigger at all, even for matching pods:

```yaml
objectSelector:
  matchLabels:
    controller.devfile.io/creator: "foo"
```

It is currently documented that resources that cannot have labels are not supported for matching https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/extensible-admission-controllers/#matching-requests-objectselector

This issue has been previously discussed in:
- #91732 – originally raised but closed due to inactivity
- #132287 – related discussion on webhook filtering limitations, where I got feedback to use `namespaceSelector`

Actually, `namespaceSelector` does not help in our scenario, as our workloads often share namespaces. We require pod-level granularity, which only objectSelector can provide.

Supporting `objectSelector` for CONNECT operations would bring consistency to webhook behavior and allow for more precise and efficient admission control logic.

If there is an alternative way to achieve this targeted behavior, we would appreciate any guidance.

### What would you like to be added?

The CronJob status lastScheduleTime and lastSuccessfulTime timestamps would be a useful addition to the Downward API, i.e. being allowed as env > valueFrom > fieldRef > fieldPath and related options.

Example:

```
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: {{ .name }}
spec:
  schedule: {{ .schedule }}
  timeZone: {{ $.Values.cronJobs.timeZone }}
  concurrencyPolicy: Replace
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      parallelism: 1
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: Never
          containers:
            - name: example
              image: ...
              env:
                - name: LAST_SCHEDULE_TIME
                  valueFrom:
                    fieldRef:
                      fieldPath: status.lastScheduleTime
status:
  lastScheduleTime: '2025-06-30T00:00:00Z'
  lastSuccessfulTime: '2025-06-30T00:01:14Z'
```

Note that there is a scenario where one or both is unset. In this case, the environment variable would need to be unset or empty.

### Why is this needed?

Cronjobs can use the timestamp for various purposes. For example, a job that scans a database every night can filter by some timestamp > LAST_SCHEDULE_TIME to get only rows that were changed since the last run.

Right now, this is possible by hardcoding (or having an environment variable for) the schedule interval into the app and calculating the schedule time. But this does not take potential startup delays for both the current and previous job.
Alternatively, the job can store its previous schedule or completion time in some form of database (e.g. key value store). But this requires a database to exist and the maintenance overhead that entails.
issues.title: Expose status.lastScheduleTime and status.lastSuccessfulTime to Downward API

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

When the API server calls multiple validating webhooks, it should surface all errors to the client, not just the first error returned by a webhook.

The validating webhook dispatcher was implemented in [#58381](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/58381). It calls multiple webhooks in parallel. When more than one webhook returns an error, the dispatcher only surfaces the first error to the API client. It [logs](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24877f96fbb60f34c1c808e7ac76870019eee86b/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/webhook/validating/dispatcher.go#L242) the remaining errors.

The original commit included a [TODO](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24877f96fbb60f34c1c808e7ac76870019eee86b/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/webhook/validating/dispatcher.go#L241) to merge the errors, presumably because all errors should be surfaced to the API client.


### Why is this needed?

As a user of a resource that associated with more than one validating webhook, I know that all these webhooks are called in parallel when I try to create the resource. If more than one webhook rejects my create request, I want to know the reasons behind all of the rejections. That is, I the API server to surface the errors returned by all the webhooks.
issues.title: When the API server calls multiple validating webhooks, it should surface all errors to the client, not just the first error returned by a webhook

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Add sharding to the List and Watch API options. Specifically, add 2 fields: `Shard int` and `TotalShards int` to the `ListOptions`.

When determining if an object should be sent via list we can apply the following logic:

```go
func shouldSend(o metav1.Object, shard, totalShards int) bool {
        if totalShards == 0 {
		return true
        }
	h := fnv.New64a()
	h.Write([]byte(o.GetUID())) // could optionally do name+namespace so the same object (if deleted) goes to same controller
	return jump.Hash(h.Sum64(), totalShards) == shard
}
```

### Why is this needed?

Issue #109667 explored this issue briefly, but with a perspective of reducing latency. I'd argue that this is more needed to allow controllers to implement HA, scalability, and avoid OOM's.

KSM has sharding features, but still requires listing out all of the objects, consuming network and memory. Other recommended sharding options here focus on splitting by namespace, or resource type which is cumbersome and error prone.

Otel Collectors/prometheus allow for sharding, but again need to perform full Lists to determine sharding in memory, consuming unnecessary resources, and leading to potential OOM's in large clusters.

Instead of having every controller implement a half-baked sharding solution that still requires a full List, we should push sharding into the API Server.
issues.title: Add Sharding to List/Watch API

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Given that [IPVS is not maintained](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/132689#issuecomment-3031585314), we would like to support stable hashing (like maglev) in kube-proxy - which IPVS currently supports.

### Why is this needed?

This is primarily to support non-cloud load balancers - which is useful for bare metal k8s, or on providers that allow for BGP peering (e.g. Vultr). Though nftables will support routing (some kind of hash?) IP packets between pods that back a service of type LoadBalancer currently, it is required that stateful connections (like TCP) have the same connection end up on the same pod.

While any 3-tuple or 5-tuple hash would allow TCP connections to be routed to the same pod (IPs, ports & protocol) - stable hashing minimizes how many connections would be disrupted when the number of backing pods changes.

This [blog post](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2025/02/28/nftables-kube-proxy/#future-plans) mentions that IPVS's schedulers (responsible for choosing which backend to send to) were really not that useful - since they do not synchronize their decisions (thus breaking the requirement that a TCP connection ends up on the same pod reliably). My understanding though is this is not true for algorithms that are only based on the set of backends (some hash of it), rather than measurements (e.g. latency or conneciton about them). Maglev additionally has the benefit of minimizing the number of connection disruptions.
issues.title: Support stable hashing (e.g. Maglev) in a post-IPVS world

/kind feature
/kind cleanup
/sig auth

Previously since >= 1.29, we have promoted the feature gate `KMSv2KDF` to GA and currently the KDF enablement is locked to true via:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/05a596033cbe507053d6de79b8066c7f16076080/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/encryptionconfig/config.go#L128-L130

With the KDF feature on, the cardinality of the cache for holding DEK seeds should be low and stable (unless the kube-apiserver keeps re-generating DEK seeds in pathological cases), so far most of the clusters we have seen have lower than 50 DEK seeds in the cache even though the cluster has been running for many years. 

Hence, we can consider replace the current expiring cache implementation with **non-expiring LRU cache** (e.g. with 1024 size) so that we don't need to rotate the cache on a day basis --- this helps improving the cluster's resilience to KMS service failures, say the KMS service is down for 5 minutes and if the cluster happens to rotate the cache during the time, it will result in unavailability drop unnecessarily.


Additionally, we can also consider pruning all the occurrences of `useSeed` checks from KMSv2 provider as it's no longer used.
issues.title: [KMSv2] Replace DEK seed cache with non-expiring LRU cache

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Prometheus protocol expects that metric values are fetched ad-hoc. It fetches the metric from endpoint and assign timestamp based on scape time. However there are cases where calculating metric is very expensive.

Apiserver has multiple such metrics, where getting metric value would require processing large amount of data and even fetching data from etcd. In such cases the metric is calculated periodically and cached for prometheus to scape. This however means that metric values are stale. Example metrics:
* [apiserver_storage_objects](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b1b15a57e68338099daa4b934b6235db4c429a66/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/metrics/metrics.go#L70-L77)
* [storage_db_total_size_in_bytes](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b1b15a57e68338099daa4b934b6235db4c429a66/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/metrics/metrics.go#L78-L87)
...


Even if we agree that such metrics don't need to be fresh, serving metric based on cached values creates a problem, how to represent cache being stale. What if the periodic calculation has not succeeded for 10 minutes? We cannot just expose the same value. Example solution used by [apiserver_storage_objects](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b1b15a57e68338099daa4b934b6235db4c429a66/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/metrics/metrics.go#L70-L77) is to set metric value to -1. This however causes issues with aggregation. Other solution would be to remove the metric, however this would result in metric totally disappearing causing user confusion.

Proper solution would be to acknowledge that metric is not calculated ad-hoc, but was calculated some time ago. That way if the cache is stale, old metric value will be still exposed, but will stop calculations and breaking aggregations. This should be achievable by using https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/prometheus/client_golang/prometheus#NewMetricWithTimestamp

/sig instrumentation
/cc @richabanker @jpbetz 

### Why is this needed?

Fixes freshness and aggregation of metric calculated based on cache.
issues.title: Expose timestamp for metric based on cached value

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?


I propose adding explicit RBAC rules to the built-in `ClusterRole/admin` to grant access (e.g., get, list, watch, create, update, patch, delete) to `HTTPRoute` resources in the `gateway.networking.k8s.io` API group. This would align the `admin` role with the evolving standard for networking in Kubernetes, as Gateway API is positioned as the successor to the deprecated Ingress API.

Proposed addition to the `admin` ClusterRole (simplified YAML for illustration):

```yaml
- apiGroups: ["gateway.networking.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["httproutes"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]
```

This change would only apply when the Gateway API CRDs are installed, maintaining the deny-by-default principle.

### Why is this needed?

Due to the growing popularity of Cilium's Gateway API implementation, `HTTPRoute` resources are increasingly used for advanced routing (e.g., vs. simpler NodePort services), making them a common requirement in modern clusters.

- **Current Behavior**: The `admin` ClusterRole provides broad permissions for core resources and legacy networking (e.g., `networking.k8s.io/ingresses`), but it does not include access to Gateway API resources like `HTTPRoute`. Users with `admin` bound to a namespace (via RoleBinding) cannot manage `HTTPRoute` without custom RBAC, even though `admin` is intended for namespace-level administration.
  
- **Rationale**:
  - Gateway API is maturing rapidly (e.g., v1.0 stable release in 2023) and is recommended as the future of Kubernetes ingress/egress routing. It's supported by major implementations like Istio, Contour, Envoy Gateway, and Cilium.
  - Many users expect the `admin` role to cover common networking tasks within a namespace, similar to how it handles `Ingress` or `NetworkPolicy`. Without this, cluster operators must create and maintain custom Roles/RoleBindings for every namespace, increasing administrative overhead.
  - Tools like FluxCD use the `admin` ClusterRole for restricted users/service accounts (e.g., in GitOps workflows), so including `HTTPRoute` access would enable seamless management of Gateway API resources without elevating privileges or adding custom RBAC.
  - This aligns with Kubernetes' goal of improving usability for standard extensions. As Ingress is deprecated (per Kubernetes docs), updating `admin` would ease the transition to Gateway API.
  - Security: This wouldn't grant cluster-wide access (since `admin` is typically namespace-bound), and it follows least-privilege by targeting only `HTTPRoute` (not all Gateway API resources).
issues.title: RBAC Permissions for HTTPRoute to Built-in admin ClusterRole

### What would you like to be added?

This is a feature request followup for the #131085 PR.

Our use case is to use labels selector annotation in lbaas service to include only specific nodes as members of the service (see https://github.com/kubernetes/cloud-provider-openstack/pull/2601 for implementation details).

E.g. `loadbalancer.openstack.org/node-selector=env=production,az=az1` should configure loadbalancer pool members to use only nodes that have `env=production` and `az=az1` labels.

Unfortunately modifying the node labels doesn't trigger the `EnsureLoadBalancer` cloud controller method, and the only solution is to modify the service spec to add some noop data.

The idea is to modify the `shouldSyncUpdatedNode` cloud-controller func to return true on nodes' labels update:

https://github.com/kubernetes/cloud-provider/blob/ae76f69e43a855438aab6bf3e0ddc3df197b35dd/controllers/service/controller.go#L693-L711

Proposed patch:
```diff
diff --git a/controllers/service/controller.go b/controllers/service/controller.go
index 97764cb..0505303 100644
--- a/controllers/service/controller.go
+++ b/controllers/service/controller.go
@@ -26,6 +26,7 @@ import (
        "time"
 
        v1 "k8s.io/api/core/v1"
+       apiequality "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/equality"
        apierrors "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/errors"
        "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/labels"
        "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/runtime"
@@ -706,6 +707,10 @@ func shouldSyncUpdatedNode(oldNode, newNode *v1.Node) bool {
        if oldNode.Spec.ProviderID != newNode.Spec.ProviderID {
                return true
        }
+       // Check if nodes' labels have changed
+       if !apiequality.Semantic.DeepEqual(oldNode.Labels, newNode.Labels) {
+               return true
+       }
 
        return false
 }
```

This is the last week to prepare for the code freeze. I hope we can introduce this feature into 1.34.

cc @elmiko @bowei @cheftako @JoelSpeed 

### Why is this needed?

This feature enables segregation of Kubernetes worker nodes for services with `externalTrafficPolicy=Local`, excluding unused nodes from load balancer pool members and health checks, and reconciling the corresponding service whenever node labels change.

A deeper issue lies in the way F5 (used by OpenStack Octavia LBaaS) handles pool member health: it marks new members as healthy immediately upon addition to the pool, causing traffic to be forwarded to nodes that are not yet ready. By using node selectors, we can prevent new nodes from being added as pool members until they have actual workloads. Moreover, updating the load balancer when node labels change can be beneficial in other scenarios as well.
issues.title: [cloud-provider]: call "EnsureLoadBalancer" method on nodes' labels update

issues.body:
/sig security
Recently, while testing the performance of the VPA multi-instance scenario, I observed an issue: as the number of VAP(Validating Admission Policy) bindings increases, the latency for API authentication resources continues to rise, and the CPU usage of the API server grows significantly. Below are the detailed metrics:

| Binding Number | Param Number | Delay |  average CPU usage    |  QPS  |
|---------|------|-----|------------|-------|
| 1 | 64 | 315.94ms | 400%  |  151.60 |
| 1 | 256  | 1138.06ms  | 400%  | 44.30 |
|1 | 1024  | 4403.71ms  | 400%   | 11.50|
| 64 |  None | 348.32ms | 400% | 145.80 |
| 256 | None | 1205.66ms  | 400% |41.37
| 1024 | None | 4737.46ms   | 400%  |10.19 |
| 10 | None | 35.42ms | >360% | 492.10 |

The test environment is a 4-core, 8GB cloud server, and the Kind cluster is configured as follows:
```
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
nodes:
- role: control-plane
  image: kindest/node:v1.32.5
  extraPortMappings:
  - containerPort: 6443
    hostPort: 6443
    protocol: TCP
  kubeadmConfigPatches:
  - |
    kind: ClusterConfiguration
    apiServer:
      extraArgs:
        profiling: "true"
- role: worker
  image: kindest/node:v1.32.5
```
In my opinion, this level of performance is insufficient for certain large-scale production environments. Excessively high CPU usage can cause the API server to become unresponsive or even crash and restart, while high latency further impacts the API server's ability to serve other components effectively. To investigate why VAPBindings lead to high CPU consumption and increased latency, I conducted a performance analysis of the API server.

By analyzing the pprof results, I found that the performance bottleneck is the 
```
requestVal, err := convertObjectToUnstructured(request)
```
statement within the `newActivation` function, which is defined in the file `staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/cel/activation.go`.

```
+---------------------+
| (c *dispatcher)     |
| Dispatch()          |
+----------+----------+
           |
           v
+---------------------+
| (v *validator)      |
| Validate()          |
+----------+----------+
           |
           v
+---------------------+
| (c *condition)      |
| ForInput()          |
+----------+----------+
           |
           v
+---------------------+
| cel.newActivation() |
+---------------------+
```

Through investigating the call chain of this function, I found that the root cause of the performance degradation actually lies in the loop within the following function:
```
func (c *dispatcher) Dispatch(ctx context.Context, a admission.Attributes, o admission.ObjectInterfaces, hooks []PolicyHook) error
```
Specifically, the performance bottleneck stems from the iterative processing of vapbinding objects and policy parameters inside this method. As the number of vapbinding instances increases, the loop's execution time grows significantly, leading to higher latency and increased CPU consumption.

To concisely describe this issue, I've omitted irrelevant code and included only the core portion directly related to the problem:

```go
for _, binding := range hook.Bindings {

	// ignore....

	params, err := generic.CollectParams(
		hook.Policy.Spec.ParamKind,
		hook.ParamInformer,
		hook.ParamScope,
		binding.Spec.ParamRef,
		a.GetNamespace(),
	)
	// ignore....

	for _, param := range params {
		var p runtime.Object = param
		// ignore....
		validationResults = append(validationResults,
			hook.Evaluator.Validate(
				ctx,
				matchResource,
				versionedAttr,
				p,
				namespace,
				celconfig.RuntimeCELCostBudget,
				authz,
			),
		)
	}
}
```

From this code, we can observe that for every incoming request, the API server iterates through all VPA bindings associated with the policy, retrieves the corresponding parameters via each binding, and then performs the admission check. This repeated iteration becomes increasingly expensive as the number of VPA bindings grows, leading to higher latency and CPU usage.

```
[In dispatcher.Dispatch function]
 |
 +-> Loop over each 'ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding'
 |   |
 |   +-> Loop over each 'policy parameter'
 |   |   |
 |   |   v
 |   |   hook.Evaluator.Validate
 |   |           |
 |   |           v
 |   |   +-----> v.validationFilter.ForInput
 |   |   |
 |   |   +-----> v.messageFilter.ForInput
 |   |   |
 |   |   +-----> v.auditAnnotationFilter.ForInput
 |   |           |
 |   |           v
 |   |   activation, err := newActivation(...)
 |   |           |
 |   |           v
 |   |   requestVal, err := convertObjectToUnstructured(request)
 |   |
 |   <-- (End of policy parameter loop)
 |
 <-- (End of VAPBinding loop)
```

Back to the original statement where the performance bottleneck occurs:
```
requestVal, err := convertObjectToUnstructured(request)
```
By analyzing the source of the request, we can observe that the request object remains unchanged throughout both the outer loop over vapBindings and the inner loop over params. This means that the same request context is being repeatedly processed in redundant iterations without any modification.

```
versionedAttr --+
                |--> cel.CreateAdmissionRequest() --> request
matchResource --+
```

This immutability of the request presents a clear opportunity for optimization — we can avoid unnecessary reprocessing by caching or pre-evaluating request-specific data, or by restructuring the loops to minimize redundant checks. For example, moving invariant computations outside the loops or using early exit conditions could significantly reduce CPU overhead and improve overall performance.

## Profile result

[profile-256-binding-none-params.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/21598461/profile-256-binding-none-params.pdf)
[profile-1024-bindding-none-params.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/21598460/profile-1024-bindding-none-params.pdf)
[profile-one-binding-with-64-params.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/21598459/profile-one-binding-with-64-params.pdf)
issues.title: Exploration and Recommendations on Kubernetes Validating Admission Policy Performance Optimization

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Hi,

I'm starting this as a thought on how Topology Spread should work when it is already failing (having skew above max): I think the answer is it should consider scheduling any single pod that doesn't make situation worse, and preferably improves the skew even if it doesn't meet the max skew requirement, instead of a direct no (current behavior). Do let me know if this is already discussed as alternative to [#3990](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/3990). I think this can be an easier and coherent approach that doesn't break what's already working, and to leave space for other components to improve stuff other than skew.

Given that this is different from existing behavior never-the-less, it might be a good idea to add a toggle (e.g., whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotScheduleWorse/ScheduleImprovements/ScheduleNoWorse)

/sig scheduling

### Why is this needed?

Given situation below as a 3 zone spread with max skew of 1, for simplicity sake, each pod schedules on a separate node (with minDomains 3 configured):

zone 1: 3 pods
zone 2: 3 pods
zone 3: 3->0 pods caused by zone failure
3 pending pods due to zone 3 failure

How this proposal helps:

1. No pending pods will be scheduled to zone 1 or zone 2, since a single schedule will make skew worse (3 -> 4).
2. When zone 3 recovers, this proposal is coherent on bringing new nodes back gradually, as scheduling any of the pending pods improves the skew (3 -> 2), which is a lower requirement than considering scheduling 2 pods at once, makes the skew under max, and eventually can recover.
3. If zone 2 encounters additional 1 node failure, this proposal helps bringing a new node into zone 2 (potentially through cluster-autoscaler), which improves replica count and doesn't make skew worse (3 -> 3).

Overall it makes this approach still somewhat rigor and limiting on maintaining the spread (not falling back to ScheduleAnyway), but helpful during and post zonal outage without human intervention.

Do let me know if any counter-examples.
issues.title: Topology Spread should greedily allow scheduling to a node that doesn't make a bad skew worse

It's becoming increasingly common to add new feature gates for extensions on features that still have a feature gate. Today we handle this in an ad-hoc way, where we sometimes check both feature gates (the one directly controlling the new extension, and the one for the original feature), but in lots of cases we just check the direct feature gate.

Rather than checking multiple feature gates wherever the extension feature is used, I propose:
1. Codify inter-FeatureGate dependencies, so if feature B depends on feature A, we make this explicit in the feature gate spec, and validate it on startup
    - Only allow a feature to be enabled if all it's dependent features are also enabled. Enforced in [`featureGate.Validate`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9da4b7ecfb60ea484f8e6c89c42e63506571bc68/staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/featuregate/feature_gate.go#L304).
    - Only allow a feature to graduate, if all it's dependent features are at least the same level of maturity. In other words, if feature A is beta, feature B can graduate to beta, but it cannot graduate to GA. (What does this mean for deprecation?). Enforced in unit test.
3. Wherever we need to check if feature B is enabled, we only check feature B, and rely on the validation to ensure that feature A is also enabled.

For an example, the new `InPlacePodLevelResourcesVerticalScaling` (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132919) depends on _both_ `InPlacePodVerticalScaling` and `PodLevelResources`.

/kind feature
/sig architecture
/cc @JoelSpeed @liggitt @jpbetz @siyuanfoundation
issues.title: Codify inter-FeatureGate dependencies

### What would you like to be added?

Introduce a way to disable automatic allocation of healthCheckNodePort for LoadBalancer services when externalTrafficPolicy: Local is set, particularly for on-premises environments where external load balancers do not rely on this port.

### Why is this needed?

In on-premises Kubernetes/OpenShift clusters using MetalLB with BGP and external load balancers (e.g., F5), the healthCheckNodePort is not used. However, Kubernetes still allocates and exposes this port when externalTrafficPolicy: Local is set.

**This leads to:**

Unnecessary open ports on nodes.
Potential security concerns.
Port exhaustion risks in large-scale clusters.
Operational confusion for administrators.
There is currently no native way to disable this behavior while preserving externalTrafficPolicy: Local, which is often required for source IP preservation.

**Proposed Solution**
Introduce an opt-out mechanism for healthCheckNodePort allocation, such as:

**Option 1: Annotation-based opt-out**

metadata:
  annotations:
    service.kubernetes.io/disable-healthcheck-nodeport: "true"

**Option 2: API field**

spec:
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local
  disableHealthCheckNodePort: true

**Risks and Mitigations**
Misconfiguration could lead to traffic being sent to unhealthy nodes if the external load balancer is not properly configured.
Clear documentation and validation should accompany the feature to ensure safe usage.
**Additional Context**
This enhancement would benefit on-premises setups where:

MetalLB is used with BGP.
External load balancers perform their own health checks.
healthCheckNodePort is not required and adds unnecessary complexity.
issues.title: Make healthCheckNodePort Optional for On-Premises LoadBalancer Services with externalTrafficPolicy: Local

When implementing the KEP and the corresponding code, we referred to a specification for .env files that is not widely recognized as authoritative. 
Current syntax: https://smartmob-rfc.readthedocs.io/en/latest/2-dotenv.html#formal-specification
  
Moreover, the scope of this specification is quite simplistic and does not appear to cover all use cases.

For example, we have the following user scenarios:
1. Users need to define a PEM-formatted private key as the value of an environment variable. This requires support for multi-line values (since the PEM format requires at least three lines: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privacy-Enhanced_Mail, and no extraneous characters should be inserted into the multi-line values. This necessitates the ability to insert multi-line values losslessly.
2. In a multi-container pod, multiple containers need to use the same environment variable defined by an initContainer, but each container needs to substitute the value based on its own variables. This requires the ability to interpolate environment variables.

Therefore, we propose to extend and modify the current envFile format:
1. Multi-line values containing line breaks can be enclosed in double quotes. Parsing should not terminate until the second corresponding double quote is encountered.
Example:
    ```
      PRIVATE_KEY="-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
      ...
      -----END DSA PRIVATE KEY-----"
    ```
2. During parsing, environment variables should support interpolation.
Example:
    ```
    DATABASE_URL="mysql://${USER}@localhost/my_database"
    container1: USER=user1 -> mysql://user1@localhost/my_database
    container1: USER=user2 -> mysql://user2@localhost/my_database
    ```

I believe the first point is a necessary addition, and the current method of introducing multi-line values (where a line ending with a backslash "" indicates the value continues on the next line, and implementations must concatenate lines without line endings, treating the backslash as a single space) should be deprecated.

The second point is an improvement feature request. We can choose to implement it, or remind users to define multiple similar environment variables as a workaround.
issues.title: [FG: EnvFiles] Proposal for env file syntax extension and improvement

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Enhance ValidatingAdmissionPolicy to enable validation of incoming requests against on-cluster resources. This feature would allow CEL expressions in ValidatingAdmissionPolicy to reference and evaluate the state or existence of other Kubernetes resources (e.g., ConfigMaps, Secrets, other CRs) during admission, enabling richer policy enforcement that reflects the real state of the cluster.

Currently, ValidatingAdmissionPolicy only allows validation based on the incoming object, its previous state (for updates), and an optional Param resource. Adding support for referencing arbitrary on-cluster resources would provide parity with what is possible in custom validating admission webhooks, but in a declarative and auditable fashion.

Potential approaches could include limiting which resources may be referenced, restricting the scope (namespace/global), or caching reads for performance and security. The design will need to address concerns around API server performance, consistency, and security boundaries.

### Why is this needed?

Many advanced policy use cases require validating an incoming resource based on the state of other objects in the cluster. For example:
- Ensuring a Deployment only references existing and approved ConfigMaps/Secrets
- Enforcing uniqueness or quotas based on other resource counts
- Cross-resource consistency (e.g., only allow creating a Pod if a related custom resource exists)

Currently, these use cases require a validating admission webhook, which adds operational complexity and reduces transparency. Enabling first-class support for cross-resource lookups in ValidatingAdmissionPolicy would make Kubernetes policy management more powerful, easier to audit, and more accessible to cluster operators.

This enhancement would benefit security, compliance, and operational use cases by bringing more workload policy scenarios into the core API machinery, reducing the need for custom webhook code and infrastructure.

### Proposal

An independent controller with declarative configuration, allowing users to specify which on-cluster resources to sync or cache. The controller aggregates this data into a CR, which can then be referenced through `paramRef`.
issues.title: Enhance ValidatingAdmissionPolicy to support cross-resource validation

**What happened:**

When modifying only metadata (labels or annotations) in a StatefulSet's pod template spec, the StatefulSet controller unnecessarily recreates all pods, causing service disruption for workloads that are otherwise healthy and functioning correctly.

**What you expected to happen:**

Changes to pod metadata (labels/annotations) in the StatefulSet template should be applied directly to existing pods without recreation, similar to how kubectl can directly modify pod labels/annotations without restart.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):**

1. Create a StatefulSet with 3 replicas:
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: test-sts
spec:
  replicas: 3
  serviceName: test-svc
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: test
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: test
        version: v1
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.20
```

2. Wait for all pods to be Running
3. Update only the metadata in the template:
```bash
kubectl patch statefulset test-sts -p '{"spec":{"template":{"metadata":{"labels":{"version":"v2"}}}}}'
```

4. This triggers the StatefulSet controller to recreate pods one by one due to template hash change

**Anything else we need to know?:**

This is the documented behavior of StatefulSets where any template change triggers a rolling update based on template hash comparison. However, this creates operational challenges:
- Production workloads suffer unnecessary downtime when adding operational labels (monitoring, alerting, compliance tags)
- The same metadata changes can be applied directly to pods using `kubectl label` or `kubectl annotate` without restart
- This creates inconsistent behavior where direct pod updates work fine but template updates cause recreation
- Forces operators to choose between:
  - Accept downtime for metadata changes
  - Use direct pod modification (which gets overwritten on future updates)
  - Use external operators/controllers to manage pod metadata, which is actually an anti-pattern to have more than one controller manage the pods.

**Additional Context:**

This enhancement would:
1. Reduce operational overhead when managing StatefulSet metadata
2. Improve availability for stateful services
3. Align StatefulSet behavior with the principle that metadata-only changes shouldn't require pod recreation
4. Provide consistency with how direct pod label/annotation modifications work

**Question for Maintainers:**
Is restarting pods for metadata-only changes a conscious design decision? If so, what's the reasoning behind it - implementation simplicity, consistency guarantees, or specific technical concerns?

/kind feature
/sig apps
/area statefulset
/priority normal
issues.title: In-Place Updates for StatefulSet

### What would you like to be added?

The suggestion is to add a `lastFailureTime` to mimics the `lastSuccessfulTime`, that is updated when a job has the JobFailure condition.

#### Alternative

An alternative would be to have Conditions for the CronJob that gives more information on the last job result, and for which generation the job was created, but this seems like a bigger refactor.

### Why is this needed?

It is currently hard to know if a CronJob last execution was successful or a failure. We can usually check for `if status.lastSuccessfulTime < status.lastScheduledTime`, then assume it is a failure, but as soon as a new Job is scheduled, we lose the information to know if the last one failed or not.
issues.title: CronJob status should keep track of lastFailureTime

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

An extra new mode for `imagePullPolicy` named  `IfNewerNotPresent` that pulls image if image ID (ref/digest) on remote is not matching.

### Why is this needed?

This gives a solution to issues such as:

- Pods that are running with an image for example v1.0.0 and a backport fix - update is released, on that image v1.0.0, without changing the tag. 
Currently, the pod will continue run with the non-backported image (that may be faulty) even if imagePullPolicy is set to IfNotPresent. IfNotPresent doesnt check the integrity of the image if pod is restarted and keeps using the older (non-backported) image. 
With this feature you can have a combination of the functionality of IfNotPresent and Integrity check that pulls image if changed in the remote registry.

A prototype - working code: 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/133677
issues.title: Add new imagePullPolicy mode IfNewerNotPresent, that pulls image if image ID (ref/digest) on remote is not matching.

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Below is what happens when there are more than one device class for an extended resource. For Alpha, we just picked one random device class. We should implement what KEP says for Beta.

https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-scheduling/5004-dra-extended-resource#device-class-api

The same extended resource name should be given to at most one device class. If there are more than one device classes, the one created later is picked at scheduling time, if two are created at the same time, the name lexicographically sorted first is picked.

### Why is this needed?

it provides more predicatable device class for an extended resource, hence better UX
issues.title: Pick predicatable device class when multiple device classes use the same extended resource name

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

The scheduler should generate an OTEL trace for a single scheduling attempt of a pod.

### Why is this needed?

We've observed slow scheduling attempts for pods which can be cumbersome to investigate with multiple scheduling plugins enabled. It would be very useful to have a trace for a single pod scheduling attempt. The trace context could also be propagated to custom scheduler plugins. 

One benefit of this over the existing log-based `utiltrace` is downstream clients that have already instrumented OTEL tracing (ie. http clients) could now be visualised in the context of a scheduling attempt.

The existing `utiltrace` is quite useful, but is k8s specific. Given [other k8s components](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/cluster-administration/system-traces/#component-traces) standardising around OTEL traces, feels appropriate for the scheduler to as well.
issues.title: Add support for tracing in scheduler

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Thanks to @serathius, kube-apiserver now supports the streaming Protobuf list encoder (see PR [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/129407)). However, it currently uses the SimpleAllocator as the default memory allocator, which allocates a new byte slice on every encoding operation for every single item in list Objects. Under high-concurrency list request workloads, this results in a significant number of short-lived heap objects, increasing garbage collection (GC) pressure and potentially leading to out-of-memory (OOM) conditions.

We propose switching the default memory allocator for Protobuf serialization encoder to [runtime.AllocatorPool](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ddd8e70b1e04ade755f3a37e008ff057ca2f1197/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/allocator.go#L35) This change would significantly reduce memory allocation overhead and alleviate GC pressure, especially in streaming list scenarios. 

### Why is this needed?

reduce memory allocation overhead and alleviate GC pressure for apiserver
issues.title: use `AllocatorPool` to reduce memory allocation in protobuf stream list

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

GetPodFromTemplate currently drops any ownerReferences specified in the pod template:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f28b4c9efbca5c5c0af716d9f2d5702667ee8a45/pkg/controller/controller_utils.go#L575-L582

This means that workload authors do not have a generic way to establish belongs-to relationships between the eventual pods and other objects.

### Why is this needed?

Controllers / schedulers can require visibility to connections from higher-level ancestor objects grouping sets of related pods.

There are implications to propagating owner references we would need to think through and derisk:
* if controllerRef is nil and all template.OwnerReferences are missing, new pods would get GCed immediately
* if controllerRef is non-nil, and template.OwnerReferences has a `isController:true`, pod creation would fail validation
* if controllerRef is non-nil and the controller was counting on generic GC to clean up pods, it would now wait until all template.OwnerReferences are gone too

/sig api-machinery
/sig apps
cc @erictune
issues.title: Consider having controllers propagate OwnerReferences from pod specs → pods

We moved all interfaces, types etc from k/k to the staging repo. 
The next discussion is whether we want to move our in-tree plugins to the staging repo. 
Some external components (such as descheduler, the cluster autoscaler, Kueue etc) run the scheduling simulation today, but, for example, descheduler implements the scheduling logic on their own. 
If we can publish in-tree plugins in the staging repo and make them easier to be imported, such components may want to use in-tree plugins to run their scheduling simulation. But, we, of course, first check if this motivation is big enough before starting this initiative.

On the technical side, as summarized in [this comment of mine](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/89930#issuecomment-2566236328), plugins still have some dependencies to k/k (e.g., feature flag package). We need to think about how we remove those dependencies to make in-tree plugins able to be moved outside.

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

I'd like to be able to configure the kubelet to permit pods with specific interface-scoped sysctls on arbitrary interfaces. This would require changing `allowUnsafeSysctls` to support pattern matching within the middle of an entry.

Here's an example of a sysctl that I'd like to set on a pod:
```yaml
sysctls:
  - name: net.ipv4.conf.interface-1.send_redirects
    value: "0"
```

I'd like to do something similar on another pod that is attached to another network with a different interface name:
```yaml
sysctls:
  - name: net.ipv4.conf.interface-2.send_redirects
    value: "0"
```

If I want to configure the kubelet to allow for this today, I have two options. One is inflexible, and the other is way too broadly scoped:
```yaml
# List every interface that I might possibly want
allowUnsafeSysctls:
  - net.ipv4.conf.interface-1.send_redirects
  - net.ipv4.conf.interface-2.send_redirects
  # ...
  - net.ipv4.conf.interface-1000.send_redirects
```

```yaml
# Allow _all_ net.ipv4 sysctls
allowUnsafeSysctls:
  - net.ipv4.*
```

Really what I want to be able to do is this:
```yaml
# Allow just my desired sysctl, but on all interfaces
allowUnsafeSysctls:
  - net.ipv4.conf.*.send_redirects
```


### Why is this needed?

The current options are either too rigid or too broadly scoped.
issues.title: Add kubelet support for allowing specific interface-scoped sysctls on all interfaces

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

This proposal includes two related changes to improve egress traffic visibility from core Kubernetes components and to refine logging controls:

Add Verbose Logging to staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/net/http.go: Introduce new klog V-level logs to provide visibility into outbound HTTP requests and how they are handled by proxy settings.

A V(5) log will be added to record requests that are proxied (i.e., not matching the NO_PROXY environment variable). This helps identify traffic that would be blocked in a restricted environment.

A V(6) log will be added to record requests that are not proxied (i.e., explicitly allowed via NO_PROXY). This helps verify that allowlist rules are functioning as expected.

Rename pkg/probe/http/http.go to pkg/probe/http/http_prober.go: Rename this file to prevent a logging conflict with the file mentioned above, which is the actual target for our enhanced logging.

### Why is this needed?

Downstream distributions of Kubernetes, such as GKE, are implementing security features to strictly control and block all egress traffic originating from the kube-apiserver. A core part of this mechanism involves using HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY environment variables to route traffic through a controlled gateway or a "blackhole" proxy, while using a NO_PROXY variable to allowlist essential cluster endpoints.

To safely roll out such a feature, it is critical to have a data-driven way to discover and audit all outbound requests made by the kube-apiserver and other components. This allows operators to build a comprehensive NO_PROXY allowlist and ensure no critical functions are broken. The proposed verbose logging in net/http.go provides this essential visibility.

The second change—renaming pkg/probe/http/http.go—is necessary to avoid unintended log spam. The klog output strips the full file path, so both staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/net/http.go (our target) and pkg/probe/http/http.go (an unrelated file) show up in logs simply as http.go.

As a result, setting --vmodule=http*=5 to enable our new logs also enables verbose logging in the probe helpers, flooding the logs with messages from liveness and readiness probes. This makes it extremely difficult to isolate the critical egress traffic data needed for validation. Renaming the probe helper file to http_prober.go cleanly resolves this name collision and allows for precise, targeted logging for this important security use case.
issues.title: Add Verbose Logging to net/http for Egress Auditing and Rename probe/http/http.go

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

A k8s-native mechanism to handle Pod stuck in terminating state (with deletionTimestamp, but with phase=Running).

Currently, the core k8s contains a mechanism in the Pod Garbage-collector (PodGC) to mark such pods as "Failed", but it terminates (marks as Failed) only Pods on the [NotReady nodes with OutOfService taint](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7104c1e426b92025aa25083edcd3dac128f3e206/pkg/controller/podgc/gc_controller.go#L154-L160) (part of the [Non-graceful shutdown](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2023/08/16/kubernetes-1-28-non-graceful-node-shutdown-ga/)).

I think we could consider a timeout after which the taint `OutOfService` is added automatically, or timeout after which a Pod is marked as Failed (timeout buffer + spec.terminationGracePeriodSeconds probably), regardless of the Node state.

### Why is this needed?

Pods stuck in the terminating phase are problematic becuase:
- they block workload-level preemptions in Kueue from being finalized
- they don't allow to make progress by Jobs using [podReplacementPolicy: Failed](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2025/09/05/kubernetes-v1-34-pod-replacement-policy-for-jobs-goes-ga/)

The current OutOfService taint requires manual cluster admin intervention, or using some small controller to add the taint, or directly transition the Pod to Failed, or delete.

The lack of the mechanism in k8s core I think results in the ecosystem fragmentation:
- AppWrapper has its own solution based on [forceful Pod deletion](https://github.com/project-codeflare/appwrapper/blob/59ca67156f53bb0ed37dff65389e0eba3f58e12d/pkg/config/config.go#L55)
- there is the [self-node-remediation project](https://github.com/medik8s/self-node-remediation) using the OutOfService taints
- Kueue is considering introducing a similar mechanism in https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/issues/6757

The issue is that the "fix" is very small, and many users say of Kueue may prefer so that it is fixed inside Kueue, rather than in a new project to deploy, as deploying a new operator increases operational complexity of the cluster (upgrades etc.).

So, ideally it would be done inside the core k8s.
issues.title: Timeout-based termination of Pod "stuck" in terminating state
