issues.body: ### What would you like to be added? Following the proposal to introduce Resource Size as a new Scalability Dimension ([#134375](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/134375)), I would like to propose establishing "Pod Shape" as its own formal scalability envelope. We should clearly separate the concepts of: * **Shape:** Which fields are set and their proportions (e.g., number of init containers, sidecars, volumes). * **Size:** The size of the field values themselves, which can be adjusted independently. The goal is to align as a community on an "Exemplar Pod Shape" that we guarantee to be scalable. Once aligned, we should formally document this shape envelope in the community configurations and limits ([thresholds.md](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/main/sig-scalability/configs-and-limits/thresholds.md)). ### Why is this needed? While addressing resource size limits is crucial, [recent analyses](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/134375#issuecomment-3952087283) have shown that the types of fields set in a Pod spec can have a disproportionate, non-linear impact on resulting Pod size and control plane load. Currently, our tests generate a specific total size in etcd by using a "flat" pod shape and stuffing a large random payload into a single environment variable. However, real-world users achieve the same overall pod size by utilizing complex architectural patterns (like sidecars and init containers), which generate drastically different cascading overheads: * **Names & ManagedFields:** Labels, annotations, and the names of containers, environment variables or fields are recorded by the API server as object metadata to track controller field ownership. In practice, this often leads to a **doubling of the Pod size**. * **Init Containers or Readiness Gates:** Each forces Kubelet to send two additional status updates. Adding just one init container or readiness gate **increases scheduling cycle writes by 50%** (from 4 to 6), inflating watch events and watch cache memory for all controllers. * **Container** - Each init or sidecar container requires an individual status tracking, adding roughly **1KB of overhead** via image digests and sandbox metadata. # Current Test Shape vs. Intended Exemplar Shape To illustrate the gap, here is a comparison between the current test pod shape and the intended exemplar pod shape. Both have a total pod size in etcd of roughly 10KB, but achieve it in completely different ways: | Field | Current Test Pod Shape | Proposed Exemplar Pod Shape | | --------------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------------- | | Annotations | 0 | 10 | | Labels | 1 | 10 | | Init Containers | 0 | 2 | | Containers | 1 | 2 | | Volumes | 2 | 10 per container/init container | | Envs | 1 | 10 per container/init container | | Env Value | 6KB | Minimal to hit intended pod size| | Total Pod Size (etcd) | ~10KB | ~10KB | ## Proposed Plan 1. **Align on the Exemplar Pod Shape:** Finalize the proposed shape outlined above as the target baseline envelope to ensure realistic size overhead and API usage. 2. **Update Scalability tests and Benchmarks** Update K8s scalability tests and benchmarks to reflect exemplar pod. 3. **Fuzzing & Investigation:** Conduct fuzzing on other pod fields to identify any remaining areas with non-linear performance impacts. 2. **Document** Add this defined shape envelope to [sig-scalability/configs-and-limits/thresholds.md](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/main/sig-scalability/configs-and-limits/thresholds.md) to formally guarantee its scalability. ## Tracking Before vs After | | Before | After (Still in progress) | | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | ------------------------- | | Pod Size | 10.15 KB | 10.29 KB (+1.4%) | | Pod Resource Size | 1571 MB | 1601 MB (+2%) | | Number of Writes in Scheduling Cycle | 4 | 8 | | Managed Fields Overhead | 20.6% | 48.80% | | [API Server Memory](https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=gce-5000Nodes-1.5GB-pods&metriccategoryname=E2E&metricname=LoadResources&PodName=kube-apiserver-control-plane-us-east1-b%2Fkube-apiserver&Resource=memory) | 53.6 GB | 61 GB (+14%) | | [API Server CPU](https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=gce-5000Nodes-1.5GB-pods&metriccategoryname=E2E&metricname=LoadResources&PodName=kube-apiserver-control-plane-us-east1-b%2Fkube-apiserver&Resource=cpu) | 38 cores | 47.5 (+25%) | | [KCM Memory](https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=gce-5000Nodes-1.5GB-pods&metriccategoryname=E2E&metricname=LoadResources&PodName=kube-controller-manager-control-plane-us-east1-b%2Fkube-controller-manager&Resource=memory) | 9.3 GB | 11.9 GB (+28%) | | [Scheduler Memory](https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=gce-5000Nodes-1.5GB-pods&metriccategoryname=E2E&metricname=LoadResources&PodName=kube-scheduler-control-plane-us-east1-b%2Fkube-scheduler&Resource=memory) | 7.6 GB | 10.0 GB (+31.6%) | | [Etcd events memory](https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=gce-5000Nodes-1.5GB-pods&metriccategoryname=E2E&metricname=LoadResources&PodName=etcd-manager-events-control-plane-us-east1-b%2Fetcd-manager&Resource=memory) | 2.3GB | 3.3GB (+43%) | | Pod Shape | | | /sig scalability /sig api-machinery /cc @wojtek-t @mborsz @liggitt
issues.title: Establish "Pod Shape" as a part of Scalability Envelope

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

**Context**
We are developing a Custom Resource Definition (CRD) controller that utilizes the standard list-watch (informer) mechanism. Under high workload conditions, we are observing significant latency in the initial notification trigger for reconciliation loops.

**Observations**
Upon inspecting the Kubernetes API server logs, we identified a high volume of the following warning messages:

`"Fast watcher, slow processing. Probably caused by slow decoding, user not receiving fast, or other processing logic"
`

This suggests a bottleneck where the API server is generating events faster than they can be decoded or consumed. While the log message mentions "slow decoding," our monitoring indicates that the controller itself is not CPU-bound or busy; rather, it appears starved of events because the API server cannot push them efficiently.

**Current Investigation**
We noticed that starting in Kubernetes v1.31, the feature gate ConcurrentWatchObjectDecode was introduced to address decoding bottlenecks by parallelizing the decoding of watch events. However, the current implementation hardcodes the concurrency limit to 10 workers. And the incoming/outgoing bufSize are also hardcoded to 100.

We are seeking the guidance if we could increase the hardcoded settings to improve the watcher efficiency, and whether k8s could provide a feature or guidance how to tune this case, e.g. improve the decoding efficiency.


### Why is this needed?

The controller is being starved of timely updates because the API server cannot produce events efficiently.
issues.title: etcd watcher scalability or improve decode efficiency

### What would you like to be added?

The client-go Result type can [only unmarshal into a runtime.Object](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/03779bbd00da25c7fcd03711ddfe466a3322e1d7/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/rest/request.go#L1449) because the underlying codec [can only target them](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/03779bbd00da25c7fcd03711ddfe466a3322e1d7/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/interfaces.go#L112).

For a dynamic client like the controller-runtime one which decodes the response into the object used for the request, this means that [the raw bytes of the response have to be retrieved to then manually deserialize them](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/controller-runtime/pull/3475). This is fragile and requires to manually add support for any possible content-type, like for example CBOR in the future.

The problem doesn't exist for the generated clients, as they decode the response into a new typed object, which implements runtime.Object.

I see two possible ways out of this:
1. Make the Decoder accept `any` rather than `runtime.Object`
2. Implement `runtime.Object` for the generated applyconfigs

While 1) would be possible in principle by internally making decoders do type assertions wherever they want a `runtime.Object`, I think changing this would end up being very large scale change that has decent potential to break something along the way, so 2) is probably the better approach.

/cc @jpbetz @liggitt 

/sig api-machinery

### Why is this needed?

see above
issues.title: Allow to unmarshal into applyconfig from client-go result

### What would you like to be added?

Provide a builtin RWX supporting storage class. Potentially reusing the existing etcd store as a backend.

### Why is this needed?

Providing RWX based storage classes is a difficult endeavor, allowing write access from multiple sources at the same point. Historically various Linux filesystem tried to achieve this, with varying degree of success or complexity.


In the kubernetes world, pod-to-pod communication that is state based (pod A creates or configures something, pod B needs to have the resulting inforarmation) can be achieved, but needs reinvention in every app.

If kubernetes supported a builtin RWX storage class, even for small objects that are supported by etcd, it would allow a powerful new way of pods to submit information to each other.

Other ideas to solve the issue of pod-to-pod, stateful information would be to allow configmaps or secrets to be writable from pods. 

The suggested storageclass is mainly thought to be used to inject small pieces of information, such as configuration files, state of another pod ('I'm doing x already - use z to achieve something'), thus size restrictions of ~1MB per entity would not cause any issue.
issues.title: Add support for built-in small object RWX Storage class

issues.body:
## What would you like to be added?

Today, the total APF concurrency budget scales with:

- `--max-requests-inflight`
- `--max-mutating-requests-inflight`


However, the per-request LIST cap still appears to be bounded by a fixed global cap (`100` seats when `SizeBasedListCostEstimate` is enabled).

This means that in larger clusters or on larger control planes, very large LIST requests may still be compressed into the same top bucket even though the total APF seat budget has grown significantly.


As a result, on large clusters, very expensive LIST requests may still be under-estimated once they hit the fixed cap. This reduces the ability of APF to distinguish between "large" and "very large" LIST requests, and may still admit too many expensive requests concurrently, which could cause OOM in apiserver

## Related work


- #132233 
  - #132355 
  - #133034 increased this cap from `10` to `100`
- #138313
- #118601 made per-priority-level maxSeats dynamic based on nominal concurrency.



## Questions

1. Is a fixed global cap of `100` still considered sufficient for very large clusters?
2. Should `MaximumListSeatsLimit` be configurable by cluster operators?
3. Would it be useful to expose observability for raw estimated seats before capping, and how often estimates are clipped by the cap?

## Possible directions

- make `MaximumListSeatsLimit` configurable
- scale the cap with total APF concurrency
- keep the current cap, but add observability to understand whether clipping is common in large clusters



/sig api-machinery
/kind feature
issues.title: APF: make list max seat cap configurable or scalable for large clusters

issues.body:
## What happened

When the watch cache is temporarily behind etcd for more than 3 seconds, a consistent LIST read that would normally be served from cache can fall back to a direct etcd LIST.

Relevant code paths:
- [watch cache 3s wait window](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/watch_cache.go#L48-L53)
- [watch cache timeout returns `TooLargeResourceVersion`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/watch_cache.go#L446-L489)
- [consistent LIST fallback to etcd](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/delegator.go#L218-L224)

This becomes dangerous in degraded situations such as:
- etcd defragmentation
- leader re-election
- transient member stall
- delayed watch delivery

## Real-world impact

This failure mode was summarized well by @serathius:

> Consistent read from cache fallback, works great until defrag.  
> Defrag stalls member, watch gets delayed more than 3s, watch cache falls back reads to etcd.  
> Due to lack of APF protection (not aware of fallback), memory jumps, for 2GB pods resource we get:  
> Etcd 17GB->180GB  
> API server 50GB->160GB

This matches the current behavior: a request that is initially expected to be a cheap cache-backed consistent LIST read can become an expensive etcd LIST at runtime once the watch cache is still behind after the 3 second wait window.



## A graceful degradation may be safer

If the cache has not caught up within 3 seconds, etcd and/or apiserver are likely already under stress. In that situation, bypassing the cache and sending more expensive LIST traffic directly to etcd can make things much worse.

Kube-apiserver already has precedent for returning `429 Too Many Requests` under degraded watch cache conditions. For example, when the watch cache is not ready, LIST requests can already be rejected with `429`:
- [existing `429` on unready watch cache](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go#L763-L768)


## Proposed direction

One possible direction would be to introduce a feature gate for this fallback path.

When enabled, if a consistent LIST read cannot be served from watch cache within the current 3 second wait window, kube-apiserver would return `429 Too Many Requests` with `Retry-After` instead of falling back to etcd. This would let clients retry later, rather than turning a cache-backed read into an expensive etcd LIST while the system is already degraded.

The reasoning is:
- if the cache is behind for more than 3 seconds, etcd and/or kube-apiserver are likely already under stress
- turning a cheap cache read into an expensive etcd LIST is risky
- asking clients to retry may give etcd time to recover and the watch cache time to catch up
- once the cache catches up again, the same consistent LIST can be served safely from cache

Using a feature gate would preserve backward compatibility and keep the current fallback-to-etcd behavior as the default, while allowing operators to opt into a safer graceful-degradation mode for large or sensitive clusters.

see #138701
issues.title: apiserver: consistent read fallback to etcd can overload apiserver and etcd when watch cache is behind

### What would you like to be added?

In release 1.36, we introduced initial changes to the Workload API (including `Workload` and `PodGroup` objects) in the `v1alpha2` version of the `scheduling.k8s.io` API group. For the 1.37 release, we plan to make further changes to these APIs and eventually promote them to Beta.
To follow Kubernetes API best practices and allow for breaking changes in the next iteration without maintaining multiple alpha versions, we need to create a new `v1alpha3` version as a copy of `v1alpha2`. We will migrate all internal consumers to `v1alpha3` and remove `v1alpha2` in this release. This avoids the overhead of maintaining both versions with conversion logic for an experimental API, while allowing us to evolve the API.

### Why is this needed?

We would like to promote the Workload API to `v1alpha3` and remove `v1alpha2` by performing the following steps:
1.  **Create `v1alpha3` API Definitions**:
    *   Copy `staging/src/k8s.io/api/scheduling/v1alpha2` to `v1alpha3`.
    *   Copy `pkg/apis/scheduling/v1alpha2` to `v1alpha3`.
    *   Update package names and references to point to the new `v1alpha3`.
2.  **Remove `v1alpha2` API Definitions**:
    *   Delete the old `v1alpha2` directories in both `staging` and `pkg/apis`.
3.  **Update Internal References**:
    *   Update all imports and usages of `k8s.io/api/scheduling/v1alpha2` to `v1alpha3` across the repository (e.g., in `pkg/scheduler/`, `plugin/pkg/admission/`).
4.  **Code Generation**:
    *   Run Kubernetes code generators to create clientsets, informers, listers, and deepcopy functions for the new version.
issues.title: Promote Workload API to v1alpha3 and remove v1alpha2

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Follow-up to #138212.
/sig scheduling

For NNN pods, try the OpportunisticBatching hint when the nominated node is infeasible, before falling back to the standard scheduling cycle.

Suggested by @macsko in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138212#issuecomment-4235037702.
> We have two possible approaches with NNN and opportunistic batching. One is yours to bypass the batching, other is to try the hint when the NNN is infeasible. It's a tradeoff, because when both NNN and hint are infeasible, the latter approach would cause the scheduling to be slower due to the two synchronous calls to the filters. But, when the hint is feasible, the performance gain would be significant. I'm not fully sure which approach is better, but I may be leaning towards checking the hint after NNN in the scheduling cycle.

### Why is this needed?

Tradeoff that needs benchmarking:

- If the hint is feasible after NNN fails, we skip a full filter pass.
- If both are infeasible, we pay for two synchronous filter calls.

Whether this is a net win depends on workload characteristics.
issues.title: OpportunisticBatching: Try the batch hint as a fallback when NominatedNodeName is infeasible

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Allow the kube-apiserver's bootstrap controller ([`pkg/controlplane/controller/kubernetesservice`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.35/pkg/controlplane/controller/kubernetesservice/controller.go)) and its endpoint reconciler ([`pkg/controlplane/reconcilers/lease.go`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.35/pkg/controlplane/reconcilers/lease.go)) to **optionally emit topology metadata** (`zone`, ideally also `region`) on the EndpointSlice it manages for the `default/kubernetes` Service.

Concretely:

1. Add an opt-in mechanism (e.g. a kube-apiserver flag, or a pluggable provider hook) to associate each apiserver instance's IP with a topology zone, recorded alongside the lease in `/registry/masterleases/<ip>`.
2. When [`EndpointsAdapter.EnsureEndpointSliceFromEndpoints`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.35/pkg/controlplane/reconcilers/endpointsadapter.go#L80-L114) writes the EndpointSlice, populate the per-endpoint `zone` field (and optionally `hints`) from the recorded topology.
3. Default behavior unchanged (no topology hints emitted) — fully backward compatible.

This would let kube-proxy Topology Aware Routing / `trafficDistribution: PreferClose` work for the `default/kubernetes` Service, just like it already does for any user Service.

### Why is this needed?

In multi-zone Kubernetes deployments where the apiserver is reachable via multiple IPs distributed across topology zones, in-cluster traffic to `kubernetes.default.svc` is currently flow-hashed across all apiserver IPs regardless of where the client is. A network failure isolated to one zone affects clients across all zones.

Concrete motivating scenario (managed Kubernetes on AWS, though the abstract problem is cloud-agnostic):

- An EKS cluster has 2 control-plane apiservers, each fronted by a cross-account ENI (X-ENI) in a different AZ. The IPs of those ENIs are what the bootstrap reconciler writes into the `default/kubernetes` EndpointSlice.
- A network failure in one AZ (or unreachability of the X-ENI in that AZ) makes ~50% of client connections to `kubernetes.default.svc` fail across the **entire cluster** — including kubelet lease renewals, kube-proxy watch streams, and CNI agent watches.
- We documented this end-to-end and reported it as [aws/containers-roadmap#2804](https://github.com/aws/containers-roadmap/issues/2804). AWS confirmed the apiserver IPs are placed across AZs and that they cannot add topology hints because the EndpointSlice is reconciled by upstream code — see this detailed analysis from an AWS engineer: [EKS kubernetes service and inter-AZ traffic](https://repost.aws/articles/ARicVh-77OR3igorKZeo1vfw).

The same pattern affects any cloud provider or self-hosted multi-zone deployment whose apiservers are reachable via per-zone IPs — GKE, AKS, on-prem multi-master, etc.

### Workarounds

None at the apiserver layer. Manually patching the `default/kubernetes` EndpointSlice with `zone` attributes is futile: the reconciler overwrites it within ~10s ([`DefaultEndpointReconcilerInterval`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.35/pkg/controlplane/instance.go#L111-L113)).

Customer-side mitigations (shorter webhook timeouts, multi-AZ critical pods, topology-aware routing on user Services) are partial — they reduce the amplification of the problem but cannot eliminate the cluster-wide blast radius of a single-zone network failure on the `default/kubernetes` path.

### Prior art / context

- [Topology Aware Routing concept page](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/topology-aware-routing/) — already implemented for user Services via `trafficDistribution: PreferClose` and topology hints on EndpointSlices.
- KEP [#536 — Topology aware routing of services](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/536) (closed, implemented; intentionally scoped to user Services).
- The `default/kubernetes` Service is special-cased: its Endpoints carry `endpointslice.kubernetes.io/skip-mirror: "true"` and the EndpointSlice has no `managed-by` label — it is reconciled by the apiserver-internal bootstrap controller rather than by `endpointslice-controller`.
- Source paths most relevant to this proposal:
  - `pkg/controlplane/controller/kubernetesservice/controller.go`
  - `pkg/controlplane/reconcilers/lease.go`
  - `pkg/controlplane/reconcilers/endpointsadapter.go`

A KEP may be appropriate given the multi-SIG scope and new apiserver flag/hook surface; happy to draft one if the SIGs agree this is in scope.

/sig api-machinery
/sig network
/kind feature
issues.title: kube-apiserver: allow opt-in topology hints on the default/kubernetes endpointslices for AZ-affine in-cluster API access

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

When ForResource() is called on a DynamicSharedInformerFactory for a GVR whose 
informer has already been stopped, it should detect the stopped state and return 
a fresh informer instead of the stale cached one.

Currently ForResource() unconditionally returns the cached informer for a GVR 
with no check against IsStopped():

    informer, exists := f.informers[key]
    if exists {
        return informer // returned even if informer is stopped
    }

The proposed change would be:

    informer, exists := f.informers[key]
    if exists && !informer.Informer().IsStopped() {
        return informer
    }

    // create and cache a fresh informer
    informer = NewFilteredDynamicInformer(...)
    f.informers[key] = informer
    return informer

### Why is this needed?

The current design creates an asymmetry — the factory allows starting individual 
informers via their Run() method, and SharedIndexInformer already exposes IsStopped() 
acknowledging that an informer can reach a stopped state, but ForResource() never 
checks this before returning a cached informer.

The only current workaround is to discard the entire factory instance and create 
a new one, which is heavy-handed when only a single GVR's informer needs to be 
refreshed, and also affects all other GVRs sharing the same factory.

Since IsStopped() is already part of the SharedIndexInformer interface, using it 
in ForResource() is a natural and minimal fix that aligns the factory's behavior 
with the lifecycle that the interface itself acknowledges.
issues.title: dynamicinformer (client-go): ForResource() should return a fresh informer when the cached one is stopped

The test uses Pod objects. Although Pods are usually encoded with PB in most cases, I believe the result is still meaningful for operations on CR objects. On the other hand, I understand that newer versions have added CBOR encoding to improve performance. However, because client-go remains compatible with older versions of the apiserver, and there are many deployments in the wild where a newer client-go is used with a slightly older control plane, I believe optimizing JSON deserialization performance in client-go is still valuable.

Currently, the deserialization path inside client-go is entirely serial and single-core. Inspired by the ConcurrentWatchObjectDecode feature gate in the apiserver, I think a similar mechanism could also be applied to client-go.

In terms of implementation, after further profiling, I found that the JSON path attempts deserialization three times:

1. The JSON framer splits JSON objects from the chunked body.
2. The outer Event object is deserialized.
3. The actual object inside the Event is deserialized.

Among these, the first step cannot be parallelized, but the other two can. I verified the idea of parallelizing steps 2 and 3 locally, but also found that step 1 then became the bottleneck:

I wonder whether we could modify the JSON framer so that it does not validate the full JSON syntax, and instead uses a more relaxed approach for framing. To test this, I implemented a state machine that only matches closing braces/brackets to split the stream, and on my machine it reached around 500-900MB/s. In addition, after reading the code further, I found that Watch responses have historically never used pretty-printed output. Therefore, if we relax the semantics, we could actually split by newline. Under this assumption, throughput on my machine can be further improved to more than 5GB/s, which would completely remove the first deserialization bottleneck:

issues.title: Concurrent decoding objects for watching requests in client-go

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

1. changing decoding watching stream response in client-go to be concurrent;
2. changing JSON stream framer to use a more relaxed approach instead of full `Unmarshal` to RawMessage.

### Why is this needed?

During benchmarking, we found that deserialization in client-go appears to be a bottleneck when handling Watch requests. I built a stress test, and the results show that JSON encoding is significantly less efficient than PB or CBOR. As object size increases, JSON deserialization throughput drops rapidly.

And before formally submitting a PR or KEP, I would like to first gather feedback from the community. I’d really appreciate your thoughts on whether this direction makes sense and whether there are any concerns I may have missed. cc @wojtek-t @serathius

The test uses Pod objects. Although Pods are usually encoded with PB in most cases, I believe the result is still meaningful for operations on CR objects. On the other hand, I understand that newer versions have added CBOR encoding to improve performance. However, because client-go remains compatible with older versions of the apiserver, and there are many deployments in the wild where a newer client-go is used with a slightly older control plane, I believe optimizing JSON deserialization performance in client-go is still valuable.

Currently, the deserialization path inside client-go is entirely serial and single-core. Inspired by the ConcurrentWatchObjectDecode feature gate in the apiserver, I think a similar mechanism could also be applied to client-go.

In terms of implementation, after further profiling, I found that the JSON path attempts deserialization three times:

1. The JSON framer splits JSON objects from the chunked body.
2. The outer Event object is deserialized.
3. The actual object inside the Event is deserialized.

Among these, the first step cannot be parallelized, but the other two can. I verified the idea of parallelizing steps 2 and 3 locally, but also found that step 1 then became the bottleneck:

I wonder whether we could modify the JSON framer so that it does not validate the full JSON syntax, and instead uses a more relaxed approach for framing. To test this, I implemented a state machine that only matches closing braces/brackets to split the stream, and on my machine it reached around 500-900MB/s. In addition, after reading the code further, I found that Watch responses have historically never used pretty-printed output. Therefore, if we relax the semantics, we could actually split by newline. Under this assumption, throughput on my machine can be further improved to more than 5GB/s, which would completely remove the first deserialization bottleneck:

issues.body:
### What happened?

The `generateCSR()` function in `staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/util/certificate/certificate_manager.go` hardcodes the key type to ECDSA P-256:

```go
privateKey, err := ecdsa.GenerateKey(elliptic.P256(), cryptorand.Reader)
```

This means all kubelet client and server certificates generated via the certificate manager use ECDSA P-256, regardless of what key type the cluster CA uses. There is no configuration option to override this.

The kubelet client certificate on the first control plane node is initially generated by `kubeadm` using the same key type as the cluster CA (typically RSA 2048), but on subsequent rotations it switches to ECDSA P-256 because rotation goes through client-go's hardcoded path.

### What did you expect to happen?

The key type for CSR generation should be configurable via the `CertificateManager` `Config` struct, similar to how `GetUsages` is already a configurable function. For example:

```go
type Config struct {
    // ...existing fields...

    // GenerateKey allows overriding the default key generation (ECDSA P-256).
    // If nil, defaults to ecdsa.GenerateKey(elliptic.P256(), rand.Reader).
    GenerateKey func() (crypto.Signer, error)
}
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Deploy a Kubernetes cluster with an RSA CA (default `kubeadm init` behavior).
2. Inspect the kubelet client certificate on the first control plane node — it uses RSA (same as CA).
3. Wait for certificate rotation (or force it by shortening cert lifetime).
4. After rotation, inspect the new kubelet client certificate — it is now ECDSA P-256.
5. On worker nodes, kubelet client and server certificates are ECDSA P-256 from the start.

The hardcoded line is at:
[`staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/util/certificate/certificate_manager.go#L767`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/util/certificate/certificate_manager.go#L767)

### Anything else we need to know?

- Environments requiring RSA keys (compliance, HSM compatibility, consistency with CA) cannot use built-in certificate rotation without patching client-go.
- Some deployments require ECDSA P-384 as P-256 is not considered sufficient under their security policies. The hardcoded P-256 makes this impossible without forking client-go.
- The `GetUsages` callback already handles the key-type-dependent usage selection, so the infrastructure for key-type awareness exists — only the generation itself is not configurable.

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

I would like to discuss whether Kubernetes should expose more structured, machine-readable scheduling failure diagnostics for Pods that cannot be scheduled.

Today, kube-scheduler reports scheduling failures through `FailedScheduling` Events and the `PodScheduled` condition. However, the detailed causes are primarily encoded in human-readable messages, for example:

```text
0/3 nodes are available: 1 Insufficient cpu, 2 node(s) had untolerated taint ...
```

This is useful for humans, but difficult for automation and troubleshooting tools to consume reliably without parsing message strings.

This issue is intended to start a discussion before drafting a KEP. I understand that feature requests are unlikely to make progress as issues alone, and I plan to engage with SIG Scheduling on Slack and consider a KEP if the problem space is considered worth pursuing.

A possible direction could be to expose stable scheduling failure categories, for example:

```yaml
status:
  schedulingDiagnostics:
    result: Unschedulable
    reasonCodes:
    - InsufficientCPU
    - TaintMismatch
    failedPlugins:
    - NodeResourcesFit
    - TaintToleration
```

This is only an illustrative example. I am not proposing a final API shape in this issue.

Initial scope could be:

preserve the existing FailedScheduling Events
preserve the existing PodScheduled condition behavior
avoid changing scheduling decisions
avoid exposing per-node detailed failure data by default
define a generic diagnostics format that scheduler plugins could contribute to
avoid solving feature-specific diagnostics for Gang Scheduling, DRA, or preemption in the first step

Non-goals:

change scheduling semantics
introduce a new scheduling policy
replace existing Events
replace existing human-readable messages
expose sensitive or high-cardinality per-node scheduling details by default

Questions for SIG Scheduling:

Is this problem already covered by an existing KEP, issue, or ongoing work?
Would SIG Scheduling be interested in a generic structured diagnostics format for scheduling failures?
Should this start as a KEP, or would it be better to first prototype a smaller change in Events, Pod status, or scheduler framework status handling?
Which API surface would be most appropriate: Pod status, Events, or something else?

### Why is this needed?

Operators, SRE teams, and automation tools often need to understand why a Pod is Pending or unschedulable.

Today, many tools need to parse `FailedScheduling` Event messages or `PodScheduled` condition messages. This can be fragile because those messages are primarily designed for human readability, not as a stable machine-readable interface.

Structured scheduling diagnostics could help with:

- more reliable troubleshooting of Pending Pods
- better `kubectl` and dashboard experiences
- observability and AIOps integrations
- autoscaler and remediation tooling
- avoiding brittle parsing of scheduler event messages

I found some related areas, but I could not find a generic KEP that standardizes machine-readable scheduling failure diagnostics across scheduler plugins.

Related topics include:

- existing `FailedScheduling` Events
- existing `PodScheduled` condition with `reason: Unschedulable`
- scheduler framework plugin status
- Gang Scheduling failure handling
- DRA scheduling failures
- historical discussions around Pod failure reason visibility

This issue is meant to validate whether the problem is real and whether SIG Scheduling would be interested before any KEP is drafted.

/sig scheduling
/kind feature
issues.title: machine-readable scheduling failure diagnostics for unscheduled Pods

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Today, HPA exposes fields such as `status.currentReplicas`, `status.desiredReplicas`, `status.currentMetrics`, and `status.conditions`. These are useful, but they do not fully explain how the final desired replica count was derived or why scaling was skipped or limited.

For example, when HPA does not scale, users often need to infer whether the reason was:

- the metric was within tolerance
- the recommendation was limited by `minReplicas` or `maxReplicas`
- the recommendation was limited by `behavior.scaleUp` or `behavior.scaleDown` policies
- the recommendation was affected by a stabilization window
- metrics were unavailable or invalid
- no scale was needed

A possible direction could be to expose only the latest decision in HPA status, for example:

```yaml
status:
  lastScaleDecision:
    time: "2026-05-12T10:15:00Z"
    currentReplicas: 5
    rawDesiredReplicas: 10
    finalDesiredReplicas: 8
    direction: ScaleUp
    reason: MetricAboveTarget
    selectedMetric:
      type: Resource
      name: cpu
      calculatedReplicas: 10
    constraintsApplied:
    - MaxReplicas
```
This is only an illustrative example. I am not proposing a final API shape in this issue.

The initial scope would be intentionally narrow:

preserve the existing HPA scaling algorithm
preserve existing HPA conditions and Events
expose only the most recent scaling decision, not a full history
avoid high-cardinality per-Pod or per-sample metric details
make common constraints visible in a stable, machine-readable way

Questions for SIG Autoscaling:

Is this problem already covered by existing work?
Would SIG Autoscaling be interested in structured HPA decision status?
Should this be explored as a KEP?
Would HPA status be the right API surface, or should this remain in Events or controller logs?

### Why is this needed?

HPA behavior has become more configurable over time, including scaling behavior policies, stabilization windows, and configurable tolerance. These features are useful, but they also make it harder for users to understand why HPA made a particular scaling decision.

Operators and SRE teams often need to answer questions such as:

- Why did HPA not scale up even though CPU looked high?
- Why was the desired replica count lower than expected?
- Was the decision limited by `maxReplicas`?
- Was scale-down delayed by a stabilization window?
- Which metric determined the final recommendation?
- Did tolerance prevent scaling?

Today, users often need to combine HPA conditions, Events, current metrics, controller-manager logs, and knowledge of the HPA algorithm to answer these questions.

A structured decision status could improve:

- troubleshooting of autoscaling behavior
- `kubectl describe hpa` output
- dashboards and observability integrations
- SRE and platform engineering workflows
- automation that needs to distinguish "no scale needed" from "scale blocked by policy"

This proposal would not change HPA behavior. It would only make the most recent HPA decision easier to understand and consume programmatically.

/sig autoscaling
/kind feature
issues.title: structured HPA scaling decision status

### What would you like to be added?

As part of the graduation of the feature, we need to switch from the preliminary v1alpha1 metadata file format to v1beta1. The default for 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f830e4a2b8f02ca00bb51417d978ce2876e5e30e/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/kubeletplugin/draplugin.go#L555-L557
should be changed to "the two most recent versions", in this case v1alpha1 and v1beta1.

v1alpha1 then can be removed one release later.

/cc @alaypatel07 @liggitt 

### Why is this needed?

The versioning of the file format should reflect the stability of the feature.

Writing the same information in two different formats enables a smooth upgrade path: first update the cluster, then DRA drivers (writing v1alpha1 and v1beta1, with the not-updated-yet consumers reading v1alpha1), then finally consumers (once available, then reading v1beta1).
issues.title: KEP-5304: DRA device metadata: add v1beta1 API

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

I would like to discuss a possible enhancement for a fire-and-forget node drain workflow.

Today, `kubectl drain` is primarily a synchronous, client-driven operation. This works well for interactive use, but it is harder to use in automation where the caller wants to request a drain, return immediately, and let a controller continue the operation safely.

The user story I would like to explore is:

> As a cluster operator or automation system, I want to request a node drain through the Kubernetes API and return immediately, so that a controller can continue the drain operation, report progress, and expose blocking reasons such as PodDisruptionBudget constraints.

One possible direction could be a minimal `NodeMaintenance`-like API or CRD that represents a drain request for a Node.

For example:

```yaml
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1alpha1
kind: NodeMaintenance
metadata:
  name: drain-worker-1
spec:
  nodeName: worker-1
  reason: PlannedMaintenance
  drain:
    enabled: true
    respectPodDisruptionBudgets: true
status:
  phase: Pending
  conditions:
  - type: Draining
    status: "False"
  - type: ReadyForMaintenance
    status: "False"
```

This is only an illustrative example. I am not proposing a final API shape in this issue.

A controller could then reconcile the object by:

validating the target Node
optionally cordoning the Node
evicting Pods using the existing Eviction API
preserving existing PodDisruptionBudget semantics
updating status with drain progress
reporting blocked states such as PDB-related blocking
marking the request as ready for maintenance when the drain succeeds

The initial scope should be intentionally small:

support a fire-and-forget drain request
preserve existing eviction and PDB behavior
expose structured status for drain progress and blocking reasons
allow automation to watch the object and react to lifecycle changes
avoid requiring the original kubectl drain client process to stay alive until completion

This could also be useful as an integration point for external automation. For example, a controller could create maintenance requests based on cloud provider notices or other external triggers. Another controller could watch these objects and populate maintenance records in systems such as ServiceNow.

Admission control could help protect cluster health. For example, a ServiceAccount might be allowed to create NodeMaintenance objects only for Nodes labeled as workers, preventing automation from accidentally targeting control-plane Nodes.

If time or deadline fields are included, I think they should use UTC only and avoid timezone fields in the API.

### Why is this needed?

Node maintenance is a common operational workflow for Kubernetes clusters, especially for OS patching, kernel updates, container runtime updates, reboots, hardware maintenance, and cloud provider maintenance notices.

Today, operators commonly use `cordon` and `kubectl drain`. However, `kubectl drain` is client-driven. In automated environments, this creates several challenges:

- the caller must keep running until the drain completes
- progress and blocked states are not represented as a first-class Kubernetes object
- external systems have no standard object to watch for maintenance lifecycle changes
- automation often needs broad permissions to cordon Nodes or evict Pods directly
- it is harder to apply admission control around which Nodes can be targeted
- integrations with ITSM or change-management systems require custom state tracking outside Kubernetes

A simple API or CRD representing a drain request could make this workflow more declarative and observable.

It would allow users and automation to create a request and return immediately, while a controller performs the actual drain and updates status. It would also provide a common object that other controllers or tools can watch.

Potential benefits include:

- safer automation for planned Node maintenance
- better visibility into drain progress
- clearer blocked status when PDBs prevent eviction
- easier integration with cloud provider maintenance notices
- easier integration with systems such as ServiceNow
- better use of RBAC and admission control to limit which Nodes can be drained by automation
- less need for long-running client-side drain processes

This proposal should not change existing eviction semantics or replace PodDisruptionBudgets. The goal is to make the existing drain workflow easier to request, observe, and automate.

Non-goals for the initial scope:

- replace `kubectl drain`
- change Pod eviction semantics
- bypass or weaken PodDisruptionBudgets
- force-delete Pods by default
- automatically patch, reboot, or upgrade Nodes
- define cloud-provider-specific maintenance behavior
- define a full cluster-wide maintenance scheduler
- handle non-graceful node shutdown
- introduce timezone handling in the API

Questions for SIG Node:

- Is this problem already covered by existing or previous work?
- Would SIG Node be interested in a small fire-and-forget drain user story?
- Should this be explored as a KEP, a CRD-based proposal, a `kubectl` change, or some combination of these?
- Would a `NodeMaintenance`-like API be the right abstraction?
- Should the first step be an external CRD/controller prototype, or should this be discussed as an in-tree enhancement?
issues.title: fire-and-forget node drain using a NodeMaintenance-like API

issues.body: ## Problem Kubernetes already supports *streaming LIST encoding* for JSON collections (ref: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/5116), but the response path still performs a **whole-list version conversion** first for typed lists (e.g. internal `core.PodList` -> external `v1.PodList`). This materializes the full external `Items []T` in memory before bytes are streamed, so peak RSS/live heap is still dominated by conversion. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f830e4a2b8f02ca00bb51417d978ce2876e5e30e/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/serializer/versioning/versioning.go#L271-L275 https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f830e4a2b8f02ca00bb51417d978ce2876e5e30e/pkg/apis/core/v1/zz_generated.conversion.go#L6632-L6645 - typed list object (a Go struct list type like v1.PodList with Items []v1.Pod , as opposed to unstructured.UnstructuredList ) pprof shows a large share of allocations/retained memory in typed list conversion paths (e.g. generated `autoConvert_*List_To_*List`). ## Proposed direction When streaming JSON encoding is enabled, the server should not need to construct an entire external typed list in memory. Ideally: - convert list header once - convert items one-by-one - stream-encode items one-by-one into the JSON `items` array ## Benchmark I evaluated this under a local `local-up` apiserver setup with a synthetic large LIST workload: - **Dataset**: **30,000 Pods** in the cluster - **Load shape**: sustained LIST traffic with **staged concurrency** (1 → 5 → 10 → 20 → 25), **30s per stage** - **Measurements**: - process **RSS** over time - Go **memstats** maxima (heap_inuse / heap_sys / next_gc) - client-side LIST latency distribution (p50/p95/max) - **Profiling**: captured heap/allocs pprof snapshots around peak memory to compare conversion hotspots between baseline and experiment ## Results (30k pods, stages 1→25, 30s each) ### Summary table | Metric | Current (control) | Streamed conversion (experiment) | Delta | |---|---:|---:|---:| | RSS avg | 2.3GiB | 1.6GiB | -30.5% | | RSS max | 5.9GiB | 3.2GiB | -46.2% | | RSS min | 244.7MiB | 241.2MiB | -1.4% | | HeapInuse max | 4.6GiB | 2.4GiB | -47.4% | | HeapSys max | 5.9GiB | 3.2GiB | -45.4% | | NextGC max | 5.2GiB | 2.7GiB | -48.6% | | LIST latency p50 (avg) | 1.881s | 1.995s | +6.0% | | LIST latency p95 (avg) | 2.264s | 2.119s | -6.4% | | LIST latency max | 4.906s | 4.427s | -9.8% | ## Figures ### 1) RSS timeline (current) ### 2) RSS timeline (streamed conversion) ### 3) pprof (current vs streamed conversion) ## Why this matters For large typed LIST responses under concurrency, “streaming LIST encoding” alone is insufficient if the server still materializes the full external typed list during version conversion. Streaming conversion (header + per-item) significantly reduces peak RSS and live heap, improving stability under sustained LIST pressure. Implementation PR: #139051 /cc @xigang @serathius
issues.title: apiserver: streaming version conversion for typed LIST objects (streaming JSON encode still materializes whole lists)

### What would you like to be added?

The `scheduler_pending_pods` metric reports counts of pods in each scheduling queue, including `queue="gated"` for pods blocked by `spec.schedulingGates`. Today this aggregate is opaque: there is no way from the metric alone to tell *which* gates are holding pods back.

I'd like the scheduler to expose gate names alongside this counter, either by:

1. Adding a `gate` label to `scheduler_pending_pods` for the `queue="gated"` series and emitting one series per (gate, queue) pair, or
2. Introducing a new metric, e.g. `scheduler_gated_pods{gate="example.com/foo"}`, that reports per-gate counts.

### Why is this needed?

When `scheduler_pending_pods{queue="gated"}` ticks up, operators currently fall back to listing pods (`kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.schedulingGates)'`) or scraping pod state from another source to figure out which controllers or admission webhooks are holding pods. With gate names in the metric, dashboards and alerts can attribute the count directly to the responsible component, and detection of "stuck" gates becomes trivial.

This is especially valuable as more controllers adopt scheduling gates (cluster autoscaler / Karpenter integrations, custom admission flows, deployment snapshot gates, spot-placement policies, etc.). Multiple gates often coexist on the same cluster and the aggregate counter cannot distinguish them.

### Notes

Cardinality:
- Gate names are namespaced (`example.com/foo`), so cardinality is bounded by the number of distinct gates in use on a cluster, typically a handful.
- A pod may declare multiple gates; the metric should either pick a deterministic representative (e.g. the first remaining gate) or emit a series per gate. Whichever trade-off is chosen should be documented.

/kind feature
/sig scheduling
issues.title: kube-scheduler: surface gate names in pending_pods{queue="gated"} metric

issues.body:
### Background / Problem Statement

In default (pod-based) preemption, when a pod popped from the queue already has a `Status.NominatedNodeName`, the preemption evaluator checks the status that the pod received on that nominated node during the current `Filter` phase. If the status is `UnschedulableAndUnresolvable` (e.g., due to a new taint or nodeAffinity mismatch), the evaluator bypasses the check for terminating pods on that node and immediately allows a new preemption attempt. This ensures the pod does not idly wait for terminating victims on a node where it can no longer fit.

In Workload-Aware Preemption (PodGroup preemption), we currently do not evaluate whether the nominated nodes of the PodGroup members became `UnschedulableAndUnresolvable`. Instead, if any member pod has a nominated node with an actively terminating victim of lower priority, preemption for the entire PodGroup is paused (`"not eligible due to a terminating pod on the nominated node"`).

### Architectural Implementation Barriers

Matching the pod-based behavior in PodGroup preemption is non-trivial. During PodGroup scheduling (`schedule_one_podgroup.go`), the scheduler evaluates all pods in the group and aggregates the results into a `podGroupAlgorithmResult`. 
Currently, this structure only preserves high-level status codes and suggested hostnames. To implement the bypass in `PodGroupEvaluator.Preempt`, we would need to explicitly propagate and preserve `framework.Diagnosis` and `NodeToStatusReader` maps for all unschedulable pods in the group up to the `PodGroupPostFilter` invocation.

### Architectural Discussion & Tradeoffs: Do we actually want this?

Even if we implement the necessary framework changes, it is an open question whether bypassing the wait is the right architectural choice for Workload-Aware Preemption. During PR reviews (see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138710), we discussed the following tradeoffs:

#### Arguments in favor of the bypass (Latency Optimization)
When an `UnschedulableAndUnresolvable` status is returned for a nominated node, the PodGroup will not be schedulable on that node even after all victims terminate. Pausing preemption introduces a delay (up to the victim pods' termination grace period). Bypassing the wait allows the PodGroup to immediately initiate preemption on other nodes in the cluster.

#### Arguments against the bypass (Cluster Stability & Preemption Storms)
From an operational stability perspective, once a PodGroup has initiated a disruptive operation (evicting victims), suppressing subsequent preemption cycles until the in-flight evictions finish acts as a crucial rate-limiter against cascading disruption (ensuring only one "killing victims" disruption per PodGroup at a time). Given how disruptive PodGroup preemption can be compared to single-pod preemption, prioritizing rate-limiting over latency optimization might be the correct architectural tradeoff.


/sig scheduling
/kind feature
issues.title: [kube-scheduler][WAP] Evaluate bypassing preemption wait on UnschedulableAndUnresolvable nominated nodes for PodGroups

### What would you like to be added?

The DRA kubelet plugin [`Helper`](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/kubeletplugin#Helper) should allow drivers to enable rolling updates with driver names longer than 28 characters.

### Why is this needed?

Currently, the `Helper` includes a UID in the name of the kubelet plugin registration socket, resulting in a name of the form `{kubelet_registry_path}/{driver_name}-{uid}-reg.sock`, e.g. `/var/lib/kubelet/plugins_registry/gpu.example.com-f358c92b-e974-4f29-a84f-6c64bec0949d-reg.sock`.

With the default registry path at `/var/lib/kubelet/plugins_registry` and a 36-character UID, 28 characters are left for the driver name to stay under the [108-character limit](https://manpages.ubuntu.com/manpages/resolute/man7/unix.7.html#Address_format).

The DRA example driver [wants to use a `*.sigs.k8s.io` name](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver/issues/174) for the driver and `dra-example-driver.sigs.k8s.io` is 30 characters long, causing the driver to fail to start with an error like this:

```
Error: start registrar: start gRPC server: listen on "/var/lib/kubelet/plugins_registry/gpu.dra-example-driver.sigs.k8s.io-ad4af911-5bcd-47c5-a554-f35cea869472-reg.sock": listen unix /var/lib/kubelet/plugins_registry/gpu.dra-example-driver.sigs.k8s.io-ad4af911-5bcd-47c5-a554-f35cea869472-reg.sock: bind: invalid argument
```

/wg device-management

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Introduce an optional parameter to the HPA configuration, for example `backupReplicas`, that would allow you to:

- Specify the exact number of backup pods the autoscaler should maintain alongside the nominal ones.
- Better monitor the average load against the _TARGETS_ thresholds via the _kubectl get hpa_ command.

The new structure of the HPA specification would look like:

```go
type HorizontalPodAutoscalerSpec struct {
	ScaleTargetRef CrossVersionObjectReference
	MinReplicas *int32
	MaxReplicas int32
	Metrics []MetricSpec
	Behavior *HorizontalPodAutoscalerBehavior
	BackupReplicas *int32
}
```


### Why is this needed?

When a pod fails, Kubernetes might take time before restoring another pod on a new node. Deploying a new pod involves time-consuming operations like starting pod processes, downloading container images or sometimes waiting for an available node. Preprovisioning one or several shared backup pods in addition to the nominal ones can reduce the service interruption since those time-consuming operations are already achieved before the pod failure occurs.

Suppose that a Kubernetes service is configured to load balance flows onto a replicaset bound with an HPA defined with the `minReplicas` parameter equal to (_1_ + _Backup_) and with the `maxReplicas` parameter equal to (_Nominal_ + _Backup_). For the shared protection to be efficient, the HPA should add a (_x_ + _1_)<sup>th</sup> pod in the replicaset as soon as the pods are loaded at a ratio (_x_ - _Backup_) / _x_ that depends on _x_, the number of pods already deployed.

Based solely on fixed _TARGETS_ thresholds, the current `v2` HPA version does not satisfy this requirement. By introducing the optional `backupReplicas` parameter, the HPA can decide to add or remove a pod at the right pod load ratio and in this way become fully compatible with the shared protection requirement.
issues.title: Proposal: Request HPA to preinstall backup pods for minimizing service interruption upon failures

/sig apps
/kind feature

The DaemonSet controller reports aggregate counts without showing whether unavailable or not-yet-updated pods are on NotReady nodes.

## What would you like to be added?

Add a DaemonSet status signal that lets rollout automation distinguish between:

- pods unavailable because the new rollout is problematic and may need rollback, and
- pods unavailable because the underlying node is NotReady, shutting down, disconnected, or under maintenance.

The second case creates problems for automation. The exact solution is up for discussion, but having a status field such as `daemonset.status.numberUnavailableOnNotReadyNodes` would be useful.

The goal is not to make the DaemonSet controller own node repair or maintenance policy. It is to expose enough information for rollout controllers, Helm hooks, operators, and humans to interpret rollout status without reimplementing their own attribution logic.

## Why is this needed?

In large clusters, DaemonSet rollout status can be ambiguous when only a few pods remain unavailable.

Example DaemonSet status from a large cluster:

```yaml
updateStrategy:
  rollingUpdate:
    maxSurge: 0
    maxUnavailable: 10%
  type: RollingUpdate
status:
  currentNumberScheduled: 100
  desiredNumberScheduled: 100
  numberAvailable: 95
  numberMisscheduled: 0
  numberReady: 95
  numberUnavailable: 5
  observedGeneration: 10
  updatedNumberScheduled: 95
```

This DaemonSet is not blocked by `maxUnavailable`; with `desiredNumberScheduled: 100` and `maxUnavailable: 10%`, the rollout budget is 10 pods. However, external rollout verification still needs to answer:

Are the remaining 5 pods unavailable because the rollout is unhealthy, or because they are on NotReady nodes?

`numberUnavailable` alone cannot answer that. It may include pods affected by rollout issues, pod readiness, `minReadySeconds`, pending/rejected pods, terminating pods, old revisions, kubelet issues, or NotReady node state.

Today, automation has to inspect Pods and often list Nodes before deciding whether the rollout should pass. That has two practical costs:

1. Every rollout verifier or operator must implement its own attribution and ignore policy.
2. In large clusters, repeated rollout checks can create additional API server and etcd load, often during periods where node lifecycle events and DaemonSet rollouts are already increasing control-plane activity.

This is especially visible for DaemonSets with broad tolerations:

```yaml
tolerations:
- operator: Exists
```

For these DaemonSets, taints do not reduce the desired node set. A NotReady node may still be counted as desired, but `numberUnavailable` does not show whether NotReady nodes are the cause of the remaining unavailability. Consumers must inspect lower-level objects to attribute the reason.

## How can we reproduce it?

One possible reproduction:

1. Create a cluster with many nodes.
2. Create a DaemonSet with `RollingUpdate`, `maxSurge: 0`, and a non-zero `maxUnavailable`.
3. Give the DaemonSet broad tolerations, such as `operator: Exists`, so node taints do not exclude most nodes from `desiredNumberScheduled`.
4. Start a DaemonSet rollout.
5. Make a small number of nodes NotReady or disconnected while leaving the Node objects present.
6. Observe that DaemonSet status reports aggregate unavailable/not-updated counts, but does not indicate whether NotReady nodes account for those counts.
7. Observe that external rollout automation must inspect Pods and often LIST Nodes to decide whether the rollout should fail or be accepted.

## Current behavior

DaemonSet status reports aggregate scheduling, availability, and update counts. It does not show how many unavailable or not-yet-updated pods are on NotReady nodes.

## Expected behavior

Kubernetes should provide a supported way to identify DaemonSet rollout unavailability caused by NotReady nodes. This could be an API status enhancement, condition, event, or documentation update.

## Related issues

- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/122912 - DaemonSet controller and Graceful Node Shutdown manager disagree when making workload placement decisions.
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/137895 - DaemonSet pod create/reject/delete loops during node deletion/shutdown.
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/117204 - DaemonSet rollout can be affected by nodes joining/leaving or becoming unavailable.
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/138240 - DaemonSet rollout can get stuck when the controller chooses bad nodes. This is related, but the scenario here is different: the rollout may not be stuck on `maxUnavailable`; the missing signal is how to interpret the remaining unavailable/not-updated pods.
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/112733 - Node lifecycle can leave pods misleadingly ready/running in some node state transitions.
issues.title: DaemonSet status should expose why rollout pods are unavailable

issues.body: ### What would you like to be added? An opt-in annotation that tells kube-proxy to skip installing REJECT/DROP rules in the filter table (`KUBE-EXTERNAL-SERVICES`) for a Service's external IPs when no endpoints exist on that node. For example: ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: ntp-anycast annotations: projectcalico.org/loadBalancerIPs: '["1.2.3.4"]' service.kubernetes.io/no-reject-on-no-endpoints: "true" <<< spec: type: LoadBalancer externalTrafficPolicy: Local ports: - name: ntp protocol: UDP port: 123 targetPort: 1123 selector: app: chrony status: loadBalancer: ingress: - ip: 1.2.3.4 # anycast VIP advertised via BGP ipMode: VIP ``` When `no-reject-on-no-endpoints: "true"` is set and no local endpoints exist, kube-proxy would not install the filter rule. Traffic would fall through to normal kernel routing, where the BGP speaker (or similar) handles failover. This allows BGP/anycast deployments to rely on routing failover to a nearby cluster/region. ### Why is this needed? kube-proxy installs filter rules in `KUBE-EXTERNAL-SERVICES` to REJECT or DROP traffic to external IPs when no endpoints are available. This is correct for standard Services — it gives clients an immediate ICMP error instead of a timeout. However, in BGP/anycast deployments this behavior prevents routing failover. The BGP speaker withdraws the route when endpoints disappear, so the kernel routing table would naturally send the packet off-node. But kube-proxy's filter rule intercepts and drops the packet before routing takes effect. Example topology: When local service is working: ```shell › kubectl get endpointslices ntp-anycast-t7n2l NAME ADDRESSTYPE PORTS ENDPOINTS ntp-anycast-t7n2l IPv4 123 100.90.14.133 ``` Output from the node in `Cluster A` with respective pod running: ```shell # iptables-save | grep 1.2.3.4 -A KUBE-SERVICES -d 1.2.3.4/32 -p udp -m comment --comment "test/ntp-anycast:ntp-udp-123 loadbalancer IP" -m udp --dport 123 -j KUBE-EXT-IL6URECE27T65EPH ``` Other node in same cluster `Cluster A` (e.g. with pods consuming this service): ```shell # iptables-save | grep 1.2.3.4 -A KUBE-SERVICES -d 1.2.3.4/32 -p udp -m comment --comment "test/ntp-anycast:ntp-udp-123 loadbalancer IP" -m udp --dport 123 -j KUBE-EXT-IL6URECE27T65EPH -A KUBE-EXTERNAL-SERVICES -d 1.2.3.4/32 -p udp -m comment --comment "test/ntp-anycast:ntp-udp-123 has no local endpoints" -m udp --dport 123 -j DROP ``` When local service fails, we expect a fallback to another region. ```shell › kubectl get endpointslices ntp-anycast-t7n2l NAME ADDRESSTYPE PORTS ENDPOINTS ntp-anycast-t7n2l IPv4 123 ``` Output any node in `Cluster A`: ```shell # iptables-save | grep 1.2.3.4 -A KUBE-EXTERNAL-SERVICES -d 1.2.3.4/32 -p udp -m comment --comment "test/ntp-anycast:ntp-udp-123 has no endpoints" -m udp --dport 123 -j REJECT --reject-with icmp-port-unreachable ``` Due to above rule: - Nodes in `Cluster A` are able to communicate with `1.2.3.4/32` service in `Cluster 2` - Pods in `Cluster A` are *not* able to communicate with `1.2.3.4/32` service in `Cluster 2` and get `connection refused` error message This proposed approach would follow the existing annotation-based extension pattern used by Service features such as `service.kubernetes.io/topology-mode` and load balancer source ranges. Use cases: anycast UDP services, anycast ingress, and active-active multi-cluster Services with shared VIPs. /sig network /kind feature /area kube-proxy
issues.title: Allow BGP/anycast Services to skip kube-proxy external no-endpoints filtering

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

### Description
When combining **Topology Aware Routing** (`service.kubernetes.io/topology-mode: Auto`) with the **HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA)**, there is a systemic architectural gap that risks localized pod starvation during scale-out events, and extreme endpoint imbalance during scale-in events. 

Currently, the HPA evaluates resource utilization (e.g., CPU, Memory) as a global, deployment-wide aggregate average. However, Topology Aware Routing deliberately isolates traffic to localized Availability Zones (AZs). 

This decoupled behavior creates a "Thundering Herd" trap during spikes, and a "Starvation" trap during downscaling, because the network routing layer is highly topology-aware while the autoscaling control loop is completely topology-blind.


### Why is this needed?


### Use Case
We run high-throughput microservices on AWS (EKS) distributed across 3 Availability Zones. To mitigate high cross-AZ data transfer costs ("Cross-AZ Tax") and lower network latency, we rely heavily on Topology Aware Routing. 

We face two distinct structural failures due to the lack of zone-aware autoscaling:

1. **The Scale-Out Trap (Localized Overload):** During localized network shifts or zone-specific traffic spikes, pods in a single AZ (e.g., `us-east-1a`) take 100% of that localized load. If `us-east-1a` pods hit 95% CPU utilization while pods in `us-east-1b` and `us-east-1c` remain idle at 10%, the cluster-wide average sits at ~38%. The HPA fails to trigger, and the pods in the stressed zone crash due to localized resource starvation.
2. **The Scale-In Trap (Zone Depletion):** When traffic drops globally and the HPA triggers a downscale event, the underlying ReplicaSet controller selects pods for termination without respecting zone distribution. It frequently terminates a disproportionate number of pods from a single zone. This leaves that specific zone entirely depleted of endpoints, breaking the path for subsequent localized traffic and forcing expensive, high-latency cross-AZ failovers.

### Proposed Solution / Architectural Approaches
We request native support for zone/topology-awareness within the core autoscaling and lifecycle framework:

1. **Topology-Aware Scale-Out Policy:** Introduce a configuration field in the HPA spec (e.g., `scalingPolicy.topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone`) that evaluates metrics per topology domain. If *any single zone* breaches the target utilization threshold, the HPA should proactively trigger a scale-up event.
2. **Topology-Aware Scale-In (Downscaling):** Ensure that when the HPA reduces the replica count, the scale-in mechanism balances pod terminations proportionally across all active topology domains. The controller must prevent downscaling from leaving a specific zone starved of healthy endpoints.
3. **Handling Soft Constraints (`ScheduleAnyway`):** If a deployment utilizes `whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway`, a Zone-Aware HPA should exploit this flexibility. During a localized spike, it should scale up replicas specifically within the hurting topology domain, allowing a temporary skew to absorb the traffic. During the subsequent scale-in event, the controller must prioritize deleting pods from the skewed zone to automatically return the cluster to its baseline balanced topology spread.

### Related Existing Issue
* **kubernetes/kubernetes #124149** 


### Additional Context
Current ecosystem workarounds require engineers to deploy entirely independent, duplicated Deployments and HPAs per AZ (e.g., `frontend-az-a`, `frontend-az-b`). This completely breaks standard GitOps principles, bloat CI/CD pipelines, and forces rigid, static replica constraints. Native lifecycle zone-awareness is required to bridge the gap between how Kubernetes routes traffic and how it manages compute capacity.
issues.title: [Feature Request] Native Zone/Topology-Aware Scaling in HPA to complement Topology Aware Routing

### What would you like to be added?

v1beta1 of the DRAResourceHealth kubelet gRPC API, migration of all in-tree usage from v1alpha1 to v1beta1, and removal of the superseded v1alpha1 package.

### Why is this needed?

The DRAResourceHealth kubelet gRPC API, used by DRA plugins to stream device health status to the kubelet — was introduced as v1alpha1. The Resource Health Status feature (KEP-4680) is nominally in beta as of v1.36, but its kubelet gRPC API remained on v1alpha1. This inconsistency was flagged in kubernetes/enhancements#4680 as a prerequisite before asking DRA driver authors to adopt the feature.

This issue tracks:
- Adding v1beta1 of the DRAResourceHealth kubelet gRPC API (schema is identical to v1alpha1, stability promotion only)
- Migrating all in-tree usage from v1alpha1 to v1beta1
- Removing the superseded v1alpha1 package

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Reduce the `watchCache.RLock` critical section during WatchList initial events setup from 2x O(N) to   O(1) (by leveraging the existing snapshot to build the event interval outside the lock).  Also, many LIST calls doesn't need to hold a lock for O(N), they can leverage the same snapshot to serve the requests.


For watch-list, currently, `newCacheIntervalFromStore` ([watch_cache_interval.go#L125-L165](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/watch_cache_interval.go#L125-L165)) performs two O(N) passes under `watchCache.RLock` ([cacher.go#L626](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go#L626)):

The equivalent List path ([`listLatestRV`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/watch_cache.go#L640-L658)) under the same RLock does a single O(N) pass:

```go
// Under watchCache.RLock:
result := w.store.OrderedListPrefix(key, continueKey)
```

Option:

** O(1)  using existing snapshots (eliminates lock contention entirely):**

Capture an immutable snapshot reference in O(1) under RLock, register the watcher, release the lock, then build the event interval outside:

```go
// O(1) under watchCache.RLock:
c.watchCache.RLock()
rv := c.watchCache.resourceVersion
snapshot, _ := c.watchCache.snapshots.GetLessOrEqual(rv) 

// Register watcher under c.Lock (same lock ordering as existing code)
c.Lock()
c.watchers.addWatcher(watcher, ...)
c.Unlock()
c.watchCache.RUnlock()
...
Iterate outside the lock
```

This mirrors the pattern already used by `waitAndListExactRV` ([watch_cache.go#L590-L615](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/watch_cache.go#L590-L615)) where List serves from snapshots, and reuses the snapshot stuff is already created on every `processEvent` ([watch_cache.go#L339](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/watch_cache.go#L339)).

Snapshots can be used for some of the LIST calls which are doing O(N) as well, would require a bigger refactor for that.

### Why is this needed?


### Narrow Benchmark data showing lock impact from LIST (vs) Init events part of watch-list

Measured on AMD EPYC 7R13, Go 1.24, comparing what runs under `watchCache.RLock`:

**Single call — no contention:**

| Operation | 500K pods | 1M pods | Allocs |
|---|---|---|---|
| WatchList (`newCacheIntervalFromStore`) | 35ms | 89ms | 500K / 1M |
| List (`OrderedListPrefix`) | 24ms | 53ms | 36-39 |
| **Ratio** | **1.5x** | **1.7x** | |

**Writer starvation : best case (writer starts after first reader acquires RLock):**

| Scenario | WatchList (writer wait) | List (writer wait) | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| 500K pods, 10 readers | 65ms | 32ms | 2.0x |
| 500K pods, 50 readers | 105ms | 32ms | 3.3x |
| 1M pods, 10 readers | 154ms | 66ms | 2.3x |
| 1M pods, 50 readers | 146ms | 75ms | 1.9x |

**Writer starvation : worst case (all readers holding RLock before writer starts):**

This simulates  where 100+ WatchList requests fire simultaneously and all acquire RLock before `processEvent` gets a chance to run, which can be true from 1.35+ if i understand correctly.

| Scenario | WatchList (writer wait) | List (writer wait) | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| 500K pods, 10 readers | 118ms | 39ms | **3.0x** |
| 500K pods, 50 readers | 510ms | 162ms | **3.1x** |
| 1M pods, 10 readers | 212ms | 81ms | **2.6x** |
| 1M pods, 50 readers | 597ms | 285ms | **2.1x** |

At 1M pods with 50 concurrent WatchList readers, `processEvent` (the writer) is blocked for **597ms** , meaning `w.resourceVersion` cannot advance for over half a second. During this time, the watch cache appears stale to all consistent read clients, which may then fall back to etcd.


The `2N` vs `N` difference under `RLock` translates to `2-3x` longer writer starvation under concurrency, and 2N to O(1) at scale makes a huge difference.

AI Disclosure:  This benchmark test results  was written in part with the assistance of claude ^^^ which I reasoned and proof read it. Debugging of issue, watch-cache stalling especially increasing since watch-lists enablement is coming from production issue we had for one of our Clusters we manage.
issues.title: WatchList holds watchCache.RLock for 2x O(N) during initial events setup (vs) O(N) for equivalent List path, causing writer starvation at scale

### What happened?

`kubectl apply --dry-run=client` fails for existing CRD resources with an error
"applying patch locally: expected a struct, but received a nil". 


### What did you expect to happen?

The command should perform successful dry-run.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run the following script, which creates a CRD and the tries to perform
an apply with the `--dry-run=client` option:

```
#!/bin/sh
set -x -e

cat > "crd.yaml" << 'EOF'
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: bugs.bug-repro.example.com
spec:
  group: bug-repro.example.com
  names:
    kind: Bug
    plural: bugs
  scope: Namespaced
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
EOF

cat > "crd-modified.yaml" << 'EOF'
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: bugs.bug-repro.example.com
  labels:
    bug-repro: "true"
spec:
  group: bug-repro.example.com
  names:
    kind: Bug
    plural: bugs
  scope: Namespaced
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
EOF

kubectl apply -f crd.yaml

kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f crd-modified.yaml
```

The output:
```
+ cat
+ cat
+ kubectl apply -f crd.yaml
customresourcedefinition.apiextensions.k8s.io/bugs.bug-repro.example.com created
+ kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f crd-modified.yaml
error: error when applying patch:

to:
Resource: "apiextensions.k8s.io/v1, Resource=customresourcedefinitions", GroupVersionKind: "apiextensions.k8s.io/v1, Kind=CustomResourceDefinition"
Name: "bugs.bug-repro.example.com", Namespace: ""
for: "crd-modified.yaml": applying patch locally: expected a struct, but received a nil
```


### Anything else we need to know?

**Other versions affected**

Reproduces also with kubectl 1.36.0

**An attempt at root cause analysis**

The problem is in 'k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/apply/patcher.go':

1. PatchLocal is called for --dry-run=client. It calls patchSimple with the localApply=true. (the last argument):

``` 
func (p *Patcher) PatchLocal(current runtime.Object, modified []byte, errOut io.Writer) ([]byte, runtime.Object, error) {
	return p.patchSimple(current, modified, "", "", errOut, true)
}
```

Below is patchSimple(). 

At lines 111 and 136 it determines whether the resource supports StrategicMergePatch using OpenAPI and OpenAPI V3 schemas and tries to produce such a patch. 

CustomResourceDefinition is one of such resource kinds, so it will create a patch and set  `patchType` to StrategicMergePatchType. 

patch!=nil, so it will not enter the block on line 149.

The applied resource differs from the current version ,so patch won't be empty,
so it will continue after the check on line 168.

localApply=true, so it will enter the block at line 171

Here on 174 it will call `scheme.Scheme.New(p.Mapping.GroupVersionKind)`, which will fail because CRD is in 'apiextensions.k8s.io/v1', apiextensions are not  builtin k8s types, so the call will fail. 

The code skips checking error status (probably it assumes (erroneously) that StrategicMerge patch always comes from line 149).

So after ignoring the error it calls `strategicpatch.StrategicMergePatch(current, patch, versionedObj)` with versionedObj==nil.

This call fails with the cryptic error "expected a struct, but received a nil" 


```
 98	func (p *Patcher) patchSimple(obj runtime.Object, modified []byte, namespace, name string, errOut io.Writer, localApply bool) ([]byte, runtime.Object, error) {
    99		// Serialize the current configuration of the object from the server.
```
