issues.body:
### What happened?

`kubectl describe pod` prints nothing for a projected volume source of type `clusterTrustBundle` or `podCertificate`. The volume is listed, but the block ends after the `Type:` line, so there is no indication of what is actually projected into the pod:

```
Volumes:
  creds:
    Type:  Projected (a volume that contains injected data from multiple sources)
```

Projected sources of type `secret`, `configMap`, `downwardAPI` and `serviceAccountToken` are printed as usual.

Both of the affected sources are GA and on by default since v1.37 (`ClusterTrustBundleProjection` and `PodCertificateRequest` in `pkg/features/kube_features.go`, both marked `LockToDefault in 1.38`), so this is not gated-off output.

Cause: `printProjectedVolumeSource` is an `if / else if` chain over the four source kinds it knows about, with no branch for `ClusterTrustBundle` or `PodCertificate` and no fallback, so those entries are silently skipped:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/58cd835870c09a025a9ee4974ec5d8e9e2415e25/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/describe/describe.go#L1076-L1097

`describeVolumes` itself already handles every `VolumeSource` kind and has a `default: <unknown>` arm; only the per-projection switch is incomplete.

### What did you expect to happen?

The projected sources to be listed in the same style as the other kinds, for example:

```
Volumes:
  creds:
    Type:                          Projected (a volume that contains injected data from multiple sources)
    ClusterTrustBundleName:        my-bundle
    Path:                          trust-bundle.pem
    Optional:                      false
    PodCertificateSignerName:      example.com/signer
    KeyType:                       ED25519
    CredentialBundlePath:          credentials.pem
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

No cluster feature configuration is needed on v1.37+. Create a pod with a projected volume:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: projected-creds
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox
    command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: creds
      mountPath: /var/run/creds
  volumes:
  - name: creds
    projected:
      sources:
      - clusterTrustBundle:
          name: my-bundle
          path: trust-bundle.pem
      - podCertificate:
          signerName: example.com/signer
          keyType: ED25519
          credentialBundlePath: credentials.pem
```

```console
$ kubectl describe pod projected-creds | grep -A5 Volumes:
```

The `creds:` block stops after the `Type:` line.

At the unit level, describing a pod whose only volume is a projected volume with a `clusterTrustBundle` source produces output containing neither the bundle name nor the path.

### Anything else we need to know?

This is the same class of gap as #142208 (`fileKeyRef` missing from the container env output): a source kind added to the API without a matching arm in the describer.

`podCertificate` is the more user-visible of the two, since a pod does not start until certificates have been issued for every `podCertificate` source in its spec, and `kubectl describe pod` is the first place an operator looks when a pod is stuck.

I have a fix with unit tests and will open a PR shortly.

/sig cli
/area kubectl

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

An extension to the Node Declared Features (NDF, KEP-5328) framework so that an individual feature can distinguish *first admission* of a pod from *re-admission* of a pod that was already admitted on this node before a kubelet restart, and choose not to require the feature in the latter case.

Today `Feature.InferForScheduling(podInfo *types.PodInfo)` receives only `Spec` and `Status`, and the same call is used in three places:

- scheduler `PreFilter` / `SignPod` (`pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/nodedeclaredfeatures/nodedeclaredfeatures.go`), with `PodInfo{Spec}` only,
- kubelet first admission (`pkg/kubelet/lifecycle/handlers.go`, `declaredFeaturesAdmitHandler.Admit`),
- kubelet re-admission after restart, which goes through exactly the same `HandlePodAdditions -> allocationManager.AddPod -> canAdmitPod -> Admit` path.

There is no signal available to the feature that would let it tell the last two apart.

Proposed change (prototyped, all additive, no behavior change for existing features):

1. `types.PodInfo` gets a new field `PreviouslyAdmitted bool` ("the kubelet holds a persisted allocation for this pod from an earlier admission; always false during scheduling").
2. `lifecycle.PodAdmitAttributes` gets `PreviouslyAllocated bool`.
3. `allocation.manager.canAdmitPod` populates it from `m.HasPodAllocatedResources(pod.UID)`. The allocation manager restores its `allocated_pods_state` checkpoint synchronously in `NewManager`, before the sync loop starts, and `canAdmitPod` runs before `SetAllocatedResources`, so on first admission the value is `false` and on re-admission after restart it is `true`. Since `InPlacePodVerticalScaling` is GA and locked to `true` in 1.35, this checkpoint is always present; it stores an entry for every admitted pod (including BestEffort), keyed by pod UID.
4. `declaredFeaturesAdmitHandler.Admit` copies the flag into `PodInfo`.

A feature that wants "soft" re-admission then implements:

```go
func (f *myFeature) InferForScheduling(podInfo *types.PodInfo) bool {
    if podInfo.PreviouslyAdmitted {
        return false
    }
    return podUsesFeature(podInfo.Spec)
}
```

### Why is this needed?

KEP-5328 currently documents a single, fail-closed policy for kubelet restarts:

> Node declared features are checked by the scheduler during scheduling and then validated again by the Kubelet's admission handlers before a pod's containers can start. This validation is critical for handling cases where a node's declared features change after a pod has been scheduled.
>
>If a Kubelet restarts with a different configuration (e.g., a feature gate is disabled), its declared features may change. Upon restart, the Kubelet re-evaluates all existing pods for admission and if a running pod requires a declared feature that the node no longer provides, the Kubelet's admission check will fail. Consequently, the pod will not be started and will be transitioned to a `Failed` phase. This ensures that a pod does not run on a node that cannot support its feature requirements. This behavior is consistent with the best practice of draining a node before making significant configuration changes, such as toggling feature gates.
>
> — keps/sig-node/5328-node-declared-features/README.md:440-442

This is the correct default for most NDF features: if the node can no longer provide something the pod fundamentally depends on, the pod should be evicted.

However, there is a class of features where this is unnecessarily disruptive:

- the feature only affects pod setup and is irrelevant once the pod is running, or
- the feature provides optional, additive functionality that a running pod can simply lose without breaking.

An example is KEP-6122 (Configurable Scaling Delay, targeting Alpha in v1.38). It uses NDF in its intended role: a kubelet with `InPlacePodVerticalScalingExclusiveCPUsScaleDownDelay` enabled declares the feature in `node.status.declaredFeatures`, and the scheduler only places pods that set `scaleDownGracePeriodSeconds` on nodes that declare it, so a pod never lands on a node that would silently ignore its grace period. The same KEP explicitly departs from the KEP-5328 default for one case ("Grace Period Not Honored" section): when the gate is turned off on a node that already runs such a pod and the kubelet restarts, the pod is not rejected, because killing a running latency-sensitive workload is worse than resizing it without the preparation window. The kubelet is instead expected to apply the next scale-down without the delay and report it via the `PodResizeInProgress` condition message and a `ScaleDownGracePeriodNotHonored` event. Its PRR rollback answer is built on this: existing pods keep running, only the delay is lost.

With today's NDF framework that behaviour cannot be implemented. The scheduler's node filter and the kubelet's admission check are driven by the same `Feature.InferForScheduling` method, so a feature that returns `true` to obtain scheduler filtering also gets fatal kubelet re-admission after a restart with the gate disabled: the pod fails with `PodFeatureUnsupported` and is killed.
issues.title: Node Declared Features: allow a feature to opt out of re-admission enforcement after kubelet restart

### What would you like to be added?

Right now, we fuzz the internal version, then convert internal -> external -> internal and verify the object didn't lose data.
In some cases, e.g. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137633, internal -> external is lossy by design (e.g. new internal fields for non-serialized types), which means we need to add fuzzer funcs to clear any such data in the internal type when fuzzing.

This leaves a little bit of a coverage gap, that could be closed by also going the other way: fuzz external, then convert external -> internal -> external, and verify equivalence.

### Why is this needed?

This would improve the coverage of some special cases of API conversion.
issues.title: Add roundtrip coverage of fuzzing an external version, ensuring a roundtrip through internal preserves data

### What would you like to be added?

I would like to propose adding a support to client-go library for creating multiple connections **to the same endpoint** and using some naive load balancing (such as round robin or power of 2) to send traffic.

The option cloud be set using one of the following mechanisms:
* In kubeconfig, via option similar to 'disableCompression' we have today
* In golang, by setting respective value, e.g. via rest.Config flag

Goal:
* In many environments, the endpoint specified in kubeconfig is an L4 load balancer that picks backend randomly. By opening multiple connections we can split the traffic from a single client / controller to multiple kube-apiserver replicas and avoid single kube-apiserver instance becoming overloaded while the other replicas are idle.
* Avoid single-replica pinning issue -- improve client experience in case of single kube-apiserver replica slowdown / unhealthiness. E.g. today kubelet sends traffic only to a single kcp replica. if the replica is slow or unhealthy (e.g. not able to process requests but alive), all connections are persistent and all kubelet's retries are still going to that replica, leading to marking the replica as unhealthy. By sending traffic to multiple replicas, we increase chances (both must be unhealthy).

Out of scope:
* Multiple endpoint support (we still want client-go to open connections to single endpoint -- we rely on L4 load balancer to assign connections to multiple backends)
* Endpoint discovery: Client-go somehow finds out what are the IPs for kube-apiserver instances.

### Why is this needed?

This is important use case for performance-heavy controllers / schedulers and similar technique is widely used by the components (see e.g. [transportHack](https://github.com/kubernetes/perf-tests/blob/1317eb81116835070beecdb2f6cb4eda3fd27b1c/clusterloader2/pkg/framework/config/client_config.go#L86) in clusterloader).

By moving this concept to core client-go library we can help the controllers to avoid this "transportHack" or similar technique. By standardising this pattern, we can make this opinionated and ensure that controllers are behaving in expected way and automatically benefit from potential improvements in this area.

issues.body:
Linux 6.7 added support for ["remote partitions"](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html#:~:text=partition%20is%20created.-,cpuset.cpus.partition,-A%20read%2Dwrite), which enables containers to allocate exclusive CPUs without modifying any other cgroups. With the deprecation of cgroups v1, we should migrate CPU manager to leverage this approach.

### Background

Currently, with static CPU policy, cpu_manager runs a reconcile loop (default 10s period) to sync CPU allocation to containers. It manages a default set, and every container that doesn't have exclusive CPUs gets assigned the default set. The default set is updated (for every container) to remove CPUs as they're allocated exclusively.

Problems with this approach:
1. Eventual consistency: When an exclusive CPU is assigned, there is up to 10s (or more!) delay before that CPU is removed from the default set of other containers.
2. No protection from system processes: Only containers managed by the Kubelet are excluded from using the assigned CPUs. System processes (e.g. the Kubelet itself) can still be scheduled to it.
3. Every static CPU assignment (or release) requires updating every other container on the node. These are all done through `UpdateContainerResources` requests, and are subject to global NRI locks.
4. Container reconciliation outside of SyncPod: the reconcile loop calls UpdateContainerResources directly. Normally, all direct container operations like that happen within SyncPod. Performing the operation outside of SyncPod makes this more prone to race conditions.

### Proposal

1. The full set of assignable CPUs is written to `cpuset.cpus.exclusive` on the full cgroup tree (`kubelet.slice`, `kubelet-kubepods.slice`), and pod-level cgroups.
2. When a container is assigned exclusive CPUs, it sets `cpuset.cpus.exclusive` to the assigned set, and `cpuset.cpus.partition=root` (some specialized workloads like DPDK may want `isolated`). This is set on container creation, or in `doPodResizeAction` on resize, both of which are in `SyncPod`.
3. Remove the cpu_manager reconciliation loop: it's no longer needed.

/sig node
/kind feature
/cc @pravk03 @ffromani @dchen1107 @Chunxia202410 @lukaszwojciechowski @esotsal
issues.title: Leverage remote partitions for exclusive CPUs (Linux 6.7+)

issues.body:
## What would you like to be added?

An exclusive mode for PodGroup topology placement in kube-scheduler: a PodGroup lands in a topology domain (one value of a node label) that no other in-scope PodGroup occupies, and keeps that domain to itself while its pods run there.

JobSet, LeaderWorkerSet (LWS) and DisaggregatedSet each implement this today by injecting pod affinity and anti-affinity. It came up in kubernetes-sigs/lws#1064 (graduating the LWS `exclusive-topology` annotation to a spec field), where the suggestion was to raise it here instead of implementing it in each controller. This issue asks a question; it does not propose an API.

### What KEP-5732 covers

`TopologyConstraint{Key}` puts all pods of one PodGroup in one domain. Its doc comment says "Different PodGroups can land on different domain instances" ([KEP-5732](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/e3340bf8f7eaa2566ff962fa425ec35d42a6d793/keps/sig-scheduling/5732-topology-aware-workload-scheduling/README.md#L252-L258), [v1beta1 types.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7708623c1a6c115ef1fd4f5f90b98cb7c49d337e/staging/src/k8s.io/api/scheduling/v1beta1/types.go#L858-L868)). Nothing keeps another PodGroup out of that domain, and in the KEP review a reviewer noted that PodGroup replicas may land in different domains "but they can also share them" ([comment](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5733#discussion_r2610398971), [reply](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5733#discussion_r2623294009)). Exclusivity is not among the KEP's [Goals](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/e3340bf8f7eaa2566ff962fa425ec35d42a6d793/keps/sig-scheduling/5732-topology-aware-workload-scheduling/README.md#L137-L151) or [Future Extensions](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/e3340bf8f7eaa2566ff962fa425ec35d42a6d793/keps/sig-scheduling/5732-topology-aware-workload-scheduling/README.md#L474-L508). I did not find an existing issue asking for it.

### Requested semantics

For a PodGroup G with exclusive placement on node label key K:

1. All scheduled pods of G are on nodes with the same value d of K. This is what `TopologyConstraint` does today.
2. G is placed only in a domain that holds no pods of another in-scope PodGroup, and while G has pods in d, no other in-scope PodGroup is placed in d.
3. d is chosen for the whole group: at least `minCount` pods must fit, as KEP-5732 Phase 2 already checks for each Placement under the Gang policy ([README.md:377-386](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/e3340bf8f7eaa2566ff962fa425ec35d42a6d793/keps/sig-scheduling/5732-topology-aware-workload-scheduling/README.md#L377-L386)).
4. It is a hard constraint checked at scheduling time only, like `requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution`.

"In-scope" is the open part, and the three controllers define it differently:

| Controller | Unit | Kept out of the domain | How |
|---|---|---|---|
| JobSet, [`alpha.jobset.sigs.k8s.io/exclusive-topology`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/jobset/blob/a4fae2847493efda10cc427a572a778bf2f1fe1a/api/jobset/v1alpha2/jobset_types.go#L42-L48) | child Job | pods of any other JobSet Job at the same priority, all namespaces | required affinity and anti-affinity on the leader pod ([pod_webhook.go:117-162](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/jobset/blob/a4fae2847493efda10cc427a572a778bf2f1fe1a/pkg/webhooks/pod_webhook.go#L117-L162)); followers get the leader's domain as a nodeSelector ([:164-198](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/jobset/blob/a4fae2847493efda10cc427a572a778bf2f1fe1a/pkg/webhooks/pod_webhook.go#L164-L198)) |
| LWS, [`exclusive-topology` and `subgroup-exclusive-topology`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/lws/blob/8dd3fd54dd4f286bf115d9214372970633dcaae8/api/leaderworkerset/v1/leaderworkerset_types.go#L28-L34) | replica, or subgroup | pods of any other LWS replica (or subgroup) in the same namespace | required affinity and anti-affinity ([pod_webhook.go:255-297](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/lws/blob/8dd3fd54dd4f286bf115d9214372970633dcaae8/pkg/webhooks/pod_webhook.go#L255-L297)); at replica level only the leader carries them and workers get the leader's domain as a nodeSelector ([pod_controller.go:298-309](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/lws/blob/8dd3fd54dd4f286bf115d9214372970633dcaae8/pkg/controllers/pod_controller.go#L298-L309)) |
| DisaggregatedSet, [`placementPolicy.type: ExclusiveTopology`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/lws/blob/8dd3fd54dd4f286bf115d9214372970633dcaae8/api/disaggregatedset/v1/disaggregatedset_types.go#L147-L183) | slice (one copy of every role, across several LWS) | pods of any other DisaggregatedSet slice in the same namespace | required affinity and anti-affinity on every pod ([affinity.go](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/lws/blob/8dd3fd54dd4f286bf115d9214372970633dcaae8/pkg/utils/disaggregatedset/affinity.go#L37-L103)) |

In all three, pods without the controller's labels (for example a plain Deployment) can still share the domain unless taints are used ([DisaggregatedSet docs](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/lws/blob/8dd3fd54dd4f286bf115d9214372970633dcaae8/site/content/en/docs/concepts/disaggregatedset/placement-policy/_index.md#L43-L45)).

## Why is this needed?

Emulating exclusivity with pod affinity in each controller has known problems:

1. **No look-ahead.** The leader (JobSet, LWS) or the first pod (DisaggregatedSet) commits the domain, and the rest of the group stays Pending if it does not fit. KEP-5732 rejects pod inter-affinity for this reason ([Alternatives](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/e3340bf8f7eaa2566ff962fa425ec35d42a6d793/keps/sig-scheduling/5732-topology-aware-workload-scheduling/README.md#L935-L946)), and the DisaggregatedSet KEP documents the same risk and defers to gang scheduling ([KEP-848](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/lws/blob/8dd3fd54dd4f286bf115d9214372970633dcaae8/keps/848-disaggregatedset-placement-policy/README.md#L194-L201)).
2. **No gang scheduling together with exclusivity.** LWS alpha rejects gang or WAS topology constraints combined with `exclusive-topology` ([KEP-666 rule 10](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/lws/blob/8dd3fd54dd4f286bf115d9214372970633dcaae8/keps/666-gang-scheduling-in-lws/README.md#L544-L546), [phase_one.go](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/lws/blob/8dd3fd54dd4f286bf115d9214372970633dcaae8/pkg/schedulerprovider/phase_one.go#L451-L453)). JobSet's docs say native gang scheduling will enable more robust topology-aware scheduling, which they call the core objective of the exclusive topology feature ([tpu_multislice.md](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/jobset/blob/a4fae2847493efda10cc427a572a778bf2f1fe1a/site/content/en/docs/tasks/tpu_multislice.md#L35)). The LWS docs ask users to pick either native exclusive placement or Kueue TAS bin-packing ([LWS docs](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/lws/blob/8dd3fd54dd4f286bf115d9214372970633dcaae8/site/content/en/docs/examples/leaderworkerset/topology-aware-scheduling/_index.md#L19-L29)).
3. **Cost.** The Kubernetes docs advise against inter-pod affinity in clusters larger than several hundred nodes ([assign-pod-node.md](https://github.com/kubernetes/website/blob/1c7aa9955e884879397ed15de88605f05eb61d1f/content/en/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/assign-pod-node.md#L261-L263)). JobSet measured 58 vs 266 pods/s at 5,000 nodes with its exclusive-placement affinities (kubernetes-sigs/jobset#174), then moved to leader-only terms (kubernetes-sigs/jobset#310) and added a manual node-label and taint mode (kubernetes-sigs/jobset#312). DisaggregatedSet still puts the terms on every pod.
4. **Controller machinery.** JobSet rejects follower pod creation until the leader is scheduled, which loads the API server (kubernetes-sigs/jobset#482). It also needed race handling (kubernetes-sigs/jobset#341) and limited exclusivity to the same priority level as part of supporting preemption (kubernetes-sigs/jobset#682, kubernetes-sigs/jobset#687).
5. **Other placers cannot see it.** Kueue TAS picks nodes without seeing the injected anti-affinity, so it can assign exclusive LWS pods a domain their anti-affinity forbids (kubernetes-sigs/kueue#15057). The direction suggested there is the WAS integration (kubernetes-sigs/kueue#13149). Kueue TAS Topology Spreading caps a domain's share within one spreading group to a value in (0, 1), so it does not exclude other workloads ([KEP-13746](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/blob/df693920cb4be96ed909ab2292966a1c7635800e/keps/13746-tas-topology-spreading/README.md#L460-L463)).
6. **Diverging definitions.** Scope has been argued separately in each project (kubernetes-sigs/lws#539, kubernetes-sigs/jobset#1057). Graduating each controller's version on its own (kubernetes-sigs/lws#1064) would fix three different scopes into three APIs.

## Question for the WG

Should WAS support exclusive topology placement for PodGroups in kube-scheduler, so controllers can express it through their PodGroup topology constraints instead of injecting pod affinity?

If yes, scope needs a single answer: same namespace or cluster-wide, PodGroups only or all pods, whether priority matters, and whether it applies to CompositePodGroups (a DisaggregatedSet slice spans several LWS).

The answer will inform whether LWS graduates its annotation to its own spec field or maps it onto WAS (kubernetes-sigs/lws#1064). I will add this to the WG meeting agenda.

KEP: kubernetes/enhancements#5732
Related: kubernetes-sigs/lws#1064, kubernetes-sigs/kueue#15057, #136207

/sig scheduling
/sig apps
/wg workload-aware-scheduling
/kind feature
issues.title: WAS: exclusive topology placement for PodGroups (one PodGroup per topology domain)

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Workload-aware (PodGroup) preemption currently operates in three steps during PodGroupPostFilter:
- **Remove all potential victims**: Identify all lower-priority workloads/pods in the cluster that the preempting PodGroup is eligible to preempt and remove them from the scheduling snapshot upfront.
- **Speculatively schedule the preemptor**: Run the standard PodGroup scheduling algorithm on this stripped snapshot to find a feasible node assignment for all pods in the preempting PodGroup.
- **Reprieve unnecessary victims**: Iterate through the removed victims (ordered from most important to least important via MoreImportantVictim) and restore any victim that can still coexist with the chosen PodGroup placement; evict the remaining victims.

During step 2, because all potential victims have already been removed from the snapshot, standard Score plugins cannot distinguish between:
- Nodes that already have sufficient free capacity (requiring no preemption).
- Nodes where capacity was only freed by removing high-priority or large PodGroup victims versus low-priority or small victims.
- Nodes whose victims have already been condemned by an earlier pod in the same preempting PodGroup (especially when preempting a victim PodGroup with DisruptionMode: PodGroup frees spots across multiple nodes).

As a result, the scheduler treats all freed nodes equally and scatters the preempting PodGroup across occupied and empty nodes alike. Step 3 (reprieveVictim) can only save victims on nodes that were not selected in Step 2, leading to:
- Unnecessary preemption of victims even when free nodes exist in the cluster.
- Preemption of higher-priority or larger workloads when lower-priority victims could have been chosen instead.
- Cascading disruption of multiple victim PodGroups instead of reusing spots freed by already-condemned victim PodGroups.


### Proposed solution
Introduce victim-aware node scoring in DefaultPreemption active only during PodGroup preemption evaluation that:
1. Track surviving vs. condemned victims across the PodGroup scheduling pass
2. Compute per-node incremental ("delta") victims in PreScore
3. Prioritize nodes by preemption cost in Score, assigning the maximum score (100) to nodes that require no new victims (either genuinely free nodes or nodes whose victims were already condemned by an earlier pod in the PodGroup), deferring tie-breaking among zero-cost nodes to standard Score plugins.
For nodes where preemption is required, we score them accordingly to the "importance" of the victims  - the more important victims needs to be preempted (priority, size, etc.), the lower the score of that node is.

The POC implementing this approach is in: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142325 (together with the results from the benchmarks being introduced in: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142679 ).

### Why is this needed?

Minimizing the "cost" of preemptions is the goal for all users and current algorithm may result in:
- Unnecessary preemption of victims even when free nodes exist in the cluster.
- Preemption of higher-priority or larger workloads when lower-priority victims could have been chosen instead.
- Cascading disruption of multiple victim PodGroups instead of reusing spots freed by already-condemned victim PodGroups.

which isn't acceptable for many users.
issues.title: Workload-Aware Preemption may result in unnecessary or cascading preemptions

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?


Topology-Aware Scheduling (TAS) for CompositePodGroups currently schedules child workloads sequentially in `compositePodGroupSchedulingDefaultAlgorithm`:
- **Enumerate candidate placements**: For each child PodGroup (or nested CompositePodGroup), enumerate all candidate topology domains (e.g., zones, racks, or nodes) matching the group's topology constraints.
- **Evaluate candidate placements from scratch**: Iterate through every candidate placement, running simulated pod scheduling (`SignPod`, `PreFilter`, `Filter`, `Score`, and tentative `Reserve`) across candidate nodes, and computing placement scores via `PlacementScore` plugins.
- **Select best placement and commit**: Normalize placement scores, select the highest-scoring candidate (breaking ties randomly), tentatively commit the child's placement to the snapshot, and advance to the next child.

When scheduling CompositePodGroups representing distributed workloads (e.g., distributed AI/ML training or HPC jobs), the hierarchy frequently consists of multiple identical child PodGroups (e.g., homogeneous worker groups with identical pod templates, resource requests, and topology constraints).
While kube-scheduler already employs opportunistic batching at the **pod/node level** (KEP-5598: reusing node evaluation outcomes across consecutive identical pods and invalidating only the chosen node), no equivalent mechanism exists at the **PodGroup/placement level**.

Because candidate placements are evaluated independently from scratch for every child in the hierarchy:
- The scheduler re-evaluates feasibility and re-runs placement scoring plugins across all candidate placements for each child, even though cluster state and capacity outside the previously selected placement remain unchanged.
- For a CompositePodGroup with $M$ child groups and $P$ candidate placements, this results in $O(M \times P)$ simulated placement evaluations. On large clusters (e.g., thousands of nodes across tens of racks or zones), this produces thousands of redundant placement evaluations.
- Non-overlapping candidate placements (placements that share no nodes with the placement selected by the previous child) retain identical feasibility and raw placement scores, but are discarded and re-evaluated from scratch in each child iteration.

As a result, the scheduler spends significant time in redundant placement simulation, leading to:
- High scheduling latency for CompositePodGroup workloads (e.g., spending dozens to hundreds of seconds in `scheduler_podgroup_scheduling_algorithm_duration_seconds`).
- Excessive CPU and memory consumption in the scheduler from repeated pod filtering and scoring across unaffected nodes.
- Head-of-line blocking in the scheduler queue for subsequent workloads waiting for scheduling cycles.

### Proposed solution

Conceptually, the proposed solution **lifts opportunistic batching (KEP-5598) from the pod/node level to the PodGroup/placement level**: instead of evaluating individual nodes for consecutive identical pods, it caches candidate topology placements across consecutive identical child PodGroups (or nested CompositePodGroups).

We propose introducing placement result and score caching in `scheduleOnePodGroup` for CompositePodGroups (guarded by an alpha feature gate `TopologyAwareCompositePodGroupOptimization`) that:
1. **Detect identical consecutive child groups**: Check equivalence between consecutive children (`arePodGroupsIdenticalWithRoot` / cached `QueuedPodInfo.PodSignature`) to determine if candidate placement evaluations can be reused across child iterations.
2. **Cache placement feasibility and unweighted raw scores**: Split placement scoring in the framework into raw plugin scoring (`RunRawPlacementScorePlugins`, computing raw scores in $[0, \text{MaxPlacementScore}]$) and normalization (`NormalizePlacementScores`). Cache feasibility outcomes and raw scores across candidate placements for identical child groups.
3. **Invalidate only overlapping candidate placements**: When child $i$ selects placement $p_{\text{last}}$, identify and invalidate only candidate placements that overlap (share nodes) with $p_{\text{last}}$ (analogous to invalidating the selected node in pod-level opportunistic batching). All non-overlapping candidate placements reuse their cached feasibility and raw plugin scores.
4. **Recalculate affected placements and re-normalize scores**: Re-evaluate feasibility and raw scores only for invalidated overlapping placements, update the cache, re-normalize scores across all surviving feasible placements, and break ties randomly to preserve identical placement distribution and quality.
5. **Support multi-level hierarchies**: Recursively propagate placement caching across both leaf `PodGroup`s and nested child `CompositePodGroup`s.

The AI based POC implementing this approach is available on [44past4/kubernetes:cpg-tas-optimization](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/compare/master...44past4:kubernetes:cpg-tas-optimization?diff=unified&w) branch (with benchmarks added to `test/integration/scheduler_perf/cpg/cpg_test.go`).

### Why is this needed?

Minimizing scheduling algorithm latency for large multi-gang workloads is essential for cluster throughput and resource utilization. The current algorithm results in:
- High algorithmic latency scaling quadratically with the number of identical child groups and candidate topology domains.
- Thousands of redundant simulated placement evaluations on nodes whose capacity and state are unchanged.
- Head-of-line queue delay for subsequent workloads in multi-tenant environments.

Extending the opportunistic batching principles of KEP-5598 from the pod/node level to the PodGroup/placement level eliminates these redundant evaluations while preserving identical placement quality and scoring semantics.

In [scheduler performance benchmarks](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1USEVtKRIKcOBdsa26qfaSGFMif4HlFVqcvtijAGx4hA/edit?usp=sharing) on a 5,000-node cluster (5 zones, 50 racks) with CompositePodGroups of 4 to 128 child groups:
- Placement feasibility evaluations were reduced by **`3.05x` to `35.56x`** (e.g., `12,800 → 360` evaluations for 256 PodGroups across 50 racks).
- Pure TAS algorithm execution time (`scheduler_podgroup_scheduling_algorithm_duration_seconds`) was reduced by **`64.1%` to `95.4%`** (**`2.79x` to `21.71x` speedup**).
- End-to-end workload scheduling duration improved by **`2.45x` to `3.90x`** with identical placement distribution.
issues.title: Optimize Topology-Aware Scheduling for CompositePodGroups with identical children

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Support an optional TLS server name override for URL-based admission webhooks, so the hostname used for TLS certificate verification and SNI can be configured independently of the hostname or IP address used to connect.

For example, an optional `tlsServerName` field in `admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1` `WebhookClientConfig` could allow:

```yaml
clientConfig:
  url: https://webhook.private.example.net:9443/validate
  tlsServerName: admission.example.com
  caBundle: <PEM-encoded CA bundle>
```

In this example, the API server would connect to `webhook.private.example.net:9443`, send `admission.example.com` as TLS SNI, and verify the server certificate against `admission.example.com` using the configured CA bundle. The HTTP Host header would continue to follow the URL. This field name and placement are illustrative; feedback on the appropriate API/configuration surface would be welcome.

When the override is omitted, existing behavior would be preserved: TLS verification uses the URL hostname. Certificate chain and hostname verification would remain enabled when an override is configured.

### Why is this needed?

A webhook's network connection address and its TLS identity can differ in deployments that use private endpoints, TCP proxies, or environment-specific routing aliases. For example, several clusters may reach the same admission service through different private DNS names, while that service presents a certificate for a stable identity such as `admission.example.com`.

Today, URL-based admission webhooks cannot express that distinction. Operators must arrange for the URL hostname to appear in the certificate's SANs, or arrange DNS/routing so the certificate's hostname reaches the intended endpoint. This couples certificate management to routing names and can require adding environment-specific SANs or coordinating DNS changes whenever a connection endpoint changes.

An explicit TLS server name would allow operators to choose the connection endpoint while continuing to authenticate the intended service identity. Kubernetes already supports this distinction for ordinary kubeconfig clients through `tls-server-name`.

### Current behavior and references

In the upstream source inspected at commit `f0126a827d42264174a7137217b52f622d8e9a98`:

- [`WebhookClientConfig`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f0126a827d42264174a7137217b52f622d8e9a98/staging/src/k8s.io/api/admissionregistration/v1/types.go) exposes `url`, `service`, and `caBundle`, without a TLS server name override.
- The [URL-based webhook client](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f0126a827d42264174a7137217b52f622d8e9a98/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/webhook/client.go) copies the resolver's REST configuration and sets the connection host from the URL.
- The [default admission authentication resolver](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f0126a827d42264174a7137217b52f622d8e9a98/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/webhook/authentication.go) reads kubeconfig `AuthInfos`; it does not load a cluster's `tls-server-name` setting. Configuring that setting in an admission authentication kubeconfig therefore does not provide this override.

Related historical issue: #52366 concerned setting the service DNS name for service-based admission webhooks. This request concerns an operator-configurable TLS identity for URL-based admission webhooks.

This limitation is blocking us from onboarding a new admission webhook. Our infrastructure supplies a routing hostname for the webhook endpoint, while the serving certificate contains infrastructure-managed service identities. Infrastructure restrictions prevent us from adding custom SANs to that certificate, including the routing hostname. The admission request therefore fails with a certificate hostname mismatch. For example, with hostnames anonymized:

```text
failed to call webhook: Post "https://webhook.private.example.net:9443/mutate-ray-io-v1-rayjob?timeout=10s": tls: failed to verify certificate: x509: certificate is valid for admission.example.com, not webhook.private.example.net
```

We need to connect using the supplied routing hostname while verifying the certificate against an existing service identity. URL-based admission webhook configuration currently provides no way to express this. This is a new-webhook onboarding limitation, not a regression. I would appreciate SIG API Machinery feedback on the configuration surface and whether a KEP is appropriate.

/sig api-machinery
/kind feature
issues.title: Support TLS server name overrides for URL-based admission webhooks

### What would you like to be added?

Add `QUERY` to the HTTP methods accepted by the API server proxy
subresources (at minimum services, ideally pods and nodes too):

- /api/v1/namespaces/{ns}/services/{name}/proxy/{path}
- /api/v1/namespaces/{ns}/pods/{name}/proxy/{path}
- /api/v1/nodes/{name}/proxy/{path}

`kubectl proxy` forwards to these endpoints, so it would gain the
support without separate changes.

### Why is this needed?

QUERY is now a standards-track HTTP method, defined in RFC 10008
(https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc10008). It is a safe, idempotent
request method that carries content, so clients can send complex
queries without putting them in the URL and without using POST. Because
it is safe and idempotent, caches and clients can safely retry it.

The proxy subresources only forward an allowlist of methods. On master,
`proxyMethods` in pkg/registry/core/service/proxy.go is:

    []string{"GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE", "HEAD", "OPTIONS"}

`ConnectMethods()` returns this list, so a QUERY request through the
proxy is expected to be rejected with 405 Method Not Allowed instead of
reaching the backend. (I have not yet confirmed this on a running
cluster.) As a result, backends that implement QUERY (search and
query-style APIs) cannot be reached through `kubectl proxy` or the API
server proxy.

I searched kubernetes/kubernetes and the kubernetes org for existing
issues about QUERY or the IETF draft (safe-method-w-body) and found
none.

### Possible approach

Add "QUERY" to the proxy method lists for the affected subresources.
Open questions for maintainers:
- Should this apply to services only, or to pods and nodes as well?
- Does the API server's request handling, authorization (verb mapping),
  or audit logging need changes for a new method?

### Workarounds today

`kubectl port-forward`, or fronting the service with a gateway or
ingress that passes arbitrary methods.
issues.title: Support the HTTP QUERY method (RFC 10008) in API server proxy subresources

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

As a follow-up and complement to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/142223
 and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/132233, we propose updating APF work estimation to reflect object estimations with a semi automated process of updating the estimates when needed.

Instead of a bespoke and manual process of adjusting request costs like we did just for large LISTs, we should standardize the process of estimating request cost that can be easier to automate and cover other methods.

Using standardized exemplar object shapes like https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/138415 and measuring allocations allows us to create a deterministic process of comparing request costs across different methods and serialization formats. We see allocations as a natural extension to the current request cost model that accounts not only for maximum live memory, but also for the additional asynchronous GC work (mark-assist and sweep contention) that is not proportional to synchronous CPU duration (seats * time) yet can be deterministically measured.

We imagine a simple benchmark that runs a for loop that executes each type of request one by one and uses metrics to measure allocations on apiserver. 

The seat assignment will now be a combination of maximum live memory, number of allocations (mallocs), and allocated bytes (allocMB) while handling a request (mapped to the signals available at admission time: input/average object size, estimated object count, and watcher count). Like before, we will separate two types of requests—streamed (WatchList and LIST with streaming responses) and non-streamed—and use different seat calculations for them based on the worst case. The seat cost will be renormalized to allow the same baseline number of requests as before.

Based on our experiments, using this method better represents the real request cost (reducing the worst-case LIST cost-per-seat discrepancy from 222x down to 3.3x) and allows up to 3x more cheap requests, while detecting and punishing unexpected heavyweights (5x–50x).

### Why is this needed?

Ensure we can systematically detect and price unexpected, allocation-heavy requests ("allocation mines") such as:

* PATCH vs. PUT: Both are charged 1 seat, yet PATCH does 2–3x more allocations than PUT on the happy path  and nearly 30x more allocations  during in-place GuaranteedUpdate transaction conflicts.
* WATCH opened on an older RV: Charged 1 seat, yet replaying history from the watch cache ring buffer does not benefit from the cachingObject serialization cache and calls DeepCopyObject() per event—requiring 100–160x more allocations than a live watcher.
* WatchList vs. Streaming LIST: Charged the same 10 seats as LIST based on peak memory, yet WatchList allocates 3–8x more bytes and 2–2.5x more objects due to DeepCopyObject() of initial events—cutting sustained kube-apiserver throughput in half and doubling P99 latency.
* No separation of DELETECOLLECTION with seats defaults to 1 seat despite allocating per object deleted 

The goal is that by systematically detecting high-allocation paths and increasing their seat cost, giving visibility to inefficient paths and motivating their optimization thus prevent hitting the Go runtime allocation ceiling (discussed in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/142223
). While we will optimize those paths over time, APF is the only mechanism that can prevent degradation of kube-apiserver performance in the meantime.

---

### Benchmark Data (For `10KB` Exemplar Pod)

#### 1. Collection & Watch Methods (Allocations per `10KB` Pod Returned)

| Request (`10KB` Exemplar Pod) | Per-Object Seat Calculation in APF? | Alloc Bytes / Pod | Alloc Objects / Pod | Ratio vs. `LIST ?rv=0` (Bytes / Objs) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`LIST ?resourceVersion=0` (Streamed)** | Yes (capped at `1 MB`) | **`2.18 KB / pod`** | **`49 objs / pod`** | **`1.0x / 1.0x` (Baseline)** |
| **`WATCH ?watch=true&resourceVersion=<current_RV>`** | No (live stream) | `0.09 KB / pod` | `0.7 objs / pod` | `0.04x / 0.01x` |
| **`WATCH ?watch=true&sendInitialEvents=true` (`WatchList`)** | Yes (capped at `1 MB`) | **`11.96 KB / pod`** | **`123 objs / pod`** | **`5.5x / 2.5x`** |
| **`WATCH ?watch=true&resourceVersion=<old_RV>`** | **No (unaware of event count)** | **`11.69 KB / pod`** | **`122 objs / pod`** | **`5.4x / 2.5x` (`130x` live `WATCH`)** |
| **`LIST ?resourceVersion=<rv>&resourceVersionMatch=Exact`** | Yes | **`55.06 KB / pod`** | **`382 objs / pod`** | **`25.3x / 7.8x`** |
| **`LIST ?resourceVersion=0` (`Accept: as=Table`)** | Yes (assumes streamed `1 MB` cap) | **`60.40 KB / pod`** | **`124 objs / pod`** | **`27.7x / 2.5x`** |
| **`DELETECOLLECTION`** | **No (unaware of object count)** | **`61.18 KB / pod`** | **`170 objs / pod`** | **`28.1x / 3.5x`** |

#### 2. Single-Object Methods (`10KB` Exemplar Pod)

| Request (`10KB` Exemplar Pod) | Alloc Bytes / Pod | Alloc Objects / Pod | Ratio vs. `PUT` (Bytes / Objs) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`GET ?resourceVersion=0`** | `4 KB` | `50 objs` | `0.03x / 0.04x` |
| **`GET ?resourceVersion=""`** | `40 KB` | `420 objs` | `0.29x / 0.31x` |
| **`DELETE`** | `50 KB` | `540 objs` | `0.36x / 0.40x` |
| **`POST`** | `90 KB` | `970 objs` | `0.64x / 0.71x` |
| **`PUT`** | **`140 KB`** | **`1,360 objs`** | **`1.0x / 1.0x` (Baseline)** |
| **`PATCH` (`merge-patch+json`, `48B` body)** | **`200 KB`** | **`1,570 objs`** | **`1.4x / 1.2x`** |
| **`PATCH` (`strategic-merge-patch+json`, `48B` body)** | **`320 KB`** | **`2,490 objs`** | **`2.3x / 1.8x`** |
| **`PATCH` (`strategic-merge-patch+json`, `3` retries)** | **`830 KB`** | **`8,750 objs`** | **`5.9x / 6.4x`** |



/cc @Jefftree @wojtek-t @p0lyn0mial

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

 A way for a gang PodGroup or CompositePodGroup to account for Pods that its owning controller intentionally creates later, after other Pods in the group are already running/complete.

Today the scheduler holds a gang's Pods until minCount of them exist on the control plane. That doesn't work for workloads with ordering dependencies inside one gang. The main example is MPI training through Kubeflow Trainer and JobSet: https://github.com/kubeflow/trainer/pull/3219#discussion_r4171153558

- The TrainJob runtime has two ReplicatedJobs: launcher and node
- With `runLauncherAsNode: true`, the launcher is rank 0. The node ReplicatedJob runs numNodes - 1 workers
- `mpirun` needs every worker's SSH server up before it starts, so JobSet only creates the launcher Pod once all workers are Ready (we [use dependsOn API for that](https://github.com/kubeflow/trainer/blob/master/manifests/base/runtimes/deepspeed_distributed.yaml#L61))
 - For one gang across launcher and workers (same topology domain, all-or-nothing), the natural setting is minCount = numNodes
 
That deadlocks. The workers wait for minCount Pods to exist before they're scheduled. The launcher Pod isn't created until the workers are Ready.

Some possible directions (open to SIG Scheduling's input):

1. Declared-but-deferred members: let a PodGroupTemplate/PodGroup declare how many extra Pods it expects later and what resources they need (for example, a reference to a Pod template or a resource shape). The scheduler would then reserve capacity for them in the chosen placement/topology domain once minCount existing Pods are schedulable.
2. Separate "gang admission count" from "reservation count": for example, keep minCount as the threshold for releasing Pods, and add a separate field for the total number of Pods (or resources) to reserve.
3. Ordered sub-groups within one Workload: let a later sub-group (the launcher) join an earlier sub-group's placement once the earlier one has been scheduled, with its capacity held in the meantime. This could build on CompositePodGroup.

I would expect we will see similar problems with [initializers or data cache](https://trainer.kubeflow.org/en/latest/user-guides/data-cache.html#architecture), when training job waits until initializer Job is complete (cc @akshaychitneni).


### Why is this needed?

  - WAS doesn't support ordered bootstrap. MPI (launcher/worker) can't be gang-scheduled with a minCount that covers the whole job. The scheduler waits for minCount Pods to exist, but the driver Pod is only created after the workers are Ready, so the job deadlocks.
- The current workaround is lossy. In https://github.com/kubeflow/trainer/pull/3219, Kubeflow Trainer plans to leave dependent ReplicatedJobs out of minCount. The launcher still joins the same PodGroup and can land in the same topology domain, but its capacity isn't reserved. On a busy cluster, the workers can be gang-scheduled and hold GPUs while the launcher stays Pending.


cc @kannon92 @tenzen-y @mm4tt @robert-bell
issues.title: WAS: Gang-schedule Pods that are created in order, like in MPI bootstrap

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Stop calling an HTTP extender for a while after its calls keep failing, so that a hung extender does not cost every pod a full `httpTimeout`.

Today every scheduling cycle calls every interested extender synchronously and waits until the call returns or times out (`http.Client.Timeout = httpTimeout`, `pkg/scheduler/extender.go`):

- Filter: `findNodesThatPassExtenders` calls `Filter`; with `ignorable: true` an error is logged and the extender is skipped for this pod only (`pkg/scheduler/schedule_one.go`).
- Prioritize: `prioritizeNodes` waits for all extender goroutines; an error is logged at V(5) and the extender's scores are dropped for this pod only.

The next pod calls the same extender again and waits again. Nothing remembers that the previous call timed out a moment ago.

A possible shape (open to other designs):

1. Per extender, count consecutive failed calls (transport errors and timeouts). After N consecutive failures (for example 3), skip the extender for a backoff period that grows from 1s up to 30-60s. While skipped, behave exactly as on an error today: an ignorable filter is skipped, a prioritizer gives no scores. When the backoff ends, the next pod probes the extender; a successful call resets the counter.
2. Apply it only where an error is already tolerated: ignorable extenders and the prioritize verb, whose errors are always tolerated. Non-ignorable filter and bind keep failing loudly, as intended in #60616.
3. Make it visible: a metric with extender call duration and result per extender and verb, and a log line (or metric) when an extender enters and leaves backoff. Today a failing prioritizer is visible only at `-v=5`.

While the extender is down the scheduling result is the same as today; only the time spent waiting changes. The difference is during recovery: an extender that comes back is used again after at most one backoff period. If that needs to be configurable, it could be an optional field on `Extender` (for example `failureBackoff`).

### Why is this needed?

A hung extender, one that accepts the connection and never answers (GC pause, deadlock, CPU starvation, a network path dropping packets), is a realistic failure. While it lasts, scheduler throughput for the whole cluster drops to about one pod per `httpTimeout`. `ignorable: true` does not help here: it only decides what happens after the timeout.

Measured on kube-scheduler v1.35.9 (1 control-plane node with 4 vCPU, 3 worker nodes), one prioritize-only HTTPS extender (`nodeCacheCapable: true`, `ignorable: true`, `httpTimeout: 2s`, `weight: 2`), bursts of 100 pause pods (1m CPU / 4Mi), median of 3 runs:

| Extender state | Pods bound per second |
| --- | --- |
| No extender configured | about 20 (1) |
| Healthy | 12.0 (11.4..13.9) |
| Service without endpoints (connection refused) | 11.2 (10.7..18.3) |
| Process stopped with SIGSTOP (TCP accepted, no response) | 0.5: 100 pods in 201.7 s, median interval between bindings 2.01 s, p50 create-to-bound 99.6 s |

(1) Bursts of 100 pods without an extender were bimodal on this control-plane node (16-18 or 32-36 pods/s, depending on its load). The medians of 250-pod bursts without an extender stayed within 20.4-21.6 pods/s over four days, so about 20 is the steady figure. The hung-extender row does not depend on it: it is bounded by `httpTimeout`, 1 pod per 2 s.

A refused connection fails fast and costs little. A hung extender costs the full timeout on every pod. Lowering `httpTimeout` reduces the damage, but it trades against the extender's legitimate tail latency, and the damage still grows with the number of pods to schedule.

Steps to reproduce:

1. Configure a prioritize-only extender with `ignorable: true` and `httpTimeout: 2s`.
2. Send `SIGSTOP` to the extender process.
3. Create 100 pods and measure the time until they are bound.

We are happy to send a PR once the shape is agreed.

/sig scheduling
/kind feature
issues.title: kube-scheduler: a hung HTTP extender limits scheduling to one pod per httpTimeout, even with ignorable: true

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

When `kube-scheduler` preempts a `Pod`, it patches the `Pod` status with the `DisruptionTarget` condition (`status: True`, `reason: PreemptionByScheduler`) and then deletes the `Pod`.
However, when `kube-scheduler` preempts a gang `PodGroup` or `CompositePodGroup` configured with `DisruptionMode: All`, it currently only sets `DisruptionTarget` on and deletes the individual member `Pod`s:

- **No group-level status signaling**: Even though the `DisruptionTarget` condition type and `PreemptionByScheduler` reason are already defined in `PodGroupStatus` and `CompositePodGroupStatus`, the scheduler does not set this condition on the preempted `PodGroup` or `CompositePodGroup`.
- **No group-level deletion**: The scheduler leaves the existing `PodGroup` / `CompositePodGroup` object alive in the API server, expecting it to be reused in-place for subsequent scheduling attempts.

Keeping the same `PodGroup` / `CompositePodGroup` instance alive across a full-group preemption causes three major problems:

- **Inconsistent group state during pod recreation and rescheduling**: While the scheduler is asynchronously deleting victim `Pod`s belonging to a preempted `PodGroup` / `CompositePodGroup`, the owning workload controller (observing individual `Pod` deletions) may immediately start recreating replacement `Pod`s attached to the same `PodGroup`. As a result, the `PodGroup` / `CompositePodGroup` enters an inconsistent state where terminating/to-be-preempted `Pod`s from the old scheduling cycle coexist with newly created `Pod`s, making rescheduling of the group problematic.
- **Topology placement pinning races in Topology-Aware Scheduling (TAS)**: During preemption, a `PodGroup` or `CompositePodGroup` using TAS often needs to be moved to a different topology domain when rescheduled. However, TAS (`TopologyPlacement.GeneratePlacements`) constrains a group's candidate placements to the topology domain of any already-scheduled `Pod`s in the group. Due to races between the scheduler deleting preempted `Pod`s and the workload controller recreating `Pod`s in the same `PodGroup` / `CompositePodGroup`, surviving scheduled `Pod`s can pin the group to its previous topology placement or cause placement conflicts, making it difficult to move the workload to a new placement.
- **Problematic lifecycle management for group-scoped resources (e.g., DRA)**: The scheduler or workload controllers may associate external or cluster resources directly with a `PodGroup` / `CompositePodGroup` instance - for example, PodGroup-level Dynamic Resource Allocation (`ResourceClaim`s generated from `ResourceClaimTemplate`s and tracked in `podgroup.status.resourceClaimStatuses`, whose lifecycle is bound to the `PodGroup`). Reusing the same `PodGroup` / `CompositePodGroup` object after preemption makes releasing, deallocating, and reallocating those group-bound resources for a new scheduling attempt problematic.

### Proposed solution

We propose updating `kube-scheduler`'s preemption execution so that preempted gang `PodGroup`s and `CompositePodGroup`s  with `disruptionMode` set to `All`  are marked with `DisruptionTarget` and deleted by the scheduler, matching the preemption lifecycle of individual `Pod`s:
1. **Scope to gang `PodGroup`s / `CompositePodGroup`s with `DisruptionMode: All`**: Apply group-level deletion only when preempting a gang `PodGroup` or `CompositePodGroup` whose disruption mode is `All`.
2. **Set `DisruptionTarget` condition on `PodGroup` / `CompositePodGroup`**: Before deleting the `PodGroup` / `CompositePodGroup`, patch its status to set the `DisruptionTarget` condition with `status: True` and `reason: PreemptionByScheduler` (consistent with `Pod` preemption).
3. **Initiate `PodGroup` / `CompositePodGroup` deletion before preempting member `Pod`s**: Issue a `Delete` request for the preempted `PodGroup` / `CompositePodGroup` (setting its `deletionTimestamp`) before setting `DisruptionTarget` and deleting the individual member `Pod`s belonging to the group.
4. **Delay final removal until all member `Pod`s are terminated via finalizers**: Because `PodGroup` / `CompositePodGroup` objects already have a protection finalizer (e.g., `scheduling.k8s.io/podgroup-protection`), the object will remain in a terminating state (`deletionTimestamp` set) until all of its member `Pod`s are deleted/terminated, after which the protection controller removes the finalizer and garbage collection completes.
5. **Preempt member `Pod`s**: Proceed with setting `DisruptionTarget` and deleting the member `Pod`s of the `PodGroup` / `CompositePodGroup`.

### Why is this needed?

Aligning the preemption behavior of gang `PodGroup`s and `CompositePodGroup`s (`DisruptionMode: All`) with standard `Pod` preemption provides a clean, atomic lifecycle per scheduling attempt:

- **Consistent preemption semantics and controller visibility**: Workload controllers receive an explicit signal on the `PodGroup` / `CompositePodGroup` itself (`deletionTimestamp` with `DisruptionTarget=True` and `reason=PreemptionByScheduler`) before individual `Pod`s start disappearing, allowing controllers to react to the group preemption as a single event rather than reacting piecemeal to individual `Pod` deletions.
- **Clean rescheduling without mixed `Pod` states**: Because the preempted `PodGroup` / `CompositePodGroup` is marked for deletion before its `Pod`s are evicted - and held by the protection finalizer until all old `Pod`s are gone - the scheduler and workload controller do not mix terminating victim `Pod`s with newly recreated `Pod`s in the same `PodGroup`.
- **Reliable relocation in Topology-Aware Scheduling (TAS)**: Recreating a fresh `PodGroup` / `CompositePodGroup` after preemption guarantees that no stale scheduled `Pod`s remain associated with the new group, allowing TAS to freely evaluate all candidate topology placements.
- **Clean lifecycle for DRA and group-bound resources**: Tying resource allocation (such as PodGroup-scoped DRA `ResourceClaim`s) to the lifecycle of a single `PodGroup` / `CompositePodGroup` instance ensures that deleting the preempted group automatically triggers cleanup of old claims/resources before a new group is created.

**Impact on workload controller integrations (urgency):**
This change affects how workload controllers (such as `Job`, `JobSet`, `LeaderWorkerSet`, etc.) integrate with Workload-Aware Scheduling (WAS), as controllers will need to watch for `PodGroup` / `CompositePodGroup` preemption/deletion and recreate the `PodGroup` / `CompositePodGroup` when rescheduling the workload. Because of this integration contract change, we should implement this as soon as possible before more workload controllers integrate with WAS.
issues.title: Delete preempted gang PodGroups and CompositePodGroups (DisruptionMode: All) during scheduler preemption

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

We propose decoupling Kubernetes internal API object manipulation from eager Go struct layout so kube-apiserver can read and modify small subsets of fields without decoding or deep-copying entire objects.

We want to introduce this incrementally in the following steps:
1. **Add codegen support to generate `<Type>Accessor` interfaces for K8s objects**
     Extend k8s.io/code-generator (e.g., via +k8s:accessors=true) to generate getter, setter, and nested cursor interfaces (such as 
core.PodAccessor
, PodSpecAccessor, ContainerAccessor) along with 1-line inlineable implementations on standard Go API structs.
2. **Generate accessors for Pod and migrate the k/k codebase to use PodAccessor**
  Generate PodAccessor on core.Pod and incrementally migrate kube-apiserver internal hot paths (registry strategies, WatchCache indexers/ToSelectableFields, table printers, defaulting) from direct field access (pod.Spec.NodeName) to PodAccessor (pod.GetSpecNodeName()).
3. **Implement `LazyPod` an alternative schema allowing for on-demand decoding and field access/mutation**
  LazyPod implement the `PodAccessor` interface while allowing read and mutation of selected fields without full decode and falling back to decode for operations requiring full-object inspection (JSON serialization) while maintaining 1:1 byte compatibility with normal pod.
4. **Iteratively expand the set of fields and operations supporting lazy evaluation**


### Why is this needed?

In [#134375](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/134375) and [#138415](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/138415), we started introducing **Resource Size** as a new scalability dimension, moving from the historical 4 KB single-container Pod to a realistic **10 KB Exemplar Pod** (2 init containers, 2 app containers, 10 volumes, 10 envs/container, ~49% `managedFields`), with a target of supporting **100 KB Pods**.

Already at **10 KB**, `kube-apiserver` hits a severe **memory allocation bottleneck** ([#142223](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/142223)):
- **Small intent vs. whole-object memory cost**: Most apiserver operations express a tiny intent—setting `spec.nodeName` (~20 B), updating a container status, setting `deletionTimestamp`, or updating `metadata.resourceVersion`. Yet `kube-apiserver` operates on the whole object, eagerly allocating, deep-copying, and re-serializing every struct, slice, and map in `Pod`.
- **WatchCache vs. remaining memory allocation hotspots**: WatchCache removes per-request decode cost on steady-state reads by decoding each object once on watch ingest. However, `O(PodSize)` allocated bytes still dominates during ingest and every write. Each Pod scheduling cycle triggers 4–8 writes ([#138415](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/138415)); every write decodes the 10 KB wire payload into **74.4 KB** of heap memory while really changing only miniscule part of object.

#### Benchmark: Allocated Bytes per Operation (10 KB Exemplar Pod)

| Operation (10 KB Exemplar Pod) | Intent (Fields Read / Modified) | Standard (`core.Pod`) | Lazy (`LazyPod`) | Allocated Bytes Reduction |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. With Etcd Decode (WatchCache Ingest & Etcd Fallbacks)** | | | | |
| **WatchCache Ingest + Default + Index** | Read 6 fields, modify 1 (`resourceVersion`) | **74.4 KB** | **16.1 KB** | **-78% B/op** |
| **Graceful Delete (with Etcd Fallback Decode)** | Read 3 fields, modify 3 metadata fields + encode | **89.6 KB** | **28.6 KB** | **-68% B/op** |
| **Uncached `LIST` 100 Pods (Protobuf)** | Read 0, modify 1/pod (`resourceVersion`) + encode | **8.81 MB** | **2.78 MB** | **-68% B/op** |
| **Uncached `LIST` 100 Pods (`Table` Wide)** | Extract 9 summary fields/pod | **7.51 MB** | **1.52 MB** | **-80% B/op** |
| **2. From WatchCache (Already Decoded Once, 0 Etcd Decode)** | | | | |
| **`DeepCopy` from WatchCache** (per cached read/patch) | Clone object before mutation | **26.2 KB** | **0.6 KB** | **-98% B/op** |
| **Graceful Delete from WatchCache** (`DeepCopy` + mutate + encode) | Read 3 fields, modify 3 metadata fields + encode | **42.7 KB** | **14.3 KB** | **-66% B/op** |

/cc @liggitt @wojtek-t @Jefftree
issues.title: Generated object accessors and on-demand Protobuf decoding for Pod (LazyPod)

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Apply higher or equal level nominations to the cluster state before the scheduling starts (before `PreFilter`) instead of applying the node-local ones only during per-node `Filter` simulation.

The proposal requires further investigation and providing more details on the proposed implementation mechanics, but filing it FTR

### Why is this needed?

The `kube-scheduler`’s scheduling (and preemption simulation) currently assume single-node scoping when reserving resources for higher or equal priority workload nominations. During scheduling, it applies nominations only during per-node `Filter` simulation, so it's not able to detect nominations that may block the scheduling if only they were applied on a different node.

This causes the scheduling or preemption simulation scheduling to ignore such reservations and schedule or nominate lower priority workloads in placements reserved (conflicting) for a higher priority workload that is waiting for preemption to complete.

The issue manifests only in cases where nominated pods have cross-node dependencies like anti-affinity, topology spread (or multi-node DRA resource nominations that may be added in the future). It's important to note that this problem exists already and current nomination mechanism is not able to protect cross-node dependencies. So far the preemption mechanism also wasn't able to identify victims that are not node-local, but WAP added such possibility as it is cluster-scoped preemption.

/sig scheduling
/wg workload-aware-scheduling

/cc @kubernetes/sig-scheduling-leads @wojtek-t @mm4tt @tosi3k
issues.title: Protect NominatedNode reservations in cluster-scoped preemption

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

When kube-scheduler preempts, it picks victims in one scheduling cycle. The scheduler cache, however, keeps counting the victims' resources until their Pod objects are gone, which is long after that cycle. In the meantime, later preemption decisions can plan against capacity that is already being released.

This proposal: when preemption is actuated, mark the selected victims as releasing in the scheduler cache. Preemption and nomination logic then treat that capacity as already freed, and the preemptor's nomination holds it. Binding still waits for the victims to actually terminate.

- When preemption is actuated, mark victims as releasing in the scheduler cache. Do this synchronously in the scheduling cycle, before any API call is sent.
- Planning view (preemption dry runs, validation of existing nominations): releasing victims are treated as gone, and the preemptor's nomination holds the freed capacity. The existing priority rules for nominated pods decide who can see or take that capacity.
- Binding view (Filter before bind): releasing victims are still present. Kubelet admission rejects a pod that doesn't fit while terminating containers may still be running, so released capacity can be used for planning but not for binding until the victims are gone.
- Rollback: if a delete call fails, or the victim's deletionTimestamp isn't observed within a timeout, restore the victims in the cache. Then activate every pod nominated on the affected nodes, plus the rest of their pod groups, so they re-plan. Narrowing this to the original preemptor isn't safe. Later preemptors may have planned around the same released capacity, and with mixed priorities the capacity left after rollback goes to the higher-priority nominations first, so a lower-priority pod may no longer fit.
- Releasing victims are not attributed to the preemptor. Its nomination already holds the capacity, and the rollback above doesn't depend on who triggered the eviction.

With this, a preemptor retried during the actuation window sees its nominated placement as still feasible in the planning view and becomes a no-op. The PreEnqueue gate is then no longer needed.


### Why is this needed?

The scheduler's view lags behind its own decisions in two windows:

1. Actuation window: from victim selection until the victims' deletionTimestamp reaches the cache through the informer. With async preemption this covers goroutine scheduling, API latency, client throttling, and the number of victims.
2. Termination window: from deletionTimestamp until the Pod object is removed. This is the graceful termination period: 30s by default, and possibly much longer.

Throughout both windows, the cache counts victims as fully occupying their nodes. This leads to:
- Over-eviction under bursty preemption. Examples:
  - Preemptor P1 evicts victims that free more than it needs. Preemptor P2 has lower priority than those victims, so its dry run cannot count the leftover capacity. P2 evicts pods elsewhere, even though it would fit on the same node once the victims are gone.
  - Candidate selection treats victims that are already terminating as a new disruption. It may pick a node that needs fresh evictions over a node where capacity is already being released.
  - When a higher-priority preemptor targets a node, the nominated node name (NNN) of every lower-priority pod nominated there is cleared, even if there is room for both. Those pods then preempt again somewhere else.
- Async preemption depends on PreEnqueue gating. The preemptor is held at PreEnqueue until its delete calls have been issued. PreEnqueue is meant to gate on pod or cluster state. Here it gates on the progress of an internal goroutine, and that goroutine emits no cluster event when it finishes. This needs workarounds: tracking the last victim, Activate on error, and similar fixes. It also leaves a race: a pod gated during the actuation window ignores events not registered by the gating plugin until a pod deletion or the periodic flush.
- Stale plans while victims terminate. A preemptor waiting for its victims short-circuits re-evaluation ("victims still terminating") and keeps its nomination. This holds even if the plan has become infeasible, for example after a new taint, a pod bound directly to the node, or an in-place node downsize. The preemptor re-plans only after the victims are gone.

### Benefits
- Less over-eviction: capacity released by earlier preemptions can be shared by later preemptors instead of each one evicting its own victims.
- Lower-priority pods can use released capacity: when a higher-priority preemptor frees more than it needs, a lower-priority pending pod can nominate itself into the leftover space without evicting anything. This works even when the pod's priority is below the victims', so it could never preempt them itself. Today such a pod stays unschedulable until the victims are gone.
- Cluster Autoscaler counts a nominated pod as fitting into the capacity it's nominated to. Without a nomination, it still sees the terminating victims occupying the node and looks for extra capacity, which can mean an unnecessary scale-up. The pod may also preempt pods on another node.
- Simpler async preemption: drop the PreEnqueue gate and its related workarounds. Re-attempting preemption becomes idempotent.
- Stable nominations: a higher-priority preemptor doesn't have to clear lower-priority nominations on a node that still fits them. A re-attempted preemption keeps the same placement as long as it stays feasible, instead of picking a different set of victims.
- Re-planning on wake-up: when a waiting preemptor is woken, it re-validates its placement against the planning view instead of waiting out the grace period of victims it may no longer need.
- Within a single workload, workload-aware preemption (KEP-5710) already shares victims among all pods of the pod group in one cycle. The benefits above therefore apply mainly across preemptors and cycles: pods that don't belong to a pod group, separate pod groups preempting one after another, and the race windows between cycles.

### Relation to workload-aware preemption GA
This proposal is not a blocker for KEP-5710 GA:
- It's an optimization, not a correctness fix. Without it, preemption is sometimes not optimal. In burst scenarios it may evict more than needed, or wait out grace periods it didn't need to. It doesn't cause lost pods, deadlocks, or wrong placements.
- It doesn't add API or change user-visible semantics. It changes scheduler-internal accounting only, so it can come later behind its own feature gate. Shipping WAP GA without it doesn't lock in anything that would have to be undone.
- The WAP-specific issues seen so far can be fixed without it:
  - make the "waiting for victims" check consider only victims actuated for this pod group, and re-check the nominated placement before keeping it;
  - re-evaluate the PreEnqueue gate when async preemption finishes, so a gated group doesn't ignore unrelated events until a pod is deleted or the periodic flush runs.

What would change this: a scheduler_perf result showing significant cross-workload over-eviction under bursty pod group arrivals, or a GA criterion in KEP-5710 that depends on sharing victims across cycles.

### Drawbacks and open questions
- Two views of a node. Planning and binding see different pod sets on the same node. Where does this live (NodeInfo, snapshot, or preemption-only), and which plugins must handle it?
- Failure handling. Rolling back by node is complete, because only the planning view uses released capacity, and the planning view uses it only through nominations. A rollback can still cascade: a lower-priority pod that loses its place may preempt again elsewhere. That only happens on the failure path, but it should be limited, for example by not starting new preemptions until the affected nominations have re-planned.
- Victims that never terminate (finalizers, a NotReady node, a stuck kubelet). Victims with a deletionTimestamp already block today. Should the cache keep treating them as releasing, or give up after some time?
- Reacting to events that make things worse. Waking a waiting preemptor when its plan breaks (new taint, direct binding, node downsize) needs reverse queueing hints, as proposed for in-place node downsize in KEP-3953. This is optional and separate from this proposal.

### Related work
- [Implement pod group preemption (#142932)](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142932): applies the same idea within a single workload's preemption cycle. This proposal extends it across cycles and preemptors.
- [scheduler: activate preemptor when last victim is already deleted (#142623)](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142623): would no longer be needed once PreEnqueue gating is removed.
- [KEP-3953: In-place Node Resource Resize](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/3953-in-place-node-resource-resize): wakes up unschedulable pods waiting for victims when a node is downsized in place, which is the reverse-hint mechanism mentioned above.
- [KEP-5229: Asynchronous API calls during scheduling](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-scheduling/5229-asynchronous-api-calls-during-scheduling/README.md): an earlier attempt at this was blocked by the need to keep re-sending victim deletions until the scheduler saw them confirmed (or a grace period set). The async API dispatcher could handle that tracking.

/sig scheduling
/wg workload-aware-scheduling

/cc @kubernetes/sig-scheduling-leads @wojtek-t @sanposhiho @wasylkowski-a @mm4tt
